en: The Scripture on the Chapter of Transcending the World, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha, staying at the Universal Radiance Lecture Hall in the Dharma-Quiescent Bodhimanda.
In the hall, upon the Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne—having realized the ultimate truth, there is no dualistic practice;
having transcended the realm of non-conceptual phenomena, one dwells as a Buddha does to achieve equanimity;
all Buddhas advance, retreat, and traverse it without obstruction or concealment.
The Dharma is without regression and their practice is peerless; that which they perceive and revere is inconceivable.
They manifest equality with the three periods of time, and the manifestations of their bodies pervade all worlds.
They discern all phenomena, and their wisdom is free from hesitation.
Fully endowed with all dharmas, they sit beneath the Bodhi tree to thoroughly expound the sutras;
they harbor no doubt regarding Perfect Enlightenment and do not conceive of or calculate a self. The aspirations, the wisdom of the Path, and the Buddha-conduct of all bodhisattvas are non-dual.
Their salvation is supreme as they cross to the other shore, never destroying the Tathāgata’s established gates of liberation.
The lands of the Buddhas are immeasurable; their sphere of activity is equal, and the realm of the Dharma they cultivate is as vast as empty space.

The number of Bodhisattvas in the countless billions of *nayutas* of dust-motes throughout the lands of the ten directions is likewise so great. These Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have all been born in the stage of "one more birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*) and shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path. Each has come from various Buddha-lands of the ten directions to assemble in this land—they have all become *kai-shi* (Bodhisattvas), have all opened the eye of wisdom, and possess boundless gates of virtue.

They transform and enlighten all realms of sentient beings, preaching the Way in accordance with the precepts through the gate of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), understanding how to act according to the times, and abiding in the Bodhisattva Dharma.
Ascending through the wisdom-concentration that transcends all world-halls, pavilions, and towers, one observes the ground of parinirvāṇa;
one honors the wisdom of the Way, eliminates all verbal expressions and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), and relinquishes the conditions for the clear consciousness of discernment;
one gathers in sentient beings and enters the immeasurable, roaming therein upon the Way.
The misfortunes and blessings created by all sentient beings all have their retributions, which never decay;
when distinguished according to the proper time, even through diligent observation, nothing can be found [that is not accounted for].

Understanding the various realms, aspirations, and natures of sentient beings, and penetrating their faculties, one examines those who may be saved and administers medicine according to the illness, following the convenience of their conditions.

Regarding the chapters and verses proclaimed by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as their underlying principles, he immediately receives and upholds them; having received their definitive resolution, he maintains an attitude of equanimity and brings forth the understanding of the True Treasury.
As for that to which one should take refuge, he enters into the immeasurable worlds of this life and beyond;
having entered the Dharma itself, he has fully and correctly understood it, perceiving the conditioned and the unconditioned as non-dual.

They are able to manifest all the sites of enlightenment entered by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present—all Tathāgatas—who, at one and the same time, govern the path, establish peace and liberation, and achieve equal enlightenment.
Whether the mind is at ease or anxious, one has already realized the Buddha-way.

Without departing from the resolve for enlightenment directed toward all sentient beings, upon entering the mind of a single person, one is able to universally enter into all that is known and all that is desired by all sentient beings.
They themselves remain unshakable within that wisdom.
Having attained universal knowledge and the mind of all-encompassing insight, the bodhisattvas abide in those stages without regressing.
The power of the bodhisattva’s practice is without rest or weariness; though he circulates and comes and goes, his wisdom has no object of action because all people [are as such].
Abiding in birth and death throughout incalculable kalpas, he understands and establishes [the path], yet he is difficult to encounter or behold even in uncountable kalpas.

These jewels of the bodhisattvas are truly difficult to encounter; they constantly turn the wheel of Dharma without ever wearying or ceasing, transforming and enlightening sentient beings so that they enter the ranks of discipline. The Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present purify this place and bring sentient beings to fulfillment therein.
Fully endowed with fundamental practices, their vows are already perfected, and their meritorious deeds are extraordinary.
Such Bodhisattvas and other scholars are praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions; for incalculable eons they have been extolled without limit, being peerless and transcending all others.
Their names were:

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantahetu (also known as Samantanetra) Bodhisattva, Samantaprasāda Bodhisattva, Samantajñāna Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Samantaprabha Bodhisattva, Samantadarśin Bodhisattva, Samantāvabhāsa Bodhisattva, Samantapuṣpa Bodhisattva, and Samantabodhi Bodhisattva. Such as these were as numerous as the atoms in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, numbering in the hundreds of billions of nayutas, beyond all calculation.
In this way, Samantabhadra accomplishes his vows—his pledged aspirations being most transcendent:
whenever Buddhas arise, he goes everywhere to seek and entreat them;
understanding the appropriate times, he maintains all the Dharma-eye teachings manifested by the Buddhas, never interrupting the instruction of all Tathāgatas.
When the Buddhas appear in the world, they swiftly receive the prediction of their attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment; their names and lands are already purified and perfected.

Abiding in the wheel of Dharma, they manifest as Buddhas even in Buddha-less lands, thoroughly adorning and purifying all worlds that are malevolent, defiled, and difficult to transform. They bring to rest and eliminate the obstacles, calamities, and fortunes of the assembly of bodhisattvas, entering the true dharma-realm free from the five aggregates and hindrances.
Thereupon, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva entered the meditative absorption of the Buddha-treasury (*buddhagarbha-samādhi*).

Having attained this samādhi, he immediately and universally entered the abodes where the Buddhas of the ten directions dwell; there was nowhere it did not pervade and penetrate, reaching every land without exception. It extended to the lecture halls, the realms of the Dharma, and the entire expanse of space, reaching to their very limits.
The lands of the ten directions shook in six ways, and a great radiance shone everywhere without exception; a profound sound resounded so that its voice was heard by all.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva arose from samādhi and, seeing that all the bodhisattvas had come together in assembly, was filled with great joy.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra-mati, beholding all the bodhisattvas gathered like clouds, was likewise filled with joy; he stepped forward and asked the Great Being Samantabhadra:
"Excellent, Son of the Buddha!"
Now these bodhisattvas have gathered from the ten directions, thirsting for and yearning for the scriptures, looking up to you, O Benevolent One, as those in darkness long for light.

Pray explain the practices of the bodhisattvas so that from beginning to end there may be no doubt—so that those who are bound may become suddenly liberated, like one cured of illness or a blind man regaining his sight.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva having that upon which they rely yet being without attachment?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s thought of the unprecedented?
And what is meant by their practice?"
What is meant by a virtuous friend?
What is meant by diligence?
What is meant by encouraging faith?
What is meant by transforming sentient beings?
What is meant by the prohibitive precepts?
What is meant by receiving the prediction of enlightenment?
What is meant by a bodhisattva not seeking out the faults of others?
What is meant by entering into the Tathāgata?
What is meant by attaining entry into the nature and conduct of sentient beings?
What is meant by "entering into all worlds"?
What is meant by "clearly entering into the reckoning of all thoughts and eons, reaching everywhere"?
What is meant by "eloquently expounding upon the matters of the three periods of time"?
What is meant by "attaining entry into the three spheres"?
What is meant by "never becoming weary of the resolve one has generated, being without deficiency or omission"?
And what is meant by "the bodhisattva’s discernment of various eloquences"?
"What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining *dhāraṇī*?
What is meant by a bodhisattva proclaiming the Buddha-way?
In response to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s question regarding universal wisdom, [the Buddha], wishing to enable all who come to attain understanding and liberation, spoke these words of praise:
“Excellent! All you bodhisattvas gathered here, listen together with one mind.
There are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva has something to rely upon, yet remains free from attachment.”

What are these ten? They are: relying on the bodhisattva-mind so as not to lose it; relying on virtuous friends to always cultivate diligence; relying on the roots of virtue to plant blessings and merit; being able to practice and uphold the *pāramitās* in accordance with them; relying on all dharmas because there is nothing to which they return; relying on one’s vows to remain close to the Path; focusing on all practices to bring their cultivation to fulfillment; associating with bodhisattvas who are in their last birth before Buddhahood; revering all Buddhas with a joyful heart; and honoring all Tathāgatas as if they were one’s own father. These are the ten dharmas of a bodhisattva, by relying upon which one becomes free from attachment.
When a bodhisattva abides in this, they swiftly attain the unsurpassed great wisdom of the Tathāgata and reach the ultimate refuge.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“The refuge is that which has no basis; One takes self-refuge in all Buddhas.”
Understanding the Dharma without expectation, even unto great vows;
seeing all Buddhas with joy, relying upon them to offer reverence;
taking refuge in all Tathāgatas, thereby fulfilling the practices of the Path.
"Bodhisattvas have ten matters regarding which they never harbor thoughts of the extraordinary. What are these ten?
They regard all roots of virtue as no different from their own; they accumulate manifold goodness within themselves to bestow upon sentient beings."
To regard all meritorious training as the thought of the Way;
to understand and penetrate sentient beings as the thought of vessels for the Way;
and to vow to deliver all beings as the thought of one's own vow.
They regard all dharmas as being no different from the thought of giving;
they contemplate all dharmas as being like the Buddha-dharma;
and they treat all practices as if they were serving their own bodies.
All verbal expressions are free from conceptual construction regarding all modes of conduct;
one views all Buddhas with the thought of them being one's parents;
and one regards all Tathāgatas with the thought of their non-duality.
It is so, son of good family!
Among the assembly of bodhisattvas, there has never been such a thought; when a bodhisattva dwells in this, they swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed and attain the root of all virtues.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"For the sake of all, one accumulates merit, Regarding them as one's own body;
One observes sentient beings As if they were vessels for the Dharma."
All sentient beings create vows; these are no different from their own bodies.
They take refuge in the Dharma of the Path, so as to bring about the state of non-arising.
There are ten matters that constitute the practice of a Bodhisattva.

What are these ten? They are: expounding and discerning the conduct of sentient beings; seeking the practice of all dharmas; universally studying the prohibitions and precepts and immediately putting them into practice; accumulating the roots of merit from various practices; single-mindedly and diligently cultivating samādhi; clearly understanding the destination toward which noble wisdom leads; being earnest and cautious so as not to err or fail; roaming through buddha-fields for the sake of adornment; cultivating spiritual friends without abandoning reverence; and practicing the conduct of the Tathāgata with the respect due to a lion—these are the ten matters.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"In all activities one undertakes, one should transform and guide sentient beings;
diligently seeking all dharmas, one should observe and practice the precepts."
Accumulating the roots of all virtues, With single-minded devotion returning to a concentrated mind,
Thoroughly understanding noble and brilliant wisdom, One wanders through pure buddha-fields.
There are ten things that constitute a bodhisattva’s good friend.

What are these ten? They are: establishing the aspiration for the Way; being able to cultivate the roots of virtue; entering the perfections (pāramitās); proclaiming the Dharma of the Way; transforming and enlightening sentient beings; discerning eloquence; extolling all living beings; eliminating various delusive thoughts; abiding in freedom from weariness or aversion; and establishing the conduct of Samantabhadra to enter the wisdom of all Buddhas—these constitute a virtuous friend. These are the ten matters.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“The mind established upon the Path, Diligently cultivating the roots of virtue,
Entering into the various *pāramitās*, And proclaiming all the scriptures.”
To transform and deliver sentient beings, to resolve the doubts of the multitude through eloquence,
to bring praise among the common people, and to eliminate all conceptual thoughts—
these are the ten matters in which a bodhisattva practices diligence.

What are these ten? They are: to expound upon the realms of all sentient beings; to be mindful of the ultimate destination of the sūtras; to adorn and purify all Buddha-worlds; furthermore, to practice and uphold the precepts of all bodhisattvas; to always endure all hardships and afflictions; to sever the agonizing pains of burning, boiling, and cooking in the hells, among hungry ghosts, and among animals; to subjugate all hosts of Māras and their retinues; to ensure that sentient beings do not harbor thoughts of anger or resentment; to serve the World-Honored Buddhas of the ten directions; and to constantly encounter the Buddhas to take refuge in them, seek instruction, and receive their teachings. These, noble son, are they.
"One should practice the ten matters of bodhisattva diligence.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"I take refuge in all Buddhas, Who adorn and purify all Buddha-lands."
Diligently practicing the bodhisattva path, Enduring all suffering and affliction,
Severing the hardships of the three miserable realms, Subduing the hosts of Māra’s officials,
Able to gladden all sentient beings, And constantly beholding all Tathāgatas.
“There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva encourages faith. What are these ten?
Constantly establishing the intention, and also encouraging others to give rise to the mind of enlightenment;”
Being foremost in benevolence and harmony, they are free from contention and dispute, and they transform others so that they too may abide in joy;
they eliminate ignorant teachings and transform others to cause them to discard heterodox scriptures, leading them to dwell in the Buddha-way;
they strive to seek the roots of virtue and likewise exhort others to set their will upon the source of goodness.
In the Perfection of Returning, one also encourages others to seek the pāramitās;
having personally generated the seed of Buddhahood, one also induces others to devote themselves to the Buddha-nature;
having personally entered the dharma of non-existence, one opens the way for and advances others so that they may establish themselves in the dharma of emptiness.
They praise the wisdom of all Buddhas without disparagement or slander, and they demonstrate and proclaim it to others without defaming the Perfectly Enlightened One;
they are fully endowed with universal wisdom and their vows are perfectly complete, and they likewise guide others to achieve all-encompassing penetrating wisdom;

having made the ultimate vow for the path, they shall attain the adorned and pure, Tathāgata, Truly Realized, and inexhaustible wisdom, and they shall also establish all people so that they enter the path of the Tathāgata.
"These are the ten matters.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Having established oneself in the Path, one also transforms others."
With a mind free from contention, he harmonizes those who are angry and resentful.
Abandoning all ignorance and darkness, he enlightens those on deluded and evil paths;
constantly seeking the roots of all virtues, he leads them to abide in the Way and its righteousness.
“Bodhisattvas have ten ways of transforming and guiding sentient beings. What are these ten?
A bodhisattva uses generosity to attract and advance sentient beings, encouraging them with a serene countenance and a pleasant expression.”
Proclaiming the Way of the Sūtras so that it may extend everywhere;
inducing others to advance and discern that their own bodies are no different [from those of others];
and bestowing immeasurable gifts to initiate the realm of persons.
Manifesting the seeds for sentient beings to plant through the practices of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
demonstrating that all worlds are like a blazing fire;
and instructing sentient beings in the unsurpassed Dharma of the Path.
They manifest various transformations through the bases of supernormal power;
they are thoroughly proficient in various skillful means and expedients;
and they deliver sentient beings in accordance with their local customs and habits.
"These are the ten matters.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva practices giving, having already used it to transform sentient beings."
Always with a serene and joyful countenance, he guides those who have not yet attained.
Beholding the world as like a blazing fire, he reveals the Great Way of the Buddha,
manifesting transformations through his supernormal powers and employing various skillful means.
“There are ten matters regarding the prohibitive precepts of a bodhisattva. What are these ten? They are: not abandoning the mind of enlightenment;

relinquishing the intentions of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; observing all sentient beings with compassionate conduct; transforming and edifying the multitudes so that they abide in the Buddha-dharma; reverently practicing what a bodhisattva should learn; understanding that all dharmas are ultimately unobtainable; encouraging the roots of merit one has cultivated toward the ultimate Way; never being attached to the bodies of the Buddhas; being able to endure all dharmas without dependence; and protecting the sense faculties as one’s prohibitive precepts.”
"These are the ten matters.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Always harmonize with the mind of the Way; Abandon the paths of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
Compassionately pitying sentient beings, they exhort them to establish the Buddha-dharma;
learning the practices of all bodhisattvas, they understand that phenomena have no inherent existence;
and regarding all virtues they practice, they encourage others toward the path of the Buddha.
“There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva receives the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa), and the prediction they receive can be known by themselves.

What are these ten? They are: to give rise to a mind of benevolence and harmony; to naturally cultivate the aspiration for the Way; never to grow weary of the bodhisattva practices; to abandon all false conceptualizations while being able to reverently practice the Dharma of all Buddhas; to maintain firm faith in everything proclaimed by the bodies of all Tathāgatas; to thoroughly investigate and fully accomplish the roots of virtue; to transform all beings so that they abide in the Buddha-way; to regard friends and relatives with equal respect and without dualistic thoughts; to view all virtuous friends as if seeing the Buddhas; and to protect the Buddha-way according to vows made in the past. These are the ten matters by which one receives the prediction.”
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"With an impartial mind, honor your virtuous friends; All benefit and righteousness arise from them.
Guarding the vows of antiquity, With purity and harmony, give rise to the aspiration for the Way."
Not wearying of the bodhisattva practice, discarding all deluded thoughts,
causing others to abide in the Buddha-dharma, and having profound faith in the Tathāgata’s teaching.
There are ten things by which a bodhisattva does not seek out the faults of others.

What are these ten? They are: entering into the original vows made in past lives; entering into practice at the appropriate time to guide and habituate oneself to skillful means; not losing the correct principle so as to achieve universal entry; fully accomplishing the various perfections (*pāramitās*); acting according to what is suitable and convenient; entering into that which accords with one's vows; transforming beings according to their inclinations; adorning the buddha-fields and exhorting others to enter the Way; manifesting supernatural transformations to follow one's teaching; and universally manifesting the places where one is born. These are the ten matters for not seeking out the shortcomings of others.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Entering into the vows of former lives, Worldly conduct according to what is appropriate,
Cultivating practice without losing the proper measure, In accordance with the various perfections (pāramitās)."
Having attained great accomplishment, through various forms of faith and joy,
they adorn the Buddha-fields by means of supernatural transformations.
There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva enters into the Tathāgatas, that which all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have realized.

What are these ten? They are: entering the path of immeasurable equality; turning the wheel of the infinite Dharma of the scriptures; proclaiming the essentials of the meaning of immeasurable wisdom; following and harmonizing with boundless sounds and voices; transforming and enlightening the classes of bottomless sentient beings; manifesting and displaying countless supernatural transformations; appearing in various forms at all times according to the occasion; entering incomparable samādhis; illuminating and awakening those who are incalculable; and demonstrating the powers and fearlessnesses to manifest the infinite and lead them into nirvāṇa. These are the ten matters in which the Tathāgata enters.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"All Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present have entered the path of immeasurable teachings and turned the wheel of Dharma without limit."
Following the path of boundless phenomena, they proclaim the field of bottomless wisdom;
they transform and enlighten countless people, their supernormal powers being beyond calculation.
There are ten matters by which Bodhisattvas enter into the nature and conduct of sentient beings.
What are these ten? They are:
entering into the practices according to what sentient beings understand;
and delivering them at the appropriate time for those who are to receive a body in the future.
All people pervade the multitude of sentient beings;
their present actions enter into all living beings;
this is the beginning and end of virtuous conduct.
One should provide timely relief to all who act contrary to the Dharma;
one should proclaim the Way;
and one should understand the inclinations of the mental natures of sentient beings, as well as the origins and destinies of all their faculties.
Discriminating among various [beings] according to their inclinations and preferences;
giving rise to various obstructions, afflictions, and desires, and repeatedly preaching the Dharma to deliver them—
these are the ten matters for entering the nature of sentient beings.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Thoroughly understanding the conduct of past ages, And likewise knowing what is to come,
He discerns the affairs of the present And all that sentient beings may do."
Entering into all virtuous practices, yet also roaming in the absence of virtue,
their minds are omnipresent, causing all faculties to reach fulfillment.
There are ten matters by which Bodhisattvas enter the world.

What are these ten? They are: always knowing contentment; dwelling in the world while practicing purity without being defiled; remaining among the laity with few desires in mind; spreading the fragrance of the infinite to perfume all who are deluded; entering various regions as if they were a single speck of dust; encompassing immeasurable and subtle meanings; pervading vast and infinite worlds; delivering beings from the afflictions of the four great elements that constitute the physical body; reverently taking refuge in the path of the Buddhas; and furthermore, wandering into worlds where no path exists. These are the ten matters for entering the worlds.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"In this world, one knows contentment; One's conduct is always pure;
Entering [the world], one seeks little; One's all-pervading karma is infinite."
"Just as in a world-system of dust, one understands subtle and wondrous conduct;
there is nothing, whether small or great, that is not mastered, as one enters into all that exists.
"Bodhisattvas have ten matters through which they clearly enter into all thoughts and kalpas, reaching mastery in everything."

What are these ten? They are: knowing past kalpas; understanding future counterparts; knowing present affairs; knowing finite worlds; recognizing infinite obstructions; entering into matters both finite and infinite; comprehending all matters of numbered and unnumbered kalpas; causing those within the numbered to enter the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); causing those who are non-conceptual to freely enter into conceptualization; and causing all conceptualizations to flow freely so as to enter into non-conceptuality. These are the ten matters through which one thoroughly understands all kalpas, reaching everywhere without exception.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Entering into the recollection of the past, The future is likewise so;
Moving through the present world, One recollects them all."
Wandering through immeasurable eons, whether they have number or are without number;
entering thoughtlessness from within thought, and regarding all perceptions as non-perception.
"The Bodhisattva has ten matters by which he eloquently explains the three periods of time without dualistic speech."

What are the ten matters? To proclaim the past by means of the present; to pre-announce the future by means of what has long since passed away in antiquity; to expound the present state by means of that which has long been extinguished; to pre-announce the past by means of what has not yet come; to suddenly proclaim the present by means of what has not yet arrived; furthermore, to disseminate the teachings regarding those born in the future; to transmit the present by means of the past; to understand the present as being the future; to proclaim with equanimity that which is seen by the eyes; and to realize that the three periods of time are all fully attained simultaneously. These are the ten matters through which the three periods of time are eloquently explained.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"He can recount past events, Expounding on how the ancients came to be;
He speaks of the past as being present, And also elucidates matters of the future."
Past, future, and present— Birth is prefigured in the not-yet-arrived;
Understanding birth through the past manifests it in the present, And one sees with the eye that which is now and yet to come.
“There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva enters into the three stations.

What are these ten? Entering into the reckoning of all existences; reaching the state of non-conceptualization; arriving at that which has attainment; proceeding toward all teachings; roaming through the realms of manifold perceptions; returning to the various worldly customs; expressing a multitude of verbal expressions; mastering the inexhaustible; extolling the profound stillness; and manifesting a multitude of tranquilities—these are the ten matters by which one enters into the three stations.”
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"When entering the assembly, there are thoughts; there are instructions received.
When dwelling amidst perceptions and worldly conventions, the objects of thought are inexhaustible."
Proclaiming the matter of tranquility, one also enters into serene stillness;
by extinguishing all evil matters, one thus fulfills the aspiration for the Way.
"Bodhisattvas have ten matters through which their arousal of the mind is never weary and remains without deficiency or flaw."
What are the ten? They are:
making offerings to all Buddhas while dwelling amidst various forms without weariness;
and reverently following all virtuous friends.
Seeking among the various sutras, he did not consider it difficult;
though he had extensively heard many scriptures, his capacity for receiving and understanding them was still insufficient;
yet, in the mere instant of forming a thought, he proclaimed the Way of the Sutras.
To transform and enlighten sentient beings by demonstrating the laws and teachings;
to inspire all beings to reach the path of the Buddha;
and to dwell in a single world for incalculable eons while practicing the bodhisattva conduct.
He travels everywhere through all lands, leaving none unvisited;
he never harbors doubt regarding the Buddha’s various scriptures, resolving them whenever he asks about them.
These are the ten matters for which he generates the mind of awakening without weariness and without deficiency.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Making offerings to the bodies of all Buddhas, Never becoming weary or satisfied;
Furthermore, following all virtuous friends, He diligently seeks out all the sutras."
Never weary in their pursuit, they see those who have resolved to attain awakening and provide them with instruction in the path; thus do they enlighten and transform all bodhisattvas.
There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva distinguishes various eloquences.

What are these ten? They are: the analytical eloquence that discerns the realms entered by sentient beings; the eloquence that clearly understands the faculties of others and their proper destinations; the eloquence that comprehends all transgressions and merits, as well as their respective retributions; the eloquence that perceives the specific places where beings are born; the eloquence that knows all that exists and does not exist in the world; the eloquence that beholds the abodes where the Buddhas dwell; the eloquence that understands the depth and shallowness of the principles of the sūtras and dharmas; the eloquence that thoroughly explains the existence and non-existence within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); the eloquence that masters the events of the three periods of time—past, future, and present; and the eloquence that can distinguish immeasurable modes of conduct expressed through loving-kindness. These are the ten matters of a bodhisattva’s various forms of eloquence.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"He understands what sentient beings know;
he perceives the inclinations of their faculties; according to the offenses or merits they have established, he beholds the places where they shall be reborn."
They distinguish all worlds;
they also clearly understand the categories of phenomena, thoroughly master the wisdom of the Buddha-way, and comprehend the beginning and end of the three periods of time.
"There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva attains dhāraṇī."
What are these ten? They are:
to immediately receive and uphold whatever one has heard extensively;
to cherish the scriptures in one's heart, never forgetting or losing them;
They uphold the torch of the Dharma and employ skillful means in all their teachings to explain and interpret the various sutras;
they understand the naturalness of phenomena, attain the radiance of the Dharma, and reach the inconceivable path of the Buddhas;
they maintain various states of meditative concentration, and upon hearing of a Buddha in the present, they receive his instructions face-to-face and immediately practice the Dharma accordingly.
Entering the Dharma-assembly, they are able to produce inconceivable speech according to local customs;
they contemplate the three periods of time and the immeasurable teachings of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, proclaiming them at the appropriate times;
and they harbor manifold eloquence regarding the essentials of all the Buddha’s scriptures.
The meanings heard by the ear are beyond measure; the noble wisdom that arises can fully elucidate all that is heard.
To uphold all Buddha-dharmas and to establish the Tathāgata’s ten powers and fearlessness—these are the ten matters of a bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Having heard extensively, one immediately upholds it; Never forgetting any dharma, one understands how to teach according to the occasion, And realizes the natural state of all dharmas."
By means of the great radiance of the Dharma and inconceivable wisdom,
they attain samādhi in the present and hear the sūtras before their eyes.
"There are ten matters by which Bodhisattvas proclaim the Buddha-way."

What are these ten? They are: understanding the principles of the Way; vowing with great aspirations; discerning the destinations to which sins and blessings lead; abiding eternally in perfect enlightenment; harboring no arrogance; penetrating the Dharma-realm; knowing the state of meditative concentration; clearly understanding the fundamental nature of the mind; comprehending original purity; and awakening according to that original nature so as to achieve the Buddha-way. These are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva proclaims the Buddha-way.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
“Thoroughly understanding the Buddha-way, Comprehending vows and discerning merit and demerit,
Established by all Buddhas, Understanding the Dharma without self-importance.”
"The mind of discrimination is fundamentally pure; it is that to which the concentrated mind returns.
This fundamental purity is also spontaneous; by following this foundation, one attains awakening.
When the Buddha spoke these words, the trichiliocosm shook with great intensity, and a vast radiance shone universally throughout the ten directions.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits all came to scatter flowers and brought various musical instruments to entertain the Buddha; filled with joy and delight, they all celebrated together, exclaiming:
"How fortunate! How blessed!"

"Because our merit from past lives was pure and profound, we have been permitted to participate in this assembly. To don these profound and subtle discourses and the boundless wisdom of the Way—how great is our fortune!

World-Honored One, the Benevolent One, through your compassionate grace toward the ten directions, you have opened up and revealed the treasury of the Dharma, healing those who are blind and ignorant, and dissolving the five aggregates, the six sense-decays, the three poisons, the five hindrances, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the sixty-two views."
He demonstrates five matters:

the categories of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; the five eyes; the six supernormal powers; and the six perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom—thereby attaining the Way of the Buddha.

He proclaimed and revealed the twelve divisions of the sutras, transforming those with wrong views and resolving their sixty-two doubts so that they might give rise to the aspiration for the Way; thus all Buddhas praised him from afar, and the bodhisattvas rejoiced.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadramati again asked Samantabhadra:
"What is called the arousal of the bodhicitta?
What is called the practice of the Dharma?"
What is called "great compassion"?
What is called "arousing the mind for the Way through conditions," such that one gives rise to that intention by means of its objects?
What is called "seeing a virtuous friend and giving rise to a mind of reverence and diligence"?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining purity?
What is meant by the perfections (pāramitās)?
And what is meant by the Buddha-wisdom?
What is meant by "that which is traversed"?
What is meant by "the power of a bodhisattva"?
And what is meant by "equanimity"?
What is meant by "arousing noble awakening"?
What is meant by "expounding the Dharma"?
And what is meant by "practicing and upholding it"?
What is eloquence?
What is the incalculable?
What is the practice of an equanimous mind?
"What is meant by practicing wisdom?
What is meant by a bodhisattva who is not conceited?
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva replied:
"Excellent! The question asked by you, Son of the Buddha, is most profound and subtle; how delightful it is!
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and I shall now speak for your sake."
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and the great assembly received the instruction and listened.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra said:
"There are ten matters that give rise to the bodhicitta."
What are these ten? At the moment of generating the mind [of enlightenment], one constantly harbors great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*), protecting and sustaining all classes of sentient beings;
one practices with pity, observing the afflictions and sufferings of the people as if undergoing them oneself, and is able to bestow all that one possesses as gifts.
When one recollects omniscience, the mind becomes the primary source;
because one recollects omniscience, one is able to give rise to the resolve without violating the sacred principles;
and by generating a solemn mind, one studies the essentials of the precepts of all bodhisattvas.
Their minds are firm and stable like vajra, having eliminated all defilements and impurities;
their arising thoughts are like rivers and oceans, guiding and directing all pure and wholesome dharmas;
their resolve is as strong and solid as Mount Sumeru, enabling them to endure the speech of the multitudes and sounds of both good and evil.
The resolve they have generated establishes eternal peace; they bestow upon sentient beings the karma of great sincerity and faith, while their minds stride alone.
With the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) reaching its limit, they thoroughly understand all phenomena and provide protection according to circumstances.
These are the ten matters for generating the bodhisattva mind.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Arising a heart of great compassion, He protects all sentient beings;
Seeing them in suffering and distress, He pities them as if they were his own."
Contemplating all-knowledge, adorned by the fulfillment of their aspirations,
their minds are like adamant and their wisdom is like the ocean and rivers.
"Bodhisattvas have ten practices for the Dharma of Samantabhadra."
What are the ten? They are:
to universally vow to practice benevolence together with all beings throughout future kalpas;
and to reverently honor the form-phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, and the Perfectly Enlightened Ones who have not yet arrived.
They transform and enlighten sentient beings by establishing the practices of a bodhisattva;
they accumulate the roots of all virtues and vow to emulate Samantabhadra;
and they are all able to enter and traverse all the *pāramitās*.
Their aspirations are harmonious and refined; they fulfill the practices of a bodhisattva and cultivate all dharmas.
They desire to adorn all buddha-worlds with impartial discourse, to take birth in all buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, and to master skillful means while seeking out the various sutras.
They all joyfully manifest birth in various Buddha-fields and attain the realization of unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment;
these are the ten matters of the bodhisattva’s dharma practice.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Fully knowing all future eons, I shall honor and revere all Tathāgatas;
Equal toward all sentient beings as toward myself, I shall fulfill the vows of Samantabhadra’s conduct."
Accumulating the roots of all virtues, Entering the various perfections (pāramitās),
Adorning all Buddha-lands, One swiftly attains unsurpassed enlightenment.
"Bodhisattvas have ten matters through which they constantly practice great compassion."

What are these ten? They are: observing sentient beings who are solitary and without spiritual lineage, one arouses great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); examining those who lack the Way, one transforms them through great pity (*mahākāruṇya*); seeing those in poverty and distress, one causes them to plant the roots of virtue; for those long asleep, one brings about awakening; seeing that the realm of sentient beings lacks skillful means, one transforms them according to the occasion; for those bound by various cravings, one exhorts and protects them; beholding the calamities and hardships encountered by the multitudes of living beings, one takes pity on them and enables their rescue; seeing those long afflicted by illness, one heals them with compassionate love; for those who have departed from wholesome dharmas, one reveals the principles of the Path; and if one sees sentient beings who have lost the Buddha-dharma, one feels pity and joy. These are the ten matters of a bodhisattva’s great compassion.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
“While dwelling in the world, he practices great compassion,
Observing sentient beings who have long suffered from afflictions Because they have severed the roots of virtue.”
To give rise to boundless compassion, To establish them in the Buddha-way,
The Bodhisattva practices great kindness In order to transform and enlighten sentient beings.
There are ten matters by which a Bodhisattva gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.

What are these ten? They are: teaching and admonishing sentient beings to accord with the principles of the Dharma so that they may give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; wishing to eliminate all suffering, affliction, and distress; establishing the people so that their minds may be forever at peace; seeing that the multitudes dwell in the ground of ignorance and causing them to resolve upon the Way; delighting in exhorting sentient beings to enter the Buddha-wisdom; following the True Awakening and reverently honoring all Buddhas, the Most Holy; desiring to behold all Tathāgatas, the Truly Realized Ones; likewise delighting in beholding the physical forms, marks, and majestic countenances of the Buddhas; furthermore, loving and rejoicing in entering the path of the Buddhas, thereby giving rise to the Great Resolve; and also reverently loving the Ten Powers and the Fearlessnesses. These are the ten matters that serve as conditions for giving rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Seeing sentient beings being extinguished, Bound by afflictions and suffering,
Desiring to lead them to eternal peace, I have thus resolved upon the Bodhisattva mind."
When the people are devoid of wisdom, he exhorts and instructs them with the Buddha’s insight, causing them to serve the Leader of the Three Realms and to constantly behold all Tathāgatas.

When a Bodhisattva sees a virtuous friend, he gives rise to a mind of reverence; when the Bodhisattva first resolves upon the path of true enlightenment, he remains humble and compliant in the company of that virtuous friend. Desiring to strive for the attainment of the All-Knowledge of a Buddha, he practices under the guidance of a virtuous friend and yields his will to them.
“There are ten matters for generating the resolve upon seeing a virtuous friend.

What are these ten? To pay homage and take refuge; to have a mind free from craving and desire; to be able to practice according to the teachings one has heard; to cherish them with joy in one’s heart; to have a will that is untainted by defilement; to always unify the mind; to integrate all roots of virtue into a single practice; to embrace a single aspiration and generate the intent toward the World-Honored One; to have an impartial will; and to be fully endowed in one’s conduct. These are the ten ways of generating a mind of reverence upon seeing a virtuous friend.”
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"With a mind always maintaining reverence, Practicing according to what has been heard;
With joy free from blemish, His intent is always single-minded."
Gathering together the roots of all virtues, I take refuge in the World-Honored One;
By constantly honoring impartial conduct, The mind of the Way is fully perfected.
“There are ten matters concerning the purity of a bodhisattva.”
What are these ten? They are:
being pure like space, ultimately without loss;
and regarding the purity of all forms, transforming and guiding sentient beings according to their fundamental natures.
Their voices are pure, manifesting a multitude of resonant sounds with ineffable speech;
their eloquence is pure, discerning the immeasurable teachings spoken by the Buddhas;
their wisdom is pure, having utterly abandoned all ignorance.
Their births are also pure, as they attain the mastery of all bodhisattvas through their own power;
their retinues are sublime, for they understand the past deeds of sentient beings and thereby transform them;
their retributions are also pure, as they eliminate all hindrances and obscurations.
Their vows are clear and luminous, as they understand the single stage from which all bodhisattvas are born;
their conduct is radiant, as they emerge upon the vehicle of Samantabhadra—
these are the ten matters by which they attain purity.
At that time, a verse was spoken—[the Dan edition notes that this verse is missing from all other editions]:
"The Bodhisattva has ten matters by which he attains the *pāramitās*. What are these ten?"
The perfection of giving: being able to bestow all that one possesses;
the perfection of ethical discipline: fully observing the prohibitions of the Buddha;
the perfection of patience: being able to practice benevolence and harmony, thereby attaining the pure power of the Buddha.
The perfection of vigor is to practice with diligence and never regress;
the perfection of tranquility is to bring the mind to single-minded concentration;
the perfection of wisdom is to contemplate that all phenomena are fundamentally and naturally true.
The Perfection of Wisdom enters the ten powers of the Buddha;
the Perfection of Vow fulfills the conduct of Samantabhadra;
the Perfection of Spiritual Power manifests manifold transformations, appearing in all places.
The Dharma-measure is infinite, for it equally governs the beginning and end of all dharmas;
this constitutes the Bodhisattva’s ten infinite perfections (pāramitās).
Abiding in these, the Bodhisattva attains the supreme, true, and infinite great wisdom of the Tathāgata, and becomes fully endowed with the six perfections.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"The Perfection of Giving: one can give away all that one possesses;
The Perfection of Precepts: purifying all the practices of the Buddhas."
The Perfection of Forbearance: benevolent and harmonious, harboring no resentment;
The Perfection of Vigor: diligently practicing without retreating;
The Perfection of Single-Mindedness: the will fixed and free from confusion.
The Perfection of Wisdom observes that all phenomena are naturally so;
The Perfection of Spiritual Powers universally enters the power of the Buddha-way;
The practice of vows is impartial, and the supernormal powers traverse all dharmas.
"Bodhisattvas have ten kinds of wisdom.
What are these ten? They are:
understanding that the varieties of sentient beings throughout all the worlds of the ten directions are inconceivable;..."
They discern all schools and thoroughly understand all phenomena without missing the proper timing;
they cause those of various forms to realize awakening through a single principle;
they penetrate all dharma-realms and are able to proclaim wisdom.
They have thoroughly understood the beginning and end of all space, attaining the peerless wisdom of the Buddhas without exception;
they are able to know all past events throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
and they are able to see all future events within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
To universally enter and transform the present affairs of the Buddha-lands in the ten directions;
to clearly understand the vows and all practices of the Tathāgatas, fully entering into all wisdom;
and to know and comprehend that the Buddhas of the past, future, and present all share the same single practice—this is the meaning of the bodhisattva’s ten wisdoms.

When a bodhisattva dwells herein, their great radiance shines with sovereign brilliance; they fulfill all their vows and place faith in all Buddha-dharmas, thereby understanding all Buddha-dharmas through a single wisdom.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Able to know the realms of the ten directions, And the sentient beings therein, beyond counting;
Universally causing them to enter the wisdom of the Way, So that they may be free from manifold thoughts."
They are able to discern all phenomena, which are as equal as space;
the Buddha’s wisdom is supreme, for it can penetrate the affairs of the three periods of time.
"There are ten matters through which a bodhisattva passes."

What are these ten? They are: understanding all dharmas as having the single meaning of one category; recognizing that all sūtras have their respective limits; comprehending that all wisdoms are of a single characteristic; discerning the mental activities and wisdoms of sentient beings as being unconditioned and innumerable; viewing all multitudes of beings with equal regard; clearly identifying the afflictions practiced by sentient beings and how their dispositions are bound to their actions; clearly identifying the good and evil deeds performed by sentient beings; ensuring that the vows and aspirations of all bodhisattvas are free from self-conceit; and establishing the ten powers of a Tathāgata without exception to attain supreme perfect enlightenment. These are the ten matters through which a bodhisattva passes.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Knowing all phenomena to be one, Because of understanding their ultimate limit,
The manifold wisdoms merge into a single characteristic, Yet the minds of sentient beings are countless."
Observing all people, who are deluded by the activities of afflictions and bound by various fetters, unable to attain the mind of universal wisdom—
“The Bodhisattva possesses ten kinds of power.”
What are these ten? All dharmas enter into spontaneity;
all sūtras are like emanations, and their manifold meanings are like illusions.
The enumeration of all dharmas is entirely the Buddha-dharma;
all sūtras are utterly without dependence;
and everything that exists returns to the three gates of liberation.
One beholds many virtuous friends and reverently serves them with great devotion;
one cultivates the power of the mind;
and by means of the roots of all virtues, one enters the hall of the King of the Path of Unsurpassed Wisdom.
They have never slandered the profound and subtle wisdom;
they believe in and delight in the omniscient mind of all Buddhas, and because of their skillful power, they never regress.
These are the ten matters that constitute the power of a bodhisattva.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"All phenomena are self-so, All like the power of illusions and transformations;
All dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, Their meaning returns to the three gates of liberation."
Reverently honoring all virtuous friends, constantly accumulating the roots of myriad virtues,
entering the hall of supreme wisdom, and possessing profound faith in the Buddha’s deep Dharma.
There are ten matters regarding the equanimity of Bodhisattvas.

What are these ten? They are: equanimity toward all sentient beings; equanimity toward all phenomena; universally contemplating all Buddha-lands as equal; the non-duality of their fundamental nature and conduct; being rooted in all the bases of virtue; equanimity toward all bodhisattvas; having no difference in their vows; no distinction among the various perfections (pāramitās); all practices returning to the same form; and regarding all Buddhas of the ten directions as a single Buddha. These are the ten kinds of equality.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"With an impartial mind, I contemplate all sentient beings; I universally observe all the various sutras;
I likewise regard all buddha-lands as equal, And in my nature and conduct, I harbor no duality."
All are united with the roots of virtue; the Bodhisattva constantly practices compassion.
His vows are without variation, as he fulfills all the perfections (pāramitās).
There are ten matters by which a Bodhisattva awakens to the holy state.

What are the ten? All dharmas are merely sounds; all return to stillness; all dharmas are like illusions; the meaning of the sutras is like shadows; that which is seen by the eye is entirely a conjunction of causes and conditions; the karma of all meanings is pure; all dharmas are merely provisional names based on characters; the karma of all phenomena is fundamentally pure because of its original nature; the wisdom of the Way is non-conceptual and exhaustively investigates the ultimate source; and all that has form arises from the Dharma-realm. These are the ten births of the awakened sage.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"All phenomena are utterly tranquil, Comparable to magical illusions;
Metaphorically like shadows and echoes, They all arise from causes and conditions."
All dharmas are pure from beginning to end; nothing whatsoever is produced.
All are due to their original limit (*koṭi*); non-conceptualization is the ultimate truth.
"There are ten matters regarding the Bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma."

What are these ten? They are: expounding the profound and wondrous Dharma; ensuring that the meaning of what is taught is understood according to the occasion; lecturing on various matters; extensively proclaiming the matters of the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*); being able to distinguish the various perfections (*pāramitā*); declaring the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Tathāgata; explaining the meaning of the three periods of time; constantly preaching the Dharma of the non-retrogression of Bodhisattvas; praising the meritorious virtues of the training of all Buddhas; and proclaiming the equal renunciation of Bodhisattvas, Buddhas, and Tathāgatas. These are the ten matters of a Bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Proclaiming the profound and wondrous Dharma, Causing all to enter the meaning of the Path;
Expounding manifold wisdom, Extensively teaching all-encompassing knowledge."
They manifest the various pāramitās and reveal the ten powers;
unimpeded throughout the three periods of time, these bodhisattvas do not regress.
There are ten matters by which bodhisattvas practice and carry out their conduct.
What are these ten? They are:
accumulating all the roots of merit from every virtuous deed;
and upon hearing the Tathāgatas preach the sūtras, being able to immediately receive and uphold them.
They grasp all manifestations, explaining them through parables;
they guide and lead all to practice the Dharma-gates;
and they embrace the treasury of dhāraṇīs and the wisdom-gates of the Way’s meaning.
They are all able to sever doubt and all attachments;
they are fully endowed with all the practices of Bodhisattvas;
and through the impartial eloquence of all Tathāgatas, they transform beings by preaching the Dharma and manifesting its radiant glory.
It is said that they receive the teachings of all Buddhas;
they establish the karmic activities of their enjoyment so as to cause them to reach unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment.
These are the ten matters by which they preach the gate of equality and put it into practice.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Accumulating the roots of manifold virtues, Praising the Dharma of the Tathāgata,
Contemplating the equality of all phenomena, He proclaims and disseminates the gateway of the wisdom of the Way."
Having cast aside all doubts and attachments, they fulfill the practices of a bodhisattva;
taking all dharmas as gateways to the world, they cause all beings to enter the chamber of the Way.
Bodhisattvas have ten matters for the analytical discernment of eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

What are these ten? They are: the teaching of all dharmas being forever free from conceptualization; the analysis of all sūtras being entirely without objective activity; eloquence regarding all meanings being likewise without attachment; the understanding that all dharmas are empty while proclaiming them as immeasurable; the realization that all dharmas are established by the Buddha; the fact that all existing things have no basis whatsoever; the ability to analyze the chapters and phrases of all dharmas; the thorough exposition of the meaning of the true reality of the sūtras; always regarding sentient beings with a mind of equanimity and compassion; and preaching the Dharma according to their inclinations so that they may attain joy—these are the ten types of eloquence.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"In preaching the sutras, one is without conceptualization; All mental activities are free from thought.
Not clinging to any phenomena, One understands them all to be empty."
Their eloquence is immeasurable; all dharmas are established by the Buddha.
Nothing whatsoever has any basis of dependence; understanding them, one sees they are all fundamentally non-existent.
"There are ten matters by which a Bodhisattva attains mastery."

What are these ten? They are: transforming and enlightening sentient beings; illuminating all dharmas; cultivating the roots of all virtues; practicing infinite wisdom; not being attached to prohibitive precepts; encouraging and assisting the Buddha-way with the roots of goodness one creates; practicing diligence without retreating; subduing all Māras; delighting in and thoroughly understanding the mind of the Way and all Buddha-ways; and attaining perfect enlightenment while remaining amidst false views. These are the ten attainments of mastery.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Awakening at dawn, he teaches sentient beings, Attaining illumination of all dharmas;
Practicing the roots of all virtues, He possesses sovereign and boundless wisdom."
The mind is entirely without attachment; with diligence and without weariness, one subdues all demons, and the realization of the Way is attained through one's own effort.
"There are ten matters by which Bodhisattvas bestow countless gifts."

What are these ten? They are: transforming and enlightening all the difficulties of the world; the beginning and end of sentient beings being incalculable; the matters of the scriptures being immeasurable; all that is done having no limit or bottom; the limits of all dharmas being difficult to exhaust even with calculation; the source of all virtues having no peer; all evils being such that none can be proclaimed; all aspirations being without boundary; the direction of all practices being beyond analogy; and all Bodhisattvas walking alone without companion, while the Buddhas, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, are uniquely honored and without equal. These are the ten matters through which the uncountable is bestowed.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"The world's reckonings cannot be reckoned; Sentient beings are beyond numbering;
All phenomena have no limit, And that which is created is likewise infinite."
“Virtue has no peer; all evils have no place;
the Bodhisattva has no equal; the Buddhas have no peers.
There are ten matters by which a Bodhisattva practices an impartial mind.

What are these ten? They are: equalizing the mind in the accumulation of merit; having identical aspirations; regarding the bodies and minds of sentient beings as being without duality; entering into the destinies of the merits and faults of the populace; universally traversing all dharmas; viewing all Buddha-lands—whether pure or defiled—as one and the same; exhorting and transforming sentient beings to enter into firm faith; equalizing the mind toward all practices and all manifold delusions; entering into the ten powers and fearlessnesses of all Buddhas; and all of these arising from the Tathāgata’s impartial wisdom. These are the ten kinds of equalized mind.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
“With an impartial mind, one accumulates the roots of virtue; One brings forth and manifests all vows.
With a mind of equality toward all sentient beings, Sin and merit are no different.”
Universally entering all sutras, Equanimously observing all buddha-fields,
Compassionately regarding all sentient beings, Causing them to enter the practice of non-differentiation.
"Bodhisattvas have ten practices of wisdom."
What are these ten? They are:
to clearly understand that sentient beings shall ultimately attain liberating wisdom;
and to enter all nations and various lands, entering those places not yet entered.
Wandering through the various nets of craving, they remove all foulness and impurity;
as they traverse the various realms, they know their increase and decrease;
and they clearly understand that all phenomena are each distinct from one another.
Or again, with a single grade [of voice], they are able to circulate universally;
through the sounds of all realms, they understand the various conceptions of the world, the perversions in which beings dwell, and the diverse thoughts they harbor;
by means of a single word, they universally enter into the verbal teachings of all dharmas.
The Tathāgata’s majestic transformations establish the Dharma-realm;
though all sentient beings dwell within the three periods of time, the Buddhas enter therein to instruct them without ceasing, causing them all to enter the Way.
These are the ten matters of the bodhisattva’s practice of wisdom.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Faithfully understanding the realm of sentient beings, Universally entering all Buddha-lands,
Reaching everywhere throughout the ten directions, He contemplates all worlds with equanimity."
All phenomena are not manifold; they enter into incalculable bodies.
That which is manifested by the Tathāgata brings liberation to those within the three realms.
There are ten matters in which a bodhisattva does not become conceited.
What are the ten? They are:
not treating with contempt those who crawl or breathe;
maintaining humility in body and mind, and not looking down upon others.
One does not become conceited on account of a buddha-field;
if one receives offerings and respect, one harbors no arrogance;
and one does not praise oneself for having a beautiful voice.
Fully perfecting all practices and vows without resorting to ornate embellishment;
transforming sentient beings so they are free from indolence;
and attaining supreme, perfect enlightenment.
Constantly harboring compassion while expounding the sutras;
not praising one's own person, yet establishing what is to be done without being conceited—
these are the ten matters of non-conceit.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Not disparaging sentient beings, Not finding joy in attaining a buddha-field,
Nor taking pleasure in being honored and revered, And remaining free from attachment to pleasant sounds."
Free from craving for any desires, he transforms and enlightens sentient beings,
attains supreme perfect enlightenment, and proclaims the wisdom of the Great Way. When this Dharma was spoken,
the devas, nāgas, spirits, worldly people, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas were all filled with joy, and they all resolved to attain the Way.

Lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, herds of deer, fish, turtles, tortoises, crocodiles, and all manner of small insects all possessed hearts of compassion and harbored no intent to harm one another; hearing the Dharma he preached, each was filled with joy and resolved to attain the Way.
The devas scattered flowers that fell like rain;
they burned various famous incenses, which rose in dense clouds;
lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
At that time, there was none who did not rejoice and pay homage.
*Dushi pin jing*, Scroll One;
*Dushi pin jing*, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra-mati again asked Samantabhadra: "What is meant by 'establishment'? What is meant by 'joyful faith'?
What is meant by 'deep entry'?"
What is meant by "relying on a protector"?
What is meant by "courageous intent"?
What is meant by "severing all doubts"?
What is meant by the inconceivable?
What is meant by the exposition of the ultimate truth?
What is meant by the full understanding of retribution?
What is meant by "concentrated mind"?
What is meant by "nothingness"?
What is meant by "gate of liberation"?
What is meant by supernormal powers (abhijñā)?
What is meant by penetration (prativedha)?
What is meant by liberation (vimukti)?
What are called gardens and groves?
What are called palaces?
What are called pleasure excursions?
What is meant by adornment?
What is meant by the immovability of the mind?
What is meant by the nature of having nothing to relinquish?
What is meant by contemplative wisdom?
What is meant by expounding the Dharma?
What is meant by pure vows?
What is meant by "seal"?
What is meant by "light of wisdom"?
What is meant by "practicing the formless"?
What is meant by the mind that is without phenomena?
What is meant by the mind being like a mountain?
What is meant by being like the ocean?
Samantabhadra said:
"Excellent question!
There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva establishes themselves."

What are these ten? They are: constantly setting one's will upon the Buddha; perpetually contemplating the sutras and the Dharma; exhorting and transforming sentient beings to cause them to abide in the Buddha-way; encouraging them to settle in their vocations; cultivating and establishing right practice; following and delighting in vows; constantly being mindful of dignified deportment; acting in accordance with the times wherever one travels; proclaiming the roots of goodness; and establishing the meaning of wisdom. These are the ten matters for establishing the mind.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"With single-mindedness, constantly recollect the Buddha; With focused diligence, contemplate the scriptures.
Exhort sentient beings to enter the Way, And show them the karma they have created."
Praising and assisting those who practice correctly, constantly ensuring that vows are not lost,
being complete in dignified demeanor and ritual propriety, and perfecting the roots of goodness to achieve noble wisdom—
these are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva delights in faith.
What are the ten? "The Bodhisattva’s mind spontaneously gives rise to this thought:
'Whosoever shall appear in the future as a Tathāgata, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, in the world, I shall see them all.'"
"Having seen these Buddhas, he makes offerings and serves them, setting his mind upon the Unsurpassed; he bows his head in self-refuge to these Perfectly Awakened Ones, saying:
'May you instruct me! Through this instruction, may I return to the stage of a Bodhisattva, just as all Bodhisattvas receive the teachings with a heart of reverence.'"
"Maintaining a heart of reverence and diligence, I shall immediately practice according to what I have heard.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva further reflected to himself:

"May I never be separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the various Bodhisattvas; may I eliminate the hardships of the restlessness of birth and death, and cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva for incalculable kalpas."
Furthermore, he thought to himself:

"In the past, before I had resolved upon the unsurpassed path, I was not a vessel for the Dharma; I feared the most profound meanings, I also feared the malicious slander and ill repute of the world, and I was terrified by the assemblies of the evil realms of birth and death."
I shall depart from this and never again be joined with it.
Remaining far removed from such affairs, in whatever place I am born, I shall not be separated from the mind of the Way; I shall have no fear, no dread, nor any trepidation.
Forever free from all hardships, they always remain far removed from dust and defilement;
having eternally extinguished impurity and turbidity, they move with solitary stride;
they subdue all Māras and eliminate all non-Buddhists.
"Furthermore, he thought to himself:

'I shall exhort and transform all realms of sentient beings, causing them to follow the teachings of the Vinaya, to set their minds upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and to cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva.'"

When you attain Buddhahood, I shall follow the subtle and sublime path of the Honored Sage; I shall bow my head in prostration, pay homage, and take refuge in you with immeasurable joy for as long as my life lasts.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you shall establish countless monasteries, serve the śarīras, propagate the Buddha’s teachings, and distribute the sūtras, so that the unsurpassed truth may endure forever.
"Furthermore, he thought to himself:
'I shall adorn the infinite world-systems, causing all Buddha-lands to be pure, harmonious, and gentle, with various distinct qualities that are equally pure.'"
I shall cause countless Buddha-fields to tremble, causing all beings therein to resolve their minds [for enlightenment].
I shall emit a great radiance that illuminates the ten directions, and through the transformations of my supernormal powers, there shall be nowhere it does not pervade.
Furthermore, he thought to himself:
"Once I have attained Buddhahood, I shall resolve all the doubts of sentient beings and transform their dispositions so that they are always pure and harmonious."

He quiets his will, extinguishes worldly desires, blocks the gates of all evils, and opens the door of eternal peace; he dispels the darkness of the netherworld and exerts a vast radiance; he abandons the works of Māra and attains supreme auspiciousness, manifesting these meritorious achievements universally to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, he thought to himself:
"Wherever I may be, I shall always see the Buddhas.
When I am in a state of peril or distress, should I wish to pay them a visit, may I surely see the Perfectly Awakened One as I desire, and never be separated from him."
"When one beholds the Tathāgata face-to-face as he expounds the Dharma:
'A Tathāgata is difficult to encounter; he appears but once in incalculable kalpas, like the *utpala* flower, rare and appearing only after a long time.'"
He gave rise to a pure mind, casting aside all improper schemes; his intent was upright and free from flattery.
Furthermore, he thought to himself:
"When I have accomplished the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and become the Most Perfectly Awakened One, I shall perform the Buddha-work throughout all buddha-fields."

For the sake of all sentient beings, he manifests the body of a Buddha in each case, beats the great Dharma drum, and rains down the nectar of the Dharma; he bestows the infinite Dharma, purity, and fearlessness, roars the lion’s roar, and establishes boundless vows.
Abiding in the Dharma-realm, they proclaim the Way of the sutras.
For an entire kalpa they do not rest; their bodies do not grow weary, and though their speech is inexhaustible, their minds never grow fatigued.
"These are the ten matters established by the mind.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Purifying all Buddha-lands, Exhorting sentient beings toward the Way,"
Revealing the profound and wondrous Dharma, Causing them to resolve upon the Unsurpassed Way.
Constantly wishing to behold all Buddhas, Serving, honoring, and taking refuge in them;
Listening to and receiving the teachings they proclaim, I shall accept and practice them with a single mind.
To sever the three evil destinies, you open wide the gate of peace and bliss;
for the sake of those in the deep darkness, you manifest the great radiance.
By disseminating the gift of the Dharma, you extinguish all defilements and dust.
He lets out the great lion’s roar and rains down the great ambrosia.
There are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva enters deeply. What are these ten?
They enter into all past events throughout the worlds and roam within the profound and deep Dharma of the enlightened nature;
they return to the future affairs of all Buddha-lands, being counted among the assemblies in every Buddha-realm;
their perfect awakening is non-dual, and though they exist in all lands, they remain serenely tranquil in the present.
They are able to know all that is spoken and said according to the local customs of the world, as well as the adornments and purities of all buddha-fields;
they enter deeply into the Dharma, understanding the various teachings found throughout the world;
furthermore, they can discern the differing karmas of merit and demerit of all sentient beings and calculate the diverse practices undertaken by all bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva understands and fully knows the abodes of all Tathāgatas of the past; the Bodhisattva fully knows the slow or rapid pace of the teachings of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; the Bodhisattva further knows the Dharma preached by the Buddhas, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and their assemblies of noble disciples in the lands of the present, as they transform and enlighten sentient beings.
Within the dharma-realm and empty space, which are without limit, there are the Tathāgatas of the ten directions;

furthermore, he discerns and knows the worldly dharmas, the dharmas of the Śrāvakas, as well as those of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, the Bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgatas, entering these dharmas without any seeking or aspiration for them.

To expound upon various gateways into the dharma-realm, yet neither entering therein nor conceptualizing phenomena, but rather transforming and enlightening others in accordance with the teachings of all dharmas—
this constitutes the tenth matter for deeply entering the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Knowing the past, the future, and the present,
He manifests in accordance with worldly customs To purify the Buddha-worlds."
Discerning the transgressions and merits of beings, the practices of all bodhisattvas,
the present buddha-fields, and the assemblies of bodhisattvas;
knowing the number of sentient beings, and the limits of the space where the Dharma is taught.
All the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the multitude of bodhisattvas have fully attained [realization].
"There are ten matters upon which a bodhisattva relies; by relying on these, one cultivates the bodhisattva practice."

What are these ten? They are: constantly honoring and revering the Buddha with daily taking of refuge; transforming and enlightening sentient beings; seeing all virtuous friends and relying upon them; always delighting in accumulating the roots of all virtues; likewise purifying all buddha-fields; always having compassion for all and not abandoning sentient beings; universally entering into all the *pāramitās*; desiring to fulfill all the vows of the bodhisattvas; cultivating immeasurable resolve for the path so that they may return to it; and clearly understanding that all Buddhas attain supreme perfect enlightenment. These are the ten matters upon which a bodhisattva relies to accomplish the practice of the Way.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Reverently honoring all Buddhas, Relying upon the conduct of Bodhisattvas,
Transforming and enlightening the multitudes of sentient beings, And respectfully following all virtuous friends."
Accumulating the roots of all virtues, Adorning and purifying all Buddha-lands,
Entering into the various perfections (pāramitās), And fully accomplishing the bodhisattva vows.
There are ten matters concerning the courageous mind of a bodhisattva.
What are these ten? They are:
eliminating all sins that constitute hindrances;
and receiving the bestowed instructions and teachings even though the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have entered parinirvāṇa.
With a courageous mind, they subdue all Māras;
they understand impermanence;
and without sparing their own bodies or lives, they dissolve the heretics through the conditions of the True Dharma.
With a gentle and harmonious mind, he gladdens all sentient beings;
harboring a heart of exultation, there is none among the assembled multitude who does not rejoice upon seeing him;
he tames and transforms all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, causing them all to receive his spiritual influence.
To practice with gentleness and compliance; to abide in the profound Dharma;

to constantly relinquish the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; and to perform the deeds of a Bodhisattva for incalculable eons without weariness—these are the ten matters of the courageous mind of a Bodhisattva.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Having cast off all the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), The Buddha departs, honoring the teachings he has mounted;
He subdues the hosts of Māras, Without cherishing his own body or life."
He subdues and transforms all non-Buddhists, bringing joy to sentient beings;
spirits and deities alike receive his instruction and constantly uphold the bodhisattva practice.
There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva severs all doubts, ensuring that no lingering hesitation remains.
What are these ten? "The Bodhisattva resolves his mind and thinks to himself:

'I shall rescue and gather in sentient beings through giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom; I shall guide them by means of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.'"
"Even while practicing this, there shall be no hesitation; it is impossible that I would ever falter or retreat.
Furthermore, he thought to himself:

"I shall universally behold the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the ten directions and all future Buddhas; having encountered the Unsurpassed Wisdom, I shall make offerings to these Buddhas without my mind lingering in doubt for even as long as a hair's breadth."
"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects:
