'I shall fully illuminate all Buddha-lands with various rays of light.

Hearing of the practices that Bodhisattvas shall undertake in the future, my mind shall not grow weary throughout incalculable kalpas; nor shall I consider it difficult to transform and guide immeasurable classes of sentient beings.'"
The Dharma-realm is incalculable and boundless, just like empty space;
the number of sentient beings to be delivered is likewise so, yet one never becomes weary or discouraged.
"Furthermore, he thought to himself:
'I shall cultivate the bodhisattva practices, fully perfect all vows, and achieve the wisdom of omniscience and the various supernormal powers.
He further thought:"
"When practicing as a bodhisattva, may I fully attain the light of the Dharma and the infinite radiance of the Buddha.
One should always consider all dharmas with joy, regarding them entirely as the Buddha-dharma.
“Universally knowing the thoughts and intentions of all sentient beings, they clearly understand the countless, inexhaustible phenomena, both conditioned and unconditioned.

Having attained equal enlightenment, they are profoundly adept in all dharmas that transcend the world; they eliminate inverted views and perceptions, and though there may be defilement, these are fundamentally and entirely pure.”

“The Bodhisattva clearly understands all Buddha-dharmas and attains supreme perfect enlightenment; he is free from the errors of manifold conceptualizations and inverted views, nor does he cling to even a single hair’s breadth [of attachment].
Although outflows (*āsrava*) are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), he penetrates the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); having renounced all gain and honor, he is able to roam and enter the boundless limits.”
"These are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva severs all doubts.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"Mindfulness of giving, precepts, patience, diligence, Single-mindedness, and the cultivation of wisdom;
Practicing loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, one beholds all Buddhas with reverence.
With light fully suffusing and illuminating, throughout immeasurable future kalpas,
the mind never grows weary as one attains the omniscience of Buddhahood.
All dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, and all are likewise the dharma that transcends the world;
by casting off defilement, turbidity, and inverted views, one attains the Buddha’s supreme perfect enlightenment.
There are ten inconceivable matters concerning Bodhisattvas.
“What are these ten? They are:

the roots of virtue cultivated are inconceivable; all aspirations made are immeasurable; one observes that all phenomena are entirely like illusions and transformations—having given rise to the mind of enlightenment and relying upon various wholesome karmas—one commits no transgression or failure.”

"Cultivating the bodhisattva practice, they are forever free from delusive thoughts; they cultivate the profound and essential meaning and universally enter into all dharmas. They do not grasp at extinction, and as long as the wisdom of the Way is not perfected, they never abandon their quest."

“The Bodhisattva practices the Way, entering the womb and being born, accumulating diligent asceticism, proceeding to the tree of enlightenment to subdue the hosts of Māras, attaining supreme perfect awakening and turning the wheel of Dharma, manifesting the attainment of parinirvāṇa, and displaying all Buddha-works. He establishes these manifestations without abandoning great compassion to protect all sentient beings, never deviating from his original vows.”

Furthermore, that bodhisattva establishes and manifests the ten powers of a Tathāgata; from the first resolution of mind, they remain within the dharma-realm to transform and enlighten sentient beings without ever ceasing or resting.

Furthermore, those bodhisattvas all enter into manifold perceptions by means of non-perception, and enter into non-perception by means of perception; they speak of matters involving various perceptions while remaining free from any mental recollection.
Furthermore, by means of various thoughts, one speaks of the state of non-thought; by means of non-existence, one enters into existence;

and likewise, all that exists enters into non-existence. One transforms the unconditioned into the conditioned and transforms the conditioned into the unconditioned. One speaks of attainment regarding the unattainable and speaks of non-attainment regarding the attainable, thereby understanding that all phenomena are entirely without existence.

Furthermore, those bodhisattvas maintain an impartial mind toward the Path; through the equality of the Path, they understand and know that the path-mind of sentient beings is no different [from their own].
Their minds are free from inverted views, their mindfulness is never lost, they do not follow false doubts, and all that they perceive is equal.

"Furthermore, at the very moment that bodhisattva resolves his mind, his mind becomes tranquil; he enters meditative absorption with a concentrated mind, abiding in the ultimate limit (bhūtakoṭi) without realizing it as a final attainment, for, being free from outflows (anāsrava), he does not enter eternal extinction."

They distribute all roots of virtue and clearly understand all phenomena; they preach to others that all things are without outflows (*anāsrava*), and they also proclaim to others that their own outflows have been exhausted.
"One should eliminate all outflows, and thus enter into worldly phenomena by means of the Buddha-dharma."
Though dwelling therein, they harbor no mundane thoughts nor any conceptualizations of the mundane or the supramundane.
They contemplate that all phenomena enter the Dharma-body, yet there is nothing entered; they clearly understand all phenomena as being non-dual and without any activity.
These are the ten inconceivable qualities of a bodhisattva; by abiding in these, a bodhisattva swiftly attains unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva explains the ultimate truth.
What are the ten? They are: expounding all Buddha-dharmas; being sincere at all times; abandoning unwholesome dharmas; not losing one's proper measure;

using the supernatural powers and transformations of the bodhisattvas to proclaim the teaching of perfect enlightenment; being able to enter according to circumstances into the karmic actions of the sins and merits of sentient beings; and elucidating the way for sentient beings.

"Having eliminated all defilements and transgressions, they are able to penetrate the meaning of sentient beings through the gate of unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), thereby dissolving all hindrances and cultivating the practice of tranquil seclusion."
"Furthermore, that bodhisattva abides nowhere at all, just like empty space.

In each and every entry, they do not grasp at precepts; they have no hesitation regarding the formation and destruction of heaven and earth; they do not falter within the various worlds, and they encounter no obscuration or obstruction within the realm of all phenomena."
"From that direction, he will increasingly attain the subtle and profound state of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, from his birth and renunciation until his final parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas who have entered the Dharma-realm will universally behold all the Buddhas’ movements, gestures, and deportment."

“The Bodhisattva perceives all classes of sentient beings abiding in nirvana; because there is nothing further to be created, he vows not to fall away, but shall eventually fully master all supernormal powers and wisdom.”

"Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who see that all phenomena have nothing to rely upon; they do not distance themselves from spiritual friends, nor do they become attached to those whom they ought to approach.
Their diligence is like that of the Tathāgata—unflagging and without cessation—and their deportment is uniform."
Whether toward friends or enemies, one accumulates the roots of virtue and encourages their gathering so that all become one;
through praise and accomplishment, one ensures there is no duality.
These are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva explains the eternal according to the occasion.
"When a bodhisattva possesses discerning wisdom, there are ten matters. What are these ten?

To clearly understand all Buddha-lands; to comprehend and enter the origins of the flourishing and decline of sentient beings; to discern the mental activities and dispositions of the multitudes; to proclaim the waxing and waning of the faculties of the people; furthermore, to know all karmic retributions and the fruits of action; to universally enter the path of the śrāvakas according to their respective timely meanings; to likewise descend to the level of the practices of the pratyekabuddhas; to cultivate all bodhisattva deeds through skillful means; to distinguish all things according to worldly dharmas; and to universally accord with and enter the Buddhas' teachings while clearly understanding the appropriateness of wisdom—this is the Bodhisattva’s tenfold analytical wisdom.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this, they swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
There are ten matters regarding the samādhis of a bodhisattva.
What are these ten matters?
When they settle their minds in meditative concentration, they know all that exists within the worlds of the ten directions;
they are able to pacify the bodies of sentient beings through mental concentration and attain the samādhi of all dharmas;
through this samādhi-concentration, they behold the Buddhas of the ten directions and are thus able to establish all forms of mindfulness.
According to the occasion, they stabilize their minds; through this samādhi, they are able to manifest countless bodies and likewise cause them to arise from that samādhi;
they universally enter into all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones;
and through the correct reception of samādhi, they awaken sentient beings.
His wisdom is universally vast, as he clearly understands the various samādhis of the bodhisattvas according to the times;
in a single moment of thought, he enters the wisdom of one-pointed mind, opening the wisdom of tranquility with an unconditioned mind;
he is able to universally cultivate all the wisdoms of the bodhisattvas without ever abandoning his steadfast faith.
By means of the great wisdom of their vows, they thoroughly understand samādhi;
these are the ten matters concerning the samādhis of a bodhisattva.
"What are the ten matters possessed by a bodhisattva? [They are as follows...]"
What are the ten? They are:
what sentient beings possess;
and the same applies to the lands.
One contemplates that sentient beings are likewise understood to be fundamentally non-existent;
when the kalpa is consumed by fire, heaven and earth are destroyed, or they undergo transformation through the calamity of water;
once heaven and earth have been destroyed, they again reconstitute themselves.
Even the Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, is non-existent;
various modes of practice likewise have no fixed location;
as for the body of the Tathāgata, its meritorious virtues are immeasurable.
The teachings regarding the origins and endings of all phenomena differ in their respective meanings;
yet if one can make offerings to the Buddhas and Perfectly Awakened Ones, there is likewise no place of refuge.
These are the ten matters concerning what a bodhisattva possesses.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"What exists for sentient beings? The land has no fixed location;
Thus one examines all the marks and signs."
When the kalpa-fire burns and heaven and earth are destroyed, their reformation is likewise so.
The Buddha’s body has manifold aspects, yet the Tathāgata is immeasurable; he proclaims the Dharma in manifold aspects.

“There are ten matters regarding the gateways of liberation for Bodhisattvas. What are these ten? Their bodies pervade all worlds, manifesting various forms and countless appearances throughout the ten directions; they enter the single Buddha-land by means of all dharma-realms; they establish the multitudes of all sentient beings; they encompass the various Buddha-lands of the ten directions with the forms of Buddha-adornments; they spontaneously awaken to and reach all realms; in the space of a single thought-moment, they pervade all Buddha-lands; they manifest all Buddhas within a single land; they cause all Buddha-realms to enter into a single body; and they cause all Buddhas to manifest their spiritual powers for the sake of joyful play while entering into a single mind. These are the ten matters of the Bodhisattva’s gateways of liberation.”
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“His body pervades the Buddha-fields, manifesting manifold forms;
All dharmas enter into a single field, yet he establishes all worlds.”
Manifesting the Buddha-body throughout all worlds, he knows for himself that there is nowhere it does not pervade;
all dharmas enter into a single essence, and he opens the mind of all people.
"The supernatural powers of a Bodhisattva consist of ten matters."
What are these ten? They are:
consciousness of the places experienced in the past, clearly understanding the skillful means, the entering and exiting, and the advancing and retreating;

the divine ear that distinguishes without obstruction, hearing all speech and the destinations to which beings incline; and the ability to know the thoughts and mental activities of other sentient beings.
By means of the karma of the unconditioned divine eye, they observe all that has been traversed and circled through countless events and various distinctions;
by means of great supernormal powers, they move and transform, establishing inconceivable categories of sentient beings;
manifesting according to their fundamental natures, they cause them to enter the discipline and perceive infinite Buddha-worlds.
They manifest all manner of bodies, such that in the mere instant of generating the resolve for enlightenment, they can pervade immeasurable Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions;
they are also able to adorn and establish countless realms and locations;
furthermore, they display their complete physical forms without harboring self-conceit, being fully awakened to and proficient in transcendent wisdom.
In the bottomless realm, he attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, becoming the Most Perfectly Awakened One;
his mind was inconceivable, and he manifested teachings according to the fundamental and derivative dispositions of sentient beings.

These are the ten matters of universal meaning for Bodhisattvas; dwelling in these, a Bodhisattva attains the unsurpassed, true, and correct supernormal powers of a Tathāgata, masters the skillful means of liberation, and follows toward the transformations manifested by all Buddhas. They appear to instruct sentient beings throughout the ten directions, transforming their conduct until all meanings are fully perfected.
“There are ten matters through which a bodhisattva attains thorough penetration.
What are these ten? They are:

being able to teach and transform sentient beings according to the appropriate time; discerning their transgressions and merits; understanding the various differences in the circumstances experienced by the different classes of living beings; causing them to leave the household life; and bringing their minds to a state of profound stillness.”

"Entering into all obscurations and hindrances, he causes the various inverted practices of each and every sentient being to be eliminated, thereby attaining the adamantine noble wisdom that fully establishes what is to be established."
“His voice pervades everywhere and is inconceivable.

He instructs all Buddha-lands, bringing them to a clear understanding of skillful means; he causes all those attached to worldly things to universally enter into and practice the four immeasurable minds.”

They understand the places from which things arise, yet they also cognize that there is nowhere from which they arise; they have already eliminated all perceptions, sensations, objective spheres, and locations.

Furthermore, these bodhisattvas do not contemplate phenomena, nor do they fail to contemplate them; they regard the absence of conceptualization in all phenomena as a single purity, yet even this purity does not exist.

They clearly understand various types [of teachings], are proficient in diligent practice, and throughout incalculable eons proclaim the Way of the Sūtras; they thereby equally return to the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Way, eternally abiding in the Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva understands that sentient beings are fundamentally and entirely in a state of parinirvāṇa; they do not engage in household affairs nor perform any conditioned actions, knowing that those who perceive the existence of birth are following after inversion.

He thoroughly understands the principles of causes, conditions, retributions, and responses; he recognizes what is worthy of veneration and respect. By means of various skillful expedients—regarding the origins and ends of their conduct, and the places where they arise and cease—he discriminates and transforms all classes of sentient beings. He illuminates the principle of the gate of liberation that had been blocked, and he resolves their inverted views and erroneous matters.

He also knows the source of sensory desires, anger, and strife; he distinguishes between the karma of birth and death and the karma of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); furthermore, he understands both rebellious acts and non-rebellious matters, and he knows that which is worthy of reliance and that which is not.

He also clearly investigates and thoroughly understands the specific destinations reached—knowing those who regress and return again, knowing those who reach final certainty and their ultimate destination, and recognizing those who, after undergoing destruction, shall be restored to formation.

He also understands how to transform and guide others, knowing the faculties of sentient beings so that he may lead those to be transformed into entry into the discipline; through various skillful means, he instructs the masses without causing them to become confused or lose their bodhisattva practice.
Why is this so? O Son of the Buddha!
You should wish to know the reason why a bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Why is this? It is for the sake of transforming and enlightening sentient beings; having transformed them so that they follow the teachings of the Vinaya, his body does not grow weary.
This is because the Bodhisattva, for the sake of all beings, remains free from contention and clearly understands and discerns the twelve links of dependent origination.

"Furthermore, that bodhisattva has never relied upon the Buddha, nor does he give rise to a mind that takes refuge in the Buddha; he does not cling to the Dharma, nor does he give rise to a mind of craving for the Dharma; he does not cling to buddha-fields, nor does he give rise to a mind that relies on buddha-fields; he does not cling to persons, nor does he give rise to a mind that yearns for sentient beings; he does not perceive people, nor does he give rise to a mind that observes the multitudes."

They shall cause all practices to flourish and manifest, fulfill their aspirations, cultivate boundless compassion, not harbor thoughts of merely seeing the Buddha, and mindfully recollect the Dharma proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

"Having attained the seat of the Tathāgata and planted the roots of all virtues, he is neither distressed nor weary; his mind delights in perfect enlightenment and does not succumb to fatigue or indolence.

Furthermore, he makes offerings to the Tathāgatas according to the Dharma, and his mind becomes increasingly refined, moving and establishing an inconceivable majesty throughout the worlds of the Buddhas."

“Establishing contemplation upon the supreme Dharma-realm, he analyzes and discerns the teachings of various sutras; he knows the conditioned assemblies of sentient beings and recognizes the extent of their limitations and capacities; he understands the root and end of suffering from which it arises, and he knows that the exhaustion and cessation of all phenomena is the very basis for ending suffering.”

"If there are bodhisattvas who are able to see this, their practice will likewise be like a shadow or an echo; they will cast off all evils and sever them at their root, and will immediately resolve to rescue and deliver sentient beings."
That which they practice is entirely non-practice; this is called the Bodhisattva practice, wherein they study the words of all Buddhas.

Their minds are as firm and solid as Mount Sumeru; they awaken to and eliminate all inverted perceptions and conceptualizations, establishing the gates of universal wisdom and all supernormal powers. They attain perfect enlightenment and enter the Hall of Infinite and Boundless Wisdom—what is called the Hall of Wisdom is the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path—thereby delivering sentient beings drifting in the three realms and returning them to the exhaustion of their source.
These are the ten things through which a bodhisattva attains penetration; by abiding in these, a bodhisattva achieves the unsurpassed great wisdom of a Tathāgata.
There are ten matters regarding the liberation of a bodhisattva.

What are the ten? They are: transcending the source of all afflictions and sensual desires; escaping the path of false views and deviance to rescue others from the suffering of being shrouded by the five aggregates (*skandhas*); further saving the physical body, the four great elements, and the sense bases (*āyatanas*); surpassing the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to thereby attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); initiating all appropriate dharmas for the lands of all sentient beings; thereby attaining a transcendence of all Bodhisattva practices that is beyond measure; extolling all Bodhisattva practices; entering the stage of the Tathāgata through the absence of conceptualization; universally knowing the three periods of time with a single noble wisdom; and employing impartial supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) such that there is none who is not rescued. These are the ten matters of liberation for a Bodhisattva.
When a Bodhisattva dwells herein, they transform and enlighten sentient beings, leading them to the Unsurpassed.
At that time, he spoke in verse:
"By means of crossing over the dust of desire, Erroneous views, and the five aggregates,"
The various categories of the four great elements, and the afflictions of craving for the body;
transcending the stages of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, attaining the patience of non-arising;
extolling the lands of sentient beings—these are the immeasurable practices of the Bodhisattva.
The cultivation of the Bodhisattva leads to entry into the stage of the Tathāgata;
transcending all manifold delusions, his spirit penetrates and understands the three realms.
There are ten matters concerning the Bodhisattva’s grove.
What are these ten? They are:
delighting in birth and death without ever feeling revulsion;
taking pleasure in transforming sentient beings; and having a nature free from attachment.
Abiding in the realm of all conceptualizations, they receive and undertake the Great Practice.
They constantly delight in adorning and purifying the worlds of all Buddhas while dwelling in their own abodes.
Their resolve is set upon subduing and transforming all Māras, their consorts, and their palaces; because of these towers and pavilions, they revere the Dharma they preach.

Reflecting upon and understanding the meaning of the Dharma as it has been heard, and observing its ultimate destination—the six immeasurable supernormal powers, the practice of the four debts of gratitude, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—these constitute the garden of the bodhisattva; they are his own venerable father and the place where he dwells and roams.
The ten powers of the Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities—in short, all the Buddha-dharmas constitute the garden of the bodhisattva.
He never again thinks of other extraordinary dharmas; rather, all the transformations manifested by bodhisattvas and the delights they establish constitute the garden of the bodhisattva.

They turn the wheel of Dharma, observing the great discipline without self-conceit, acting with vigilance and never erring; all their aspirations never depart from perfect enlightenment, universally manifesting before the masses as a garden for bodhisattvas.
Yet their Dharma-body pervades all Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions, and the conduct of these bodhisattvas is like empty space; these are the ten pleasure gardens of the bodhisattvas.
“There are ten matters concerning the bodhisattva’s palace. What are these ten?
To delight in the bodhisattva’s palace, with a mind free from delusion;”
The chapters and phrases of the ten wholesome paths, the karmic deeds of merit and wisdom, and the diligent accumulation thereof constitute the palace of a bodhisattva;
by transforming the various classes of sentient beings within the desire realm and cultivating the four brahma-vihāras— loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy,
and equanimity— a bodhisattva, through these instructions, leads the multitudes of the form realm to be reborn in the celestial palaces of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
By means of this, the Bodhisattva extinguishes all defilements and impurities, reaching the heavens of the Formless and the Form Realms.
Upon arriving at their palaces, he instructs those who face great hardships and leads back those common folk who were not yet disciplined;
or at times, he is born within realms of mixed impurity, where the Bodhisattva joyfully accepts such places in order to rescue all sentient beings who are gripped by craving.

The Bodhisattva may take pleasure in manifesting within the inner palace among court ladies, men, and women; because he has performed identical meritorious deeds in past lives, he thereby instructs and transforms the various Emperors, Brahmās, Śakras, and the Four Heavenly Kings throughout the four quarters and four regions.

Through this, the Bodhisattva exhorts and transforms those who are violent and perilous, leading ordinary people to abandon their distracted minds and abide in all the practices of the Bodhisattvas. Because his thought of transformation is long-standing, he freely gallops forth, sporting in supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

The Bodhisattva is always single-mindedly in the liberation-gates, *samādhi*, and right reception (*samāpatti*); he delights in them by opening and transforming through wisdom. By means of the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) and the scriptures of the unsurpassed, truly correct Buddhas, he severs all obstructions, bestows all dharmas, and attains mastery. He becomes a sovereign of a kingdom, noble and majestic according to his own will.
The Bodhisattva delights in these ten powers of the Tathāgata as his dwelling place; these are the ten palaces of the Bodhisattva.
"The Bodhisattva has ten modes of contemplation.
What are these ten? They are:
taking delight in personally examining various chapters and verses;
observing the conduct one follows with a focused mind; and employing skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
Wherever they dwell, they immediately find themselves at the feet of all Buddhas, hearing and receiving the Dharma with a mind that aspires toward the ten directions;
their minds are universally pervasive as they revere all Bodhisattvas, manifesting infinite gateways through the transformations of their supernormal powers;

they transform sentient beings who are deluded in body and mind, and by upholding the single gateway of the samādhi of concentrated intent, they attain universal entry into all gateways of meditative concentration.
Abiding in all dhāraṇīs, they are able to receive and uphold everything they hear, never forgetting it;
they expound these essential summaries for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to rejoice;
delighting in eloquence, they can praise and extol a single verse with magnificent words for incalculable eons, and in their discourse on matters of teaching, their speech can never be interrupted.
Aiming for supreme perfect enlightenment, they manifest various physical forms and immeasurable categories of teachings for the sake of sentient beings;
they long to turn the wheel of Dharma to transform those of differing doctrines, causing them to inquire into and receive the teaching.
These are the ten contemplations of the Bodhisattva’s wandering.
“Bodhisattvas have ten kinds of adornment and purification. What are these ten?
Because their power is brilliant and clear, they are able to walk alone.”
Fearless and pure, there is none who can surpass him;
his meaning is resplendent, and the words and meanings he expounds cannot be obstructed or interrupted even if spoken for incalculable eons, for his Dharma is pure.
He is able to expound the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma; his scriptural discourse is harmonious and refined, never forgetting a single principle.
Their aspirations are subtle and wondrous, for all bodhisattvas do not abandon their vows;
their conduct is pure and bright as they proclaim the sublime and elegant teachings of the sages and saints, adorning the buddha-fields;
with a single voice they universally announce themselves throughout the ten directions as if in a single field, purifying their own domain while pervading all buddha-lands.

He causes the Way to arise like clouds and rains the nectar of the Dharma, establishing the True Teaching to eliminate all conditioned delusions and the conduct of restlessness; he is without pride and is pure.

Manifesting the bodies of sentient beings through his single essence, he instructs and trains them all with diligent perseverance, tirelessly seeking all forms of penetrating and swift wisdom throughout the day and night, and displaying the images of the countless powers and fearlessnesses.
These are the ten purities of a Bodhisattva.
When a bodhisattva abides in this, they universally attain the adorned purity of all Buddhas.
There are ten matters by which the mind of a bodhisattva remains unmoved. What are these ten?
They give all that they possess without attachment; in their giving, they are entirely pure and their minds remain unmoved.
They contemplate and clearly examine the profound Dharma of the Buddhas, honoring and revering them, serving and taking refuge in them with boundless single-minded devotion.

They maintain thoughts of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, never harboring anger or resentment, and never abandoning any class of beings—whether crawling insects, breathing creatures, or human beings.
He sought all Buddha-dharmas without ever becoming weary or negligent; all sentient beings are beyond calculation.
He practiced the deeds of a bodhisattva for incalculable eons, neither drawing near nor remaining distant, never regressing in his bodhisattva conduct, being without obstruction or interruption.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva’s original resolve of faith and whatever practices he cultivated were immeasurably pure.
Those who are pure are free from defilement and possess clear understanding; they practice with earnest diligence and pay reverent homage to all Buddhas.
They cast off the body to which they were attached and, having no further longing for worldly pleasures, become their companions; they attain great exultation and boundless joy.
Taking profound faith as their guide, they take refuge in omniscience; responding to its scriptural verses, they ultimately achieve the teachings of all Bodhisattvas.
In practicing the instructions of training, one does not slander or disparage what has been heard and believed; despite vexations and shifting karmic conditions, the mind remains unmoved.
These are the ten matters by which the bodhisattva’s mind is unmoved.
Being able to abide in this, one immediately attains the various supernormal powers and sagely wisdom.
There are ten things by which a bodhisattva’s mind does not abandon anything. What are these ten?
Having attained the path of the supreme, most correct enlightenment of all Buddhas, it is called "not abandoning.
It teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to follow the Dharma and Vinaya without leaving anyone behind;
it accords with the teachings of all Buddhas, never failing in its instruction and admonition.
They rely upon and take refuge in all virtuous friends without ever straying from them;
they visit all Buddha-lands, prostrating and bowing before the Tathāgatas, the Truly Realized Ones, never abandoning the rules of propriety;
they constantly seek all dharmas of merit and never abandon the Mahāyāna.
May I encounter the era of a Buddha and purely cultivate the Brahma-faring;
may I uphold and protect the prohibitive precepts, never violating them;
and may I follow all bodhisattvas in diligently practicing the path and its tasks, never becoming indolent or negligent.
To seek and aspire to the meaning of the Tathāgata’s instructions, upholding them at all times and receiving them through consultation without forgetting;
to practice the fundamental vows and deeds of all bodhisattvas, contemplating and reflecting upon them all to penetrate the teachings of all Buddhas—
these are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva’s mind never abandons [the path].
"The Bodhisattva’s wisdom of contemplation has ten aspects.
What are these ten? They are:
contemplating all phenomena; discerning the chapters and phrases; and expounding them according to the occasion."
He examines the root of all virtues throughout the three periods of time and expounds the Dharma accordingly;
he observes the fundamental limits of the practices of all bodhisattvas and brings them to transformation and enlightenment;
and he gazes upon the various Dharma-gates to penetrate their origins.
They also behold the deeds established by all Buddhas;
they contemplate the various dhāraṇīs and take refuge in them through the gateways of wisdom;
and with clear intelligence, they universally observe the world.
They behold all dharma-realms and enter them through compliant wisdom;
they survey the ten directions with inconceivable wisdom;
they perceive the wisdom of all Buddhas, abiding in a thorough understanding of the infinite, holy brilliance of the worlds.
This is the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the ten wisdoms.
There are ten matters regarding the Bodhisattva’s exposition of the Dharma. What are these ten?
They proclaim that all phenomena arise from conditions;
they are called the "all-meaning" because they cause all things to converge therein through the accumulation of resolute conduct;
and they expound that all that exists is like an illusion or a magical transformation.
Furthermore, he proclaims that all dharmas are likewise fundamentally empty;
in his exegesis of the various sutras, the discourse is vast and uninterrupted, without limit or bottom;
and regarding all karmic actions, there is complete non-attachment.
Furthermore, it is said that all dharmas are as firm as a vajra, and all meanings are what the Tathāgata has expounded;
it is also said that all karmic actions are tranquil and serene;
and it is further proclaimed that all dharmas are entirely without arising.
To expound that all dharmas are fundamentally and uniformly pure, and to teach that they are not formed through combination—
this constitutes the ten matters for a bodhisattva’s exposition of the Dharma.
There are ten matters for the purity of a bodhisattva.
What are these ten?
Their nature is fundamentally pure and free from defilement;
they eliminate the knots of doubt and hesitation, rendering them clear and bright.
He has cast aside all hesitation and the sixty-two views; he cultivates propriety through his conduct and majestic demeanor;
he delights in universal wisdom, the various supernormal powers, and swift intelligence; his analytical eloquence is lofty and pure;
and he is courageous and radiant, possessing the four fearlessnesses.
Cultivating the bodhisattva practices, all their dwellings and travels are entirely without flaw;
they exhort all bodhisattvas to cultivate every aspiration;
their conduct is free from defilement, possessing the thirty-two marks of a hundred meritorious virtues.
The deeds of a Mahāsattva consist in seeking the unsurpassed, truly correct path;
they take refuge in the pure dharmas and adorn and purify the fundamental purity of all virtues.
These are the ten purities of a Bodhisattva.
When a bodhisattva dwells herein, they attain the unsurpassed purity of all Buddhas.

There are ten matters that constitute the seal of a bodhisattva; by means of this seal, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with bodhisattva wisdom, swiftly accomplishing the unsurpassed, truly correct path and becoming a Most Perfectly Awakened One.
What are the ten?

"The Bodhisattva fully knows that all things are suffering—suffering upon suffering, affliction upon affliction, the suffering of separation from what is loved, and the suffering of encountering what is hated."
"Though encountering such hardships, he diligently sought the Buddha-dharma; his mind remained unshaken, nor did he abandon it.

In the conduct of a Bodhisattva, one does not fear, does not dread, and harbors no trepidation; one does not forsake the original vow, does not neglect great wisdom, and is thoroughly proficient in all things, with a mind that never deviates from the essentials of the Buddha-way."

“Foolish ordinary people, out of their own afflictions and attachments to loved ones, cultivate the roots of unwholesomeness; they revile the Bodhisattva, insult and slight him, uttering coarse and violent words, and even pelt him with tiles and stones or strike him with swords and staves. It is because the Bodhisattva encounters such things that he seeks the Buddha-dharma, never becoming weary of or abandoning the Bodhisattva practice.”
“Constantly practicing patience and harboring much benevolence and harmony, they diligently practice patience in accordance with the teachings of the sūtras and fulfill right conduct.

Furthermore, these bodhisattvas proclaim the profound and wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas; they abide in omniscience and cause it to enter their own wisdom, fully manifesting all that is born, and transforming all people so that they joyfully love the Dharma.”
Furthermore, that bodhisattva contemplates the wisdom of their own essence, attains a nature of benevolence and harmony, and gives rise to the mind of universal wisdom, thinking:
"I shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of Buddhahood and become a Most Perfectly Awakened One."

"Observing sentient beings racing and circling through the hardships of the five destinies, suffering from grief, distress, and resentment, he causes them to give rise to the mind of enlightenment, to be joyful and glad, to increase their profound faith, to be thus delighted, and to become firm in their diligent exertion."
Furthermore, that bodhisattva enters into the boundless wisdom of the Tathāgata without overstepping its limits.
The holy brilliance of the Tathāgata is beyond measure, and the teachings proclaimed by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are likewise without limit or bottom.
Without limiting himself to the Buddha’s wisdom, he does not give rise to increase or decrease regarding any written words; he discerns all meanings and does not transgress the Buddha’s teachings.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva loves and delights in the unsurpassed, true, and correct path; he takes joy in profound meanings and attains subtle, infinite wisdom.

Because they were devoted to the unsurpassed [enlightenment] with such earnestness and longing, never departing from it, no hosts of Māras, nor their retinues, nor any heterodox teachers, nor any external adversaries, dared to stand before them; they never abandoned the mind of omniscience.
The benefits brought about by the practices of a bodhisattva are such that they never turn back.

Furthermore, when these bodhisattvas practice the Way, they are without fear or dread and do not cherish their own bodies or lives. They give rise to the mind of supernormal wisdom (*abhijñā*), taking the cultivation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) as their primary goal; they are all illuminated by the radiance of the Buddhas, never abandoning the principles of the Way and never distancing themselves from virtuous friends.

Furthermore, when that bodhisattva sees sons of good family or daughters of good family who are resolved to study the Mahāyāna, he causes them to practice diligently and yearn for all Buddha-dharmas; he exhorts them to establish the roots of virtue and receive all-knowledge, never ceasing or abandoning this effort.

Furthermore, wherever that bodhisattva dwells and moves among sentient beings with an impartial mind, he likewise employs even and upright wisdom to proclaim the sutras for all living beings, leading them universally to the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, advancing toward non-retrogression, and giving rise to great compassion.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva reckons all Buddhas of the past, future, and present as one; he offers up all roots of virtue to the Buddhas without ever interrupting his contemplation of their sagely wisdom.
These are the ten seals of a bodhisattva.
By means of these seals, one swiftly achieves perfect enlightenment and seals the unsurpassed Dharma.
"The light of a bodhisattva’s wisdom has ten aspects."
What are these ten?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva shall inevitably attain and perfect the unsurpassed, right, and true path, illuminating all things with the Buddha-way;
they shall constantly behold all Buddhas and their equal, perfect enlightenment.
They thoroughly understand the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings;
they clearly recognize all categories of the Dharma in the various sutras;
they give rise to the bodhicitta and constantly associate with virtuous friends.
Distinguishing the roots of the manifold virtues accumulated;
understanding that which is sealed by wisdom, constantly beholding all Buddhas;
and clearly comprehending how to enlighten and transform the various classes of sentient beings.
Establishing oneself in the stage of the Tathāgata, proclaiming the hall of the path of inconceivable Dharma-gates;
understanding all Buddhas and establishing them according to the occasion, universally being able to fully possess all the *pāramitās*;
this is the radiance of the ten wisdoms of the Bodhisattva.
“Bodhisattvas have ten practices for engaging with immeasurable sentient beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
What are these ten? In this regard, the bodhisattva cultivates the practice of the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*); until all vows are fulfilled, they will never take final realization.”
"Furthermore, that bodhisattva plants the roots of all virtues and resolves to encourage and assist the entire dharma-realm, remaining unattached to any phenomena.
Moreover, when that bodhisattva practices the path, they observe all actions as being like illusions and transformations; all dharmas are tranquil and they remain undeluded;
the Buddhas are likewise so."

Furthermore, that bodhisattva removes the attachments of delusive conceptualization from all sentient beings; throughout incalculable eons, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices and fulfill their great vows without giving rise to weariness or indolence.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva practices all dharmas with complete non-attachment; all dharmas are naturally quiescent and yet not extinguished, for he must fully master the teachings of omniscience.

"Furthermore, that bodhisattva understands all deluded thoughts as well as the absence of conceptualization and vows, proclaiming the practice of true reality from its fundamental beginning through its ultimate end over incalculable eons.

Moreover, that bodhisattva realizes that all phenomena are entirely non-existent; yet, although they understand this emptiness and nothingness, they do not abandon the practice of the Way, but continue to seek all Buddha-dharmas."

"Furthermore, at the very moment that bodhisattva resolves his mind, he universally enters the triple world and also fully understands the meaning of the three periods of time. That which his mind penetrates is utterly detached from the intermediate states, such that there is nothing it does not comprehend."

Furthermore, for the sake of even a single person, that bodhisattva remains within the perils of birth and death, practicing the bodhisattva dharma for incalculable kalpas and establishing their resolve in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Just as they endure all weariness and fatigue for the sake of one person, so too do they do so for the sake of all sentient beings;
they ultimately establish them in the Great Way (*mahāmārga*) without slackening or abandoning it out of weariness, even when facing the sufferings of the future.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva, fully equipped with the bodhisattva practices, does not seek to quickly attain unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment.
For the sake of all beings, he circulates within the realm of afflictions to transform and benefit countless sentient beings, establishing them in the Buddha-way.
These are the ten immeasurable practices of a bodhisattva.
By abiding in these, a bodhisattva swiftly attains perfect enlightenment.
There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva’s mind is not timid or weak as they resolve upon the path of enlightenment.
What are the ten? "The Bodhisattva reflects:
'All Māras and the various celestial beings of Māra shall be seen to be subdued; my mind shall not be timid or weak.'"
"I shall subdue all those of external and heterodox paths by means of the True Dharma; my body shall bring joy to the realms of all sentient beings, and my mind shall not be weak or inferior.
Thus, he fulfills all the perfections (pāramitās) and becomes fully endowed with the entire Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
"For the sake of sentient beings, one accumulates and gathers the perfections of merit.
This unsurpassed, right, and true path requires great diligence; although it is difficult to accomplish, it is nonetheless a great undertaking."

The Bodhisattva’s practice of the mind does not involve using timidity or weakness to transform the realms of all sentient beings; rather, he accords with and follows the discipline, acting as a venerable guide and instructor.

Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, where physical forms vary and the styles of dress are of countless kinds, the Bodhisattva enters among them according to what they delight in, and therein achieves supreme perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva spontaneously reflects:

"All that I have ever studied and cultivated in the practice of a bodhisattva has issued from within myself. Should anyone come to seek my hands, feet, ears, nose, flesh, bones, marrow, wife, children, sons, daughters, elephants, horses, carriages, kingdoms, cities, towns, kinsmen, or servants, I am able to give them all, never opposing the wishes of others."
Seeing that the multitude has come seeking something, in the very moment he gives rise to the thought of awakening, he allows them to have whatever they desire without feeling weariness or aversion.

Desiring to bring peace to all sentient beings, he harbors compassion for them; having given what is to be given, he harbors no expectations. With great pity as his foremost principle, he returns to infinite loving-kindness and does not consider himself timid.
Furthermore, as that Bodhisattva practices his conduct,

all those within the triple world, the teachings of all Buddhas, the buddha-fields of sentient beings, the various worlds of all living creatures, the realm of empty space, and the sounds of all phenomena are entirely quiescent, tending toward and entering into parinirvāṇa.

"All dharmas proceed gradually; in the space of a single thought-moment, one realizes their equality and responds accordingly. By discerning and understanding them, one attains supreme perfect enlightenment.
All things are directed toward analogies, aided by spiritual powers, and realized through practice. One maintains neither thought nor non-thought, ensuring no differentiation arises."

Without various modes of practice, one regulates them so that there is no accumulation of wealth or karma, and no creation of causal conditions; one does not create distinctions, nor is there non-distinction. Through the action of countless dharmas, one does not transgress;

by means of non-dual wisdom, one clearly understands all dualities; by means of signless wisdom, one dissolves all conceptualizations; by means of thought-free wisdom, one recognizes all thoughts; by means of non-various wisdom, one clearly understands the various; by means of limitless knowledge, one clarifies all limited insights; by means of supramundane wisdom, one clearly understands all worldly activities; and by means of the holy light of the world, one opens and transforms the darkness and obstructions of the various regions.
Possessing the wisdom of no-past, they are able to discern all things of the past;
returning to the ground of non-personality, they clearly recognize the realms of all sentient beings.

Having emerged from all attachments, they traverse the accumulation of all practices performed; they clearly recognize all ultimate wisdoms, understanding that which is fully developed and understanding that which is not yet fully developed.

Using pure and refined wisdom to resolve worldly afflictions, one discerns and knows the inexhaustible ultimate limit; by transforming all that is exhausted and clearly comprehending the dharma-realm, this constitutes the foremost wisdom.
His body manifests universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, entering into countless sounds and verbal teachings, and from that infinity, he proclaims instruction and admonition.
With a single wisdom of spontaneity, he enters into non-spontaneity; with a single noble and enlightened practice, he elaborates upon what has been cultivated and manifests various modes of conduct.
All dharmas are entirely unattainable; one who understands this meaning reaches the ultimate and manifests transformations.

Manifesting transformations to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment, and attaining great wisdom to display great supernormal powers, one moves all beings through universal knowledge and brings them to practice and transformation—this is to be without cowardice.
These are the ten forms of fearlessness of a bodhisattva.
There are ten matters in which the mind of a bodhisattva is like a great mountain. What are these ten?
"Thereupon, the bodhisattva constantly cultivates diligence, focusing his mind on contemplating the various supernormal powers and swift wisdom.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva contemplates that all phenomena are fundamentally pure like space, yet understands that all phenomena arise entirely from inversion."
Having cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva for incalculable eons, they have aroused that resolve and brought to full abundance all pure and white dharmas;
they understand the meaning of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable wisdom and are thus able to practice and uphold all pure and white dharmas.
"The Bodhisattva brings forth the path of the various Buddha-sūtras, which is impartial, pure, and harmonious, and accords with virtuous friends.
Regarding the cause for generating the mind of enlightenment, one should harbor no doubts or fetters;
one should revere the sūtras and not entertain divergent thoughts."

Regarding other karmic actions, one should simply be reverent, diligent, humble, and submissive; one should give away all that one possesses without stinginess, gradually drawing near to the Way and its teachings.
"The Bodhisattva takes pity on all sentient beings and endures the afflictions of various anxieties and sufferings."

Even if one encounters calamities that endanger the body, hardships that threaten life, verbal abuse and humiliation, or the infliction of blades and staves upon the person, one is able to endure them all; harboring no resentment or distress, with a concentrated mind undisturbed, one gives rise to no anger or hatred.

Conceiving boundless compassion, they take pity upon all living beings; donning the great armor of virtue, they do not retreat, nor do they abandon the resolve for enlightenment, but instead apply themselves with ever-increasing earnestness.
They give rise to boundless pity, and that pity becomes ever more expansive.
Why is this? Sons of the Buddha,
you should know that all dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas arise through causes and conditions.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfectly Endowed with Protective Practice, thoroughly understands all dharmas; he takes patience, gentleness, and harmony as his noble station.
“When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates great merit, his majestic spiritual power is most sublime.”
If he is in the heavens, he is the most honored among the devas;
if he is in the world, his status is high among men. His countenance is upright and handsome, his power is supreme, and his retinue is mighty and flourishing; whatever he desires is at his command.
If he becomes a sovereign, he belongs to an infinitely noble lineage, his meritorious achievements are boundless, and his wisdom is vast and far-reaching.
"He does not delight in sensual desires nor seek wealth; he exercises mastery over his retinue and finds peace therein.

He loves only the Dharma—rejoicing in the Dharma, delighting in the Dharma, yearning for the Dharma, and seeking the Dharma. He takes the Dharma as his dwelling, finds protection through the Dharma, takes refuge in the Dharma, and attains liberation through the Dharma. He constantly seeks the meaning of the Dharma, finds joy in the Dharma, and contemplates the sutras."
By means of such analogies, one attains *an-shu* (summer retreat) and does not follow the teachings of Māra.

Why is this? Because if a bodhisattva, at the very moment of generating the aspiration, eliminates the realm of sentient beings, the self, and the realm of Māra, causing them to abide in the domain of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, with such diligence, that bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path for incalculable eons, knowing within himself:
'Today I have attained the study of the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way; I am neither terrified, nor afraid, nor do I harbor any dread.'"

Having practiced the bodhisattva conduct and having accomplished such practice, I shall now attain the path of supreme perfect enlightenment; furthermore, throughout incalculable eons in future ages, I shall personally know and witness the practice of the bodhisattva conduct.

"Furthermore, seeing that those of other paths are difficult to transform and difficult to heal, lacking a sense of reciprocity and ignorant of gratitude, he dons the armor of virtue in order to instruct this multitude. He wanders among sentient beings with mastery; seeing those who are wicked and evil, he does not grow weary of them, nor does he turn back out of hatred for such people or because of worldly desires."
Furthermore, that bodhisattva does not rely on others, but resolves upon the Great Vehicle path, thinking:
"I shall gather the practices of a bodhisattva through this conduct; I alone shall accomplish them, without needing anyone else."

"In future kalpas, they shall uphold the dharma of the bodhisattvas; through their own aspirations and practices, they shall fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, giving rise to a mind that dwells upon the unsurpassed Great Way.
Thus, they take sole delight in transforming sentient beings and rejoice in the transformation of sentient beings;
they believe in the bodhisattva practice, purifying their own will and nature, and are likewise able to purify the nature and conduct of others.
He understands profound realms and further discerns the lands of others, perceiving the Buddhas of the past, future, and present as a single unified realm.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva does not perceive any dharmas, nor does he behold the practices of any bodhisattvas; he does not contemplate the complete meaning of all *kai-shi* (bodhisattvas), nor does he perceive the meaning of teaching sentient beings. He does not examine the honoring of the Buddha-dharmas, nor does he perceive those who have attained, are attaining, or will attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of enlightenment. Furthermore, he does not perceive the proclamation of the Way of the Sūtras, nor does he perceive any who cannot speak it, nor any who preach it.
"Do Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas not retreat from the Great Way?
Why is this? Son of the Buddha, you should know:"
This is the birth of a bodhisattva, who, seeking all dharmas, achieves supreme perfect enlightenment.

Practicing all dharmas without following inverted views, they apply themselves with even greater diligence to cultivate the roots of virtue; their conduct is pure, and they are fully endowed with wisdom.

In the mere instant of a single thought of awakening, their meritorious achievements and renowned virtue increase daily; they are neither terrified, nor fearful, nor do they harbor anxiety, and thus they swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed, true, and right path.
These are the ten matters by which the mind is like a great mountain.
There are ten matters by which the wisdom of a bodhisattva is like the rivers and seas, leading them into the unsurpassed path. What are these ten?
“Entering the immeasurable realms of sentient beings.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
The Bodhisattva universally traverses the realms of the Buddhas of the ten directions; entering the holy chamber through the great palace, he practices the state of non-conceptualization.”
Furthermore, that bodhisattva cultivates and purifies the infinite realms of all space, roaming through the void without obstruction.
The ten directions are tranquil, like water and like a net, through universal equality.
"Furthermore, that bodhisattva skillfully enters the dharma-realm and wanders in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
That which he enters is uninterrupted, yet he does not conceive of it as permanent;
that which he enters is boundless, being neither created nor extinguished."
He clearly understands that which he enters, reaching everywhere without exception.

Furthermore, he accumulates the roots of merit for himself by taking refuge in the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Bodhisattvas, Dharma Masters, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all ordinary beings of the past, future, and present; he likewise establishes roots of merit within them.
He further exhorted the multitude:

"By means of these roots of virtue, when the Buddhas of the past, future, and present—those who have already attained, are now attaining, or will hereafter attain perfect enlightenment—proclaim the Way of the Sūtras—those who have already spoken, are now speaking, or will hereafter speak—the various classes of sentient beings who receive and accept the Dharma—those who have already realized the Ultimate Way, those who desire to turn toward the Way, or those who are now attaining the Way—may they all bring about the transformation and guidance of sentient beings."
These roots of virtue, combined with these manifold merits, encourage and assist all beings without seeking any recompense; even in this present life, they do not give rise to weariness or fatigue.
Furthermore, as each thought arises, that Bodhisattva enters the past, traversing incalculable eons; in each eon, they behold ten billion Buddhas.
Throughout countless, immeasurable, and inconceivable hundreds of thousands of billions of eons, what they perceive and see is beyond all analogy.
Entering the flourishing world of Buddhas, he transcends all metaphors; he also beholds the assemblies and bodhimaṇḍas of all Buddhas as they preach the Dharma for bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
He transforms and enlightens sentient beings, yet regarding the establishment of their lifespans—whether short or long—he abides nowhere.
The number of people delivered and saved during a single eon is such that it cannot be measured or limited across all eons.

If there is a time within an eon when no Buddha appears in the world, the Bodhisattva, knowing this, should cultivate and establish the roots of great virtue within that eon; even though there is no one to exhort them or open the way to the Dharma, they shall nevertheless preach and explain it.

Beholding the pure and virtuous roots of the Buddhas of the past and future, they enter immeasurable eons to contemplate their meaning without ever feeling weary or satisfied, thus entering the eons of the past.
Furthermore, those Bodhisattvas enter into the future, contemplating and observing as they traverse the immeasurable number of eons yet to come:
"In which eon shall there be a Perfectly Awakened One?"
When will there be no Buddhas?
In which kalpa will a Buddha appear in the world?
What is the number of Tathāgatas and Arhats?
What is his name? From which buddha-field does he emerge?
What is the name of that realm? How does he transform and deliver beings? Which sentient beings does he delight? And what is the length of his lifespan?
He foresees immeasurable and incalculable eons without weariness or fatigue.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva enters into the present, observing the worlds of the ten directions, proclaiming the boundless buddha-fields, distinguishing their orientations, and calculating their distances and proportions.
The Buddhas contemplate and examine their origins and ends, thereby attaining the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Way.
They proceed beneath the Bodhi tree, seek out kusha grass, spread it upon the ground, sit beneath the tree, and subdue the hosts of Māra.

He arises and enters cities and towns, ascends to the heavens, extensively expounds the meaning of the sutras, turns the wheel of Dharma, instructs sentient beings, manifests the performance of Buddha-works, and attains supreme perfect enlightenment.
Encouraged and assisted by Śakra and Brahmā, they relinquished their lifespans until reaching the realm of nirvana without remainder, attaining parinirvāṇa.

They disseminated the Way of the sutras, protected the teachings and instructions, caused the transformation of the Dharma to flourish, adorned monasteries and temples, made offerings to sacred images, and cultivated stūpas and shrines.

Mindfully recollecting all Buddha-lands, they resolve their minds one by one to enter the countless Buddha-fields of the ten directions; they universally observe sentient beings, seeing all Buddhas therein, and listen to the Dharma being preached, receiving, chanting, reciting, and studying it, holding it within their hearts.

Choosing one's aspirations and conduct ensures that both advancement and retreat are beneficial; reaching throughout the ten directions, all shall take refuge in the Buddhas and never forget the Buddha-dharma. Why is this so?
They realize that all phenomena are merely like dreams.
For this reason, they make offerings to the Tathāgata wherever he may be.

In every place where they are born, they are always by the side of a Buddha; they personally see themselves honoring and revering the Tathāgata, yet they do not crave their own bodies nor are they attached to the Tathāgata. They do not rely upon the world, the assemblies, or the sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), nor do they harbor any desire to hear the scriptures.

They do not become weary or satisfied with seeing the Buddhas present before them; likewise, they travel to those Buddha-fields to see the Buddhas of the ten directions without harboring any expectations.
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas have made offerings to and served the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, for incalculable eons.

In each and every kalpa, they serve and take refuge in infinite Tathāgatas; from their initial birth until their final passing, they never cease their offerings throughout the three periods of time. They provide sustenance to the Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, retinues, and assemblies, continuing these offerings until the Tathāgatas enter parinirvāṇa.
After their parinirvāṇa, they continue to revere and honor their relics until the very end of time.
One gives away all that one possesses to satisfy the realms of all sentient beings.

This giving from a mind of renunciation is inconceivable; yet one does not contemplate a reward, nor does one perceive a recipient who receives anything. It is solely out of compassion that one provides for them.
They pay homage to all Buddhas and bestow gifts upon all sentient beings without weariness; in this manner they take refuge in the Buddhas.

Throughout incalculable kalpas, they transform and guide sentient beings, upholding the teachings of the Dharma and proclaiming the Way of the sutras, leading and encouraging all beings to give rise to the unsurpassed, right, and true mind of enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Sons of the Buddha!

You should know that Bodhisattvas mutually accomplish one another through the precepts, prohibitions, instructions, and exhortations, as well as the practice of the Way and the pure Dharma. They transform others according to the Vinaya, and the Bodhisattva’s equanimity arises from these."
Aspiring to the various *dhāraṇī* gates of the Bodhisattvas, they constantly behold the Buddhas, the infinite Great Sages.
Seeking out Dharma masters, they pay them respectful homage, inquiring after and receiving the teachings, reciting and chanting them without ever becoming weary or negligent.
Protecting and sustaining all sentient beings, he brings his training to ultimate completion; he proclaims the Way of the Sūtras for the sake of the multitudes, transforming infinite assemblies.

Having set out upon the path of unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment, he establishes himself in non-retrogression, purifies all Buddha-dharmas, and contemplates universal wisdom and the meaning of all supernormal knowledges. He cultivates all Buddha-dharmas, fully perfecting all practices throughout incalculable eons.
These are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva, like the ocean, achieves supreme perfect enlightenment.
*Dushi pin jing*, Scroll II; *Dushi pin jing*, Scroll III.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Bodhisattva Samantabuddhi again asked Samantabhadra: "How is it that the practices and deeds of a bodhisattva are as luminous as the night?"
What is meant by having a mind like a vajra and being resolved upon the armor of the Mahāyāna?
What is meant by the Mahāyāna?
And what is meant by being able to fully manifest great diligent cultivation?
What is meant by indestructible faith?
What is meant by receiving the prediction of enlightenment?
What is meant by encouraging the roots of virtue?
What is meant by "entering the noble state"?
What is meant by "arousing a mind that is vast and immeasurable within"?
And what is meant by the "Bodhisattva-piṭaka"?
What is meant by "guarding and protecting"?
What is meant by "sovereignty"?
What is meant by "moving and inspiring"?
What is meant by "various transformations"?
What is meant by "adorned and purified lands"?
And what is meant by "the Dharma according to the times"?
What is meant by transformation of the body?
What is meant by transformation through aspiration?
What is meant by transformation through emanation?
What is meant by the transformation of wisdom?
What is meant by the transformation of supernormal powers?
What is meant by the transformation of the bases of psychic power?
What are called the fluctuations of the powers?
What are called amusements?
What are called spheres of experience?
What are called the ten powers?
What are called the fearlessnesses?
And what are called the unique qualities of the Buddhas?
"What is meant by 'karma,' and what is meant by the 'body of a bodhisattva'?
Samantabhadra replied:
“Excellent, excellent! You have asked this matter most skillfully, for it brings enlightenment to all and bestows benefit upon those to come.

That which you have now asked is like the solar palace illuminating the world; it is like the moon rising at night; it is like entering the great ocean to gather various precious pearls; it is like a physician compounding medicine; it is like a hungry person seeking food; it is like one who is thirsty desiring to drink.”
"All you who have gathered here!
Listen attentively, listen attentively. They all said:
"I shall receive your instruction," [the king] replied. Samantabhadra said:
"There are ten things by which a bodhisattva is as clearly manifest as the night."
What are the ten? "His intention pervades countless Buddha-fields, and his mind is like empty space; he beholds all Tathāgatas and bows his head in refuge.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s stride is as it was at the first watch of the night when he was about to achieve perfect enlightenment."

Furthermore, that bodhisattva has heard the sūtras from immeasurable Buddhas; having received, upheld, recited, and contemplated them with single-minded focus, his understanding becomes vast and expansive, increasing ever further, and his mind pervades the boundless ten directions.
"Furthermore, that bodhisattva, without ever passing away from this buddha-field, manifests his body by being born in other directions, always knowing the Buddha-dharma and never forgetting it."

Furthermore, that bodhisattva understands all dharmas through a single dharma-practice, gradually proclaiming the Way of the sutras for the multitude, and entering into the single meaning by means of all meanings.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva can eliminate and also understand the various defilements; he can extinguish all cravings and also know when desire is flourishing and when it has been removed.

His actions are steadfast as he cultivates the bodhisattva practices, never producing false realizations regarding the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), and his perfections (*pāramitā*) are supreme and foremost.

Abiding in the fundamental limit, they clearly understand the study of the truths; through skillful means and expedients, they fulfill their original vows; their practice reaches ultimate completion, and their bodies never grow weary.

"Furthermore, that bodhisattva’s mind enters into all perceptions; regarding what is possible and what is impossible, he nevertheless expounds upon the matters of the possible and the impossible. He acts without any [self-]doing, and while practicing, he remains free from conceptualization as he transforms and enlightens sentient beings."

Furthermore, that bodhisattva, through a single spontaneous understanding, realizes that all phenomena are without spontaneity and without plurality; they are neither few, nor can they be named or measured; they are without form and without marks.
If one cannot even attain a single [dharma], how much less so many? The Bodhisattva clearly understands all these dharmas:

the dharmas of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and ordinary persons; wholesome and unwholesome dharmas; worldly dharmas and world-transcending dharmas; dharmas of transgression and dharmas without transgression; with outflows and without outflows; conditioned and unconditioned.

"Furthermore, that bodhisattva—whether it be the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones who have attained the Way, those who have not attained the Way, or sentient beings who lack the Dharma—does not abandon their vows, but transforms and enlightens sentient beings, thoroughly understanding all dharmas."

Why is this? Because he fully knows the causes and conditions of the thoughts and actions of others and the masses; furthermore, he clearly discerns them and provides instruction and admonition so that all people may reach nirvana, their aspirations being completely fulfilled.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva clearly understands and perceives the mental inclinations of sentient beings; comprehending their destinies, he employs skillful means to manifest himself according to the time, preaching the Dharma and demonstrating the discipline, never departing from the true and correct, nor following what is inverted.

The Bodhisattva clearly understands that all phenomena abide equally throughout the three periods of time; they are fundamentally non-existent and immovable, established at the ultimate limit (*koṭi*).

He does not perceive sentient beings, nor does he see any who might be transformed, for there is neither transformation nor non-transformation; there is no following of precepts or teachings, nor is there any practitioner.

The dharmas toward which they turn through discrimination cannot be apprehended; yet for those who arise and those who cease, their vows are never in vain, and they remain forever unattached to any dharma.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva beholds countless Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; at each and every Tathāgata’s teaching, he hears the sūtras spoken and immediately receives and upholds them. Although the practices performed are manifold with various names and different intentions, throughout those kalpas—discerning the beginning and end of each individual kalpa down to incalculable kalpas—he hears everything and recognizes it all, never forgetting or becoming confused. Regarding the inconceivable teachings of all such Tathāgatas, he hears them all and receives and upholds them without any duality.

By the power of their own practice and vows, they shall transcend all others, transforming and enlightening sentient beings so that they may all fully accomplish the path of unsurpassed, true, and most correct awakening; having fulfilled their vows, they will thoroughly understand the dharma-realm.
This is called the tenth practice of the bodhisattvas’ conduct, which is like the manifestation of light in the night.
There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva’s mind is like a diamond and their resolve is armored in the Great Vehicle.
What are these ten?

"Not abiding here, nor having any limit, the bodhisattva resolves his mind to understand all dharmas, attaining unimpeded penetration regarding the three periods of time; this is what it means for the mind to be like a vajra and to don the armor of great virtue."
Each and every pore, beyond measure or calculation, is universally able to adorn all; how much more so for sentient beings?
From the armor of virtue of all Bodhisattvas throughout the entire Dharma-realm, these words issue forth spontaneously:
"I shall bring all sentient beings to extinction [of suffering] and lead them to the path of unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment."
"Furthermore, the Buddha-worlds are bottomless and boundless, beyond measure or limit.
The bodhisattvas make such vows:
'I shall purify the unsurpassed, right, and true [Dharma] within all Buddha-worlds.'"
For this reason, he purifies all Buddha-lands.

Furthermore, as all sentient beings are bottomless, boundless, limitless, and infinite, if there is a bodhisattva who exhorts them toward these roots of virtue on such a vast scale, illuminating for all sentient beings the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are without limit, and the roots of virtue planted by the bodhisattvas are likewise so.
They encourage sentient beings to constantly behold the Buddhas, and further enable them to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, becoming the most perfectly awakened ones.

"If there is a bodhisattva who, upon seeing the Buddhas and hearing them preach the sutras, feels joy in their heart; who does not rely on a self and does not cling to the Tathāgata; who is neither near to the body of the Tathāgata nor far from it; who is neither existent nor non-existent, neither reckoning anything as 'having' nor 'not having'; who does not reckon a body nor the marks and signs of form; who understands the essence of the Tathāgata such that it neither arises nor does not arise, is neither characterized by marks nor not characterized by marks, has neither a location nor no location, and neither produces the body of the Tathāgata nor destroys it—thereby entering the state of non-existence through the body of the Tathāgata, and practicing while having nothing to practice."
Why is this? It is because they all undergo the natural course of all things.

Furthermore, these bodhisattvas constantly extend compassion to the class of sentient beings; whether their heads are cut off, their hands and feet severed, their ears and noses sliced away, both eyes gouged out, or they are reviled, insulted, struck with tiles and stones, kicked, trampled, pinched, spat upon, or mocked—they are able to endure it all. They do not give rise to anger, nor do they harbor resentment, and their countenance remains unchanged.
Having cultivated the bodhisattva practices for incalculable eons, he has never once given rise to a thought of abandoning or forsaking anything.
"Furthermore, as a bodhisattva trains in all phenomena, he studies the non-duality of things."

By training in this, one is free from all resentment; one diligently protects the masses, endures all suffering and the afflictions of various troubles, and even when the body encounters poisonous pain, one endures it all.
All things of the future are boundless and unobstructed; one dwells in faith and joy.

By means of such analogies, one should resolve upon the Bodhisattva path, extending from the future until the ultimate limit of the Dharma-realm and dwelling within the realm of empty space, practicing the Bodhisattva way in each and every Buddha-world to transform and enlighten sentient beings.
Just as the practices cultivated in one world-system are likewise so in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, extending across the dharma-realm and exhausting the limits of empty space.
Being empty and devoid of intrinsic existence, they feel no alarm, no fear, and no trepidation; thus do they give rise to their activities throughout the three periods of time.
Why is this so? Because wherever a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells and resides, he practices the Bodhisattva conduct for the sake of all beings.

Relying on the Bodhisattva mind, he has faith in the unsurpassed, right, and true path; his nature and disposition are pure, he accumulates the roots of manifold virtues, fulfills his vows, and attains mastery in the Buddha-way.

Furthermore, they may attain it through their own power; whatever they wish to accomplish for the sake of perfect enlightenment is immediately attained according to their intent. Their practice is immeasurable and reaches ultimate consummation, severing all five aggregates so that all sensations are exhausted without remainder.
In the places where he practices, he does not attain perfect enlightenment based upon those [worlds]. Why is this?
Because he fulfills his vows, completes the bodhisattva practices, transforms and enlightens sentient beings, and protects all buddha-fields.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva does not apprehend the Buddhas, nor does he apprehend the locus of the Way; likewise, he does not apprehend the loci of the bodhisattvas or all sentient beings, nor does he apprehend the mind, consciousness, or mental formations, nor does he apprehend the conditioned or unconditioned states of all sentient beings in the past, future, and present.
