The conduct of a bodhisattva is thus: profound, subtle, and sublime; tranquil, serene, and still; entirely without attainment.
Their practice is non-dual and free from contention; it is naturally such as this—pure, liberated, and characterized by parinirvāṇa.

Cultivating practice as it was at the original limit, with a mind that is truly sincere and without falsehood, they do not slacken or abandon their established vows—the mind of omniscience and the various practices of Bodhisattvas.

They transform and enlighten sentient beings through the various perfections (pāramitās), instructing the people according to the precepts, reverently honoring all Buddhas, preaching the Dharma and expounding its meaning to adorn the worlds.
Thereupon, he applied himself with diligence, never once becoming weary. Why was this?
It was because of his great vow.
By such analogies, one knows all dharmas; thus, through these characteristics of dharmas, one’s great compassion is boundless and one’s merit is immeasurable.
"Having thoroughly understood the meaning of wisdom, one takes pity on sentient beings and constantly comprehends the names and designations of all dharmas."
"Such foolish worldlings do not understand this; they are unable to comprehend that all phenomena are of their own nature. I shall now awaken them so that they may attain this knowledge."
Why is this? Because all sentient beings lack tranquil conduct.
For this reason, the Buddhas preach the sutras for them, transform and enlighten sentient beings, give rise to infinite compassion, and do not abandon great loving-kindness.
"Why should we weary of great compassion and abandon sentient beings?
If we do not attain Buddhahood, do not complete the scriptures, and do not fulfill our great vows, [it would be in vain].
Thus, they bestow the unsurpassed Dharma-gift upon sentient beings; from the very first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they purify all multitudes of living beings.

One establishes a vow of sincerity: if one cannot learn the gate of the Way through the great vows, the essential right awakening, and the arousal of the bodhicitta, then one deceives all the Buddhas.

For the sake of all beings, one arouses the mind of the Way, plants the roots of all virtues, and encourages others therein; one enters profound and subtle wisdom, universally pervading the forms and abodes of all sentient beings, and equalizes one’s mind toward them.
For this reason, by fulfilling the great vows, these constitute the ten matters whereby the mind is like a diamond and one dons the armor of the Mahāyāna.
Abiding in this, the bodhisattva swiftly accomplishes the Tathāgata’s infinite supernormal powers, as firm as a diamond.
“Bodhisattvas possess ten matters of great diligence. What are these ten?
‘I shall reverently honor all Buddhas, make offerings to them, and take refuge in them; I shall accumulate and gather together the roots of all the virtues of the bodhisattva multitude.’”

For the sake of all Tathāgatas after their parinirvāṇa, one shall adorn the divine temples and make offerings of various flowers, renowned incense, powdered incense, blended incense, unguents, robes, banners, and canopies.

Upholding the True Dharma, protecting and instructing others, and transforming all realms of sentient beings; exhorting them to aspire to the unsurpassed, right, and true path; not contravening the sublime discipline; purifying all Buddha-lands; and establishing them in the unsurpassed realm.
"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva thinks to himself:
'In every world throughout all future kalpas, for the sake of even a single person who has not yet attained liberation, as well as for all people, there shall be no one left behind;
my cultivation of the Bodhisattva practice for their sake is likewise thus.'"

"Raising great compassion, he establishes all sentient beings upon the Buddha’s true path; though passing through various hardships, he never for a moment gives rise to a mind of weariness or indolence, constantly cultivating the Buddha-dharma."

These Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have appeared throughout incalculable kalpas; if a person were to make offerings to each of them as they would to a single Buddha, their service to all these Tathāgatas would be equal and without distinction.

"After the parinirvāṇa of these Tathāgatas, for incalculable kalpas, one shall make offerings to their śarīras with all manner of jeweled canopies, bells, banners, and streamers; for each and every Buddha, one shall establish great temples in countless lands, depicting their forms and erecting images throughout immeasurable and inconceivable realms."
Diligent day and night, never ceasing for even a moment, one serves as a treasury of the Buddha-dharma.
Having served all Buddhas, one transforms sentient beings and proclaims the teachings of the Dharma.
Having rectified the Dharma, one gradually approaches the Great Way.

By means of these roots of virtue, one attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path, becoming a Most Perfectly Awakened One (Anuttara-samyak-saṃbuddha). Adhering to the single equality of all Tathāgatas, one returns to all Buddha-fields.
"Having attained perfect enlightenment, they proclaim the Way of the sutras throughout incalculable eons across all Buddha-fields.
They manifest inconceivable supernatural powers through the transformations of all Buddhas, never becoming weary; nor do their body, speech, or mind reckon the labor involved."

"When they first resolve their minds, they enter directly into the Dharma-gate; at all times they serve the Buddhas, cultivate great vows to guide and transform sentient beings, take great kindness as their foremost priority, and culminate in great compassion."

One honors the dharma of signlessness, abides in the teaching of sincerity and faith, and fulfills all dharmas as the realization to be attained; there is no opposition in anything, and in all undertakings, there is no contention or dispute.

"The Buddhas of the past, future, and present enter into a single principle; they proceed toward the Dharma-realm, which is identical with emptiness, transcending the dharma of signlessness, where there is neither attainment nor non-attainment, leading one to the ultimate."
"Never having felt weariness or aversion toward the teachings of all Buddhas, they bring about infinite vows and perform the fundamental practices of a Buddha to entice and exhort the multitudes.
These are the ten matters in which a bodhisattva is profoundly diligent; dwelling in these, a bodhisattva accomplishes the unsurpassed great wisdom of a Tathāgata."
“There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva can fully manifest great diligence. What are these ten?

To revere and honor all Tathāgatas, the Truly Realized Ones, and take refuge in them; to request that all sentient beings be protected at all times; to seek the protection of the Buddha-dharma with great earnestness and diligence; to accumulate the roots of myriad virtues without weariness; to cause the sacred scriptures to flourish and circulate everywhere; to be fully endowed with all infinite vows for the Path; to be earnestly devoted to and aspire toward the practices of all bodhisattvas; to constantly encounter virtuous friends from whom one receives instruction; to travel everywhere throughout the ten directions to behold the Tathāgatas; and to listen to the sutras they preach and enter the Buddha’s place of enlightenment. These are the ten matters by which one manifests great diligence.”
"Bodhisattvas have ten things through which their faith is indestructible. What are these ten?

They believe that the Buddhas of the ten directions have no differing intentions; they rejoice in all Buddha-dharmas and never abandon them; they love and delight in the noble Sangha and do not give rise to divergent thoughts; they take pleasure in bodhisattvas and harbor no doubts or fetters; they always associate and harmonize with virtuous friends; they compassionately regard sentient beings and do not forsake the masses; they fully practice all the vows of the bodhisattvas and fulfill the various conducts of the *kai-shi* (bodhisattvas); they revere and pay homage to all Buddhas by bowing their heads in refuge; they transform and enlighten sentient beings so that all may be delivered and liberated; and they cultivate the skillful means (*upāya*) of the bodhisattvas without violating their firm faith."
These are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva’s faith is indestructible.
“There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva receives the prediction [of enlightenment]. What are these ten?
Delighting in and firmly believing in practice;
receiving the definitive nature of one's own conduct;
cultivating the mind of the Way and cherishing the roots of virtue.
Their practice is vast and far-reaching; they receive the prediction of enlightenment through the Vaipulya sūtras, receive it before their very eyes, or receive it secretly;
they attain the prediction of supreme perfect enlightenment through mastery of the mind;
or they receive the prediction after having attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti).
To transform and enlighten sentient beings, receiving the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) from beginning to end, whereby all delusive thoughts are eliminated and forever exhausted;
to be able to manifest and display all the meritorious achievements of the practices of all bodhisattvas—only then does one receive the prediction.
These are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva receives the prediction.
"Bodhisattvas have ten matters for encouraging and assisting the roots of virtue. What are these ten?
By means of these roots of virtue, they share a single aspiration; wherever they are born, may they always be with virtuous friends, remaining thus forever and never allowing it to change."
By means of these roots of virtue, may they share a single mind with all spiritual friends, never allowing for any division;
in whatever place they are born, may they be endowed with equal vows and remain together with virtuous teachers;
by means of these roots of goodness, in whatever place they are born, may their aspirations be in harmony with those of all bodhisattvas.
By virtue of these meritorious deeds, in every life and wherever they may be, they shall be accompanied by the wise;
wherever they dwell, they shall single-mindedly focus their thoughts, never departing from the holy and enlightened;
wherever they travel or reside, they shall always remain equanimous and pure, sharing the same resolve as the wise.
In every lifetime one is born together with virtuous friends whose conduct is in accord;
in future lives one enters into a state of equality and meets with enlightened teachers;
by virtue of this original merit, one remains with good teachers, giving rise to righteousness that is indestructible.
These are the ten matters that encourage and assist the roots of virtue.
Furthermore, there are ten matters regarding the bodhisattva’s entry into the noble mind. What are these ten?
Extensively practicing giving, one attains entry into wisdom;
delighting in all the path-dharmas of the Buddhas, one roams among the Tathāgatas;
entering into the meaning of the immeasurable intermediate state, one uses the wisdom of inquiry to resolve all knots of doubt.
They clearly understand the meanings and principles, are able to enter the noble wisdom, and can discern all that is taught by the mouths of the Tathāgatas, the Truly Realized Ones;
they have deep faith in the Buddha-dharma and manifest all that exists, yet their power is slight;
because the Buddha has appeared in the world, the roots of their virtue are immeasurable, and they delight in the Tathāgata.
They all possess the pure meaning of the sūtras and are fully endowed with the inconceivable wisdom of all bodhisattva practices;
at the very moment they resolve their minds, they enter infinite buddha-lands without any obstruction;
they understand the wisdom of a single thought-moment, clearly comprehending all the matters of the buddhas' paths and entering the manifold dharma-realms.
Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, they are able to receive and uphold it all, entering into the various vocal expressions of all Tathāgatas;
these are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva enters into wisdom.
"There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva’s mind, when first aroused, becomes inwardly vast and immeasurable."

What are these ten? At the moment they resolve their minds, they broaden their inner will; they contemplate immeasurable Buddhas; they enter among sentient beings with a boundless resolve to develop the mind and roam among the multitudes of living beings and their lands; they enter the Dharma-realm and understand its non-duality; they observe all phenomena as being equal to empty space; they universally gaze upon the practices of all Bodhisattvas; they contemplate all Buddhas of the three periods of time; they enter into the inconceivable retributions of sin and merit; they observe that all Buddha-lands are entirely pure; and they universally enter all the sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) of all Buddhas to observe them therein, as well as entering the sounds, resonances, and terminology of all Tathāgatas. These are the ten matters by which a Bodhisattva universally enters the intermediate state, internally broadening and expanding immeasurably.
“Bodhisattvas further have ten kinds of treasuries.
What are the ten? They are:
the treasury of cultivating diligence by enumerating all dharmas;”
They understand that all phenomena are entirely without arising;
they illuminate and uphold the essential teachings of the Buddhas’ sutras;
and with eloquence, they proclaim the origins and endings of all phenomena, understanding them according to the appropriate time.
The infinite meanings of all phenomena are entirely ungraspable;
they cause all beings everywhere to behold with their own eyes the transformations produced by the supernormal powers of the Buddhas,
while skillfully and equitably governing all dharmas.
They constantly see all Buddhas and are never far removed from them;
they discern the inconceivable provisional meanings and the conceptualizations formed by various illusions;
and upon seeing all Buddhas and the multitude of Bodhisattvas, they rejoice with great delight and attain the treasury of the Dharma.
These are the ten treasuries of a bodhisattva.
There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva provides protection. What are these ten?
They shall never slander the Buddha’s path and Dharma, but shall protect and uphold its intent;
they shall have faith in the teachings of the Great Sage, never wavering or regretting it;
and they shall enter among the bodhisattvas, always maintaining reverence and diligence.
Upon meeting all virtuous friends, they harmonize their nature and align their aspirations with them;
they no longer cultivate or dwell upon the practices of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
they protect and uphold the chapters and phrases of the bodhisattvas, practicing them without ever regressing.
He has compassion for all sentient beings and harbors no malice;
he thoroughly elucidates the root of all virtues;
he subdues all Māras and repels all external adversaries.
To be fully endowed with all the perfections (pāramitās);
these are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva provides protection.
"A bodhisattva possesses mastery; there are ten matters through which they attain mastery over life."
What are these ten? Their lifespan is reckoned as incalculable kalpas, without end or limit;
their minds roam freely, and the meditative concentrations they arouse enter into holy wisdom beyond measure.
Their karma is sovereign, as they traverse the various Buddha-fields adorned with the infinite; they desire to manifest and establish the meaning of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Their karma is unrestrained, appearing at will according to the occasion;
they roam freely within the retributions produced by the world.
They manifest throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions with mastery of intention;
they universally behold all Buddha-worlds and gaze upon all Tathāgatas, their vows being fulfilled at will and their desires being mastered;
in whichever Buddha-land they attain supreme perfect enlightenment, they travel freely by means of their supernormal powers, able to manifest all manner of majestic spiritual transformations.
They exercise mastery over all phenomena, universally able to manifest countless internal Dharma-gates;
they possess sovereignty over wisdom, frequently appearing at the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas through the Tathāgata’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses.
These are the ten matters of a bodhisattva’s mastery; dwelling in these, a bodhisattva is fully able to perfect all the *pāramitās*.
“There are ten matters by which a Bodhisattva manifests transformations. What are these ten? They are:

manifesting as sentient beings according to their transgressions and merits; adorning and purifying buddha-lands, each being distinct; transforming the sutras and teachings to provide instruction according to the times; manifesting his presence wherever he may be; exercising mastery over his vows to establish the principles of the Way; traveling freely through his conduct while entering everywhere; employing noble wisdom in the performance of deeds to demonstrate them to all; using supernatural transformations to deliver all without exception; employing the power of spiritual feet so that there is nothing he cannot move; and cultivating majestic power until reaching the ten powers. These are the ten matters of a Bodhisattva’s transformative manifestations. There are ten matters by which a Bodhisattva transforms sentient beings.”
What are these ten? They are:
proclaiming that sentient beings are entirely non-existent; that all the multitudes of living beings are established through conceptualization;
and preaching the Dharma to all creatures according to the appropriate time.
They transform the common masses, causing them to abandon arrogance;
they protect every step taken within all realms of humanity, ensuring peace and security free from harm;
and they are universally able to manifest in all worlds, establishing all sentient beings and the realms of those beings.
He manifests as Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings;
he travels among the common people, appearing in bodily form according to the occasion;
and he likewise manifests the physical forms and appearances of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
They manifest the conduct of Bodhisattvas, understanding the spheres of all sentient beings and reaching them all without exception;
they awaken to and perfect universal knowledge of all powers of the Way, the marks and signs of the physical body, and various forms of adornment;
this is the Bodhisattva’s transformation of sentient beings.
"Bodhisattvas have ten matters for the adornment and purification of buddha-fields. What are these ten?
All buddha-fields become a single buddha-field;..."
They establish and construct karmic achievements such that all Buddha-lands enter into a single pore;
they cause all Buddha-realms to enter therein without end;
and they open up and communicate the single meaning within all Buddha-spheres.
Manifesting his own single practice, he perceives his own body universally entering all Buddha-lands;
among the various classes of sentient beings in all those Buddha-lands, none are able to move him, nor does he feel any fear.
Furthermore, all the adornments of every Buddha-land appear within a single Buddha-land, and the majesty and purity of that one land pervades all Buddha-lands.
In all Buddha-lands there is but one Tathāgata;

throughout the assemblies and places of enlightenment, the body of this single Tathāgata pervades all sentient beings, causing them to enter into that which is subtle and wondrous, infinitely sublime, vast, universal, profound, and deep.

Whether it be those who are deviant or upright, those who are dependent on others or self-governing, and whether it be in every direction, within the net of phenomena, or as karmic retribution—it is everywhere without exception, and he is able to manifest himself in all these ways.
These are the ten matters.
"There are ten matters concerning the Bodhisattva’s adaptation to the times regarding the sūtras and the Dharma. What are these ten?
To cause all dharmas to enter into a single dharma is to transform all dharmas by means of that one dharma;
to transform the nature of sentient beings so that they do not engage in contention or dispute;
and to cause all dharmas to accord with and enter into the Prajñāpāramitā, teaching them to cross over to the other shore.

All dharmas enter into sentient beings; one abandons the conceptualization of dharmas and causes all dharmas to enter into a single meaning, expounding teachings that cannot be exhausted even throughout incalculable kalpas.
By means of all dharmas entering into hundreds of thousands of countless dharma-gates, one perceives the minds of sentient beings and fully explains their origins and endings.
Furthermore, regarding the universal gate-wheel of syllables of all dharmas, one understands them according to the occasion.
All dharmas enter into a single dharma-gate, free from contention; they proclaim the meaning of incalculable eons that can never be exhausted;
all dharmas enter the path of all Buddhas to transform sentient beings;
and all Buddha-dharmas manifest infinite internal orthodox teachings.
All phenomena enter entirely into the primordial limit (*koṭi*); within the immeasurable net, the exhaustion of sentient beings throughout countless eons is manifested;
these are the ten matters according to the times.
"Bodhisattvas have ten ways in which their bodies undergo transformation. What are these ten?
They establish sentient beings within their own bodies so that they may attain liberation;..."
Furthermore, they establish themselves by conceiving of their own body as the bodies of sentient beings;
they manifest the entry of all Buddha-bodies into a single Buddha-body, and the entry of a single Buddha-body into the bodies of all Buddhas;
and they establish their own bodies within all Buddha-lands, manifesting transformations for the sake of sentient beings.
Universally encompassing the three periods of time within the single, pervasive Dharma-body, they cultivate right reception with a concentrated mind in one body;
yet manifesting various bodies, they realize the path of perfect enlightenment through a single body,
and manifest the bodies of countless bodhisattvas.
To merge the bodies of sentient beings into a single body, and to universally manifest many bodies from the body of a single person;
to manifest entry into the Dharma-body by means of the bodies of sentient beings,
and likewise to manifest the bodies of sentient beings by means of the Dharma-body.
These are the ten matters concerning the transformation of his body.
"There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva transforms and establishes his vows. What are these ten?
They take up the vows of all bodhisattvas and establish their own oaths; the Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, manifest the various bodhisattvas through the power of the path of their own vows.
According to the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings wherever they may be, they cause them to achieve the unsurpassed, right, and true path, becoming the Most Perfectly Awakened Ones.

They eliminate the cravings and desires of the mind throughout boundless eons, emerge from the body of consciousness, and establish the body of wisdom; they appear in various forms according to their sovereign vows while transcending their own physical forms.
Fully manifesting that perfected body, they transform and guide sentient beings, exhorting them toward all vows;
with the body of a bodhisattva pervading all thoughts, their various practices and kalpas continue without interruption;
treading the path of the single power, they achieve supreme perfect enlightenment, and by virtue of their power and vows, they manifest their bodies throughout all infinite buddha-fields.
To expound a single dharma-phrase within all forms, pervading the entire dharma-realm without exception;

to raise the great cloud of Dharma, raining down the flavor of ambrosia, illuminating with wisdom and understanding, proclaiming the Dharma of True Reality, thundering like a great roar, satisfying all sentient beings, fulfilling infinite vows, and being fully endowed with the joy of the Dharma—
this is the bodhisattva’s establishment of their transformative vow.
“Furthermore, there are ten matters concerning the transformative manifestations of a bodhisattva.
What are these ten? To manifest by means of practicing in accordance with the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu);”
They joyfully perform Buddha-works within the realm of sentient beings;
yet they further manifest universally before all the hosts of Māras.
While practicing the unconditioned realm as Bodhisattvas, they extract beings from the cycle of birth and death.
Practicing all-knowledge, he does not abandon the activities in which Bodhisattvas roam, yet he maintains the practice of profound stillness and detachment;

appearing among sentient beings, he appears to study with great urgency, yet he is never distracted, neither advancing nor flagging, neither dual nor singular, without speech, without thought, possessing nothing and initiating nothing, practicing in a manner equal to space—yet the Bodhisattva thus manifests all these things.

Amidst the various inverted perceptions of sentient beings that give rise to their various actions, he does not mingle with their defilements, but purely cultivates the power of practice, manifesting it all as well.
In all places where they travel, they clearly understand all affairs; realizing fundamentally that there is no person, they transform and guide sentient beings in the present.

They cultivate the gates of dhyāna-liberation, the supernormal powers, and the wisdom of the three insights; they take birth in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions in the present, accomplishing the practices of a Tathāgata and perfecting the Buddha’s majestic purity.
They manifest the deportment, etiquette, and conduct of non-conceptualization belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
These are the ten matters of transformation through which a bodhisattva effects metamorphosis.
There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva effects transformation through wisdom. What are these ten?
With inexhaustible eloquence, they proclaim the wisdom of the Way; having attained all dhāraṇīs, they manifest immeasurable light.
Their eloquence is skillfully analytical, and they discourse extensively;
they harmonize the faculties of sentient beings, delivering them through the transformations of holy wisdom.
By observing the minds of others with an unconditioned mind, one perceives the intentions and mental activities of sentient beings through a single mind;
one understands the dispositions, natures, fetters, and the afflictions of sentient beings, administering medicine according to their ailments so that they may attain healing and clear understanding,
and simultaneously attains universal mastery over the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

They are able to enter into the conduct of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, manifesting fully both kalpas with numerical limits and those without such limits, thereby transforming and enlightening them;
their minds are tranquil and serene, forever free from obscuration or hindrance, as they achieve supreme perfect enlightenment and universally deliver all beings;
through the wisdom of a single person, they attain mastery, observing sentient beings and knowing the karma they create—their good and evil, and their misfortunes and blessings.
With a single sound, they cause it to pervade and resonate throughout the voices of all sentient beings;
these are the ten matters. "There are ten matters concerning the supernormal transformations of a Bodhisattva.
What are these ten? They are:
manifesting a single body throughout all Buddha-lands; being able to harmoniously expound the teachings within every assembly of a Tathāgata;
proclaiming the bodhisattva path and the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas; and transforming and guiding all who practice the path through the conduct of a single mind.

With a single voice, they universally proclaim to the sentient beings in all Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions according to their mental inclinations, enabling each to attain what is appropriate for them;

with a concentrated mind, they perceive the good and evil deeds, calamities and blessings, performed by all living beings over incalculable kalpas of past lives, thereby delivering and liberating them; thus, they adorn all Buddha-lands with spiritual powers;
and through these spiritual powers, they perceive the three periods of time equally, without any distinction or disparity.
They know all the practices established by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, illuminating them with the radiance of the Dharma;

they also perceive through their supernormal powers the conduct of all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas, as well as the ten powers of the Tathāgata;
and there are no roots of virtue of the bodhisattvas that they do not protect.
The Bodhisattva brings all sounds to equal stillness and thereby governs sentient beings with impartiality and equanimity;
this constitutes the tenth supernormal transformation of the Bodhisattva.
There are ten matters concerning the miraculous transformations of the Bodhisattva’s psychic power (*ṛddhi*).
What are these ten? To cause countless worlds to enter into a single atom is a transformation of spiritual power (*ṛddhi*);

furthermore, to use a single atom to pervade the entire Dharma-realm while manifesting a single Buddha-land; to cause all the waters of the oceans to enter a single pore; to expand the vast Dharma-realm to enter into many Buddha-lands; and to ensure that all sentient beings suffer no harm or affliction—these constitute the ten.
Infinite worlds enter into his own body, and through the wisdom of his supernormal powers, he universally manifests all that he does;
inconceivable Iron Ring Mountains and Great Iron Ring Mountains enter into a single pore;
he travels through the lands of all Buddhas, causing all living beings to harbor no fear.

They manifest immeasurable eons as a single eon, or appear as a single day; they may manifest a single eon as immeasurable eons, combining and adjusting these durations to transform and guide sentient beings without causing them any affliction or harm.

They manifest all worlds as being struck by external calamities, or encountering the disasters of water and fire, desiring to cause sentient beings to perceive the impermanence of things; yet through the display of their supernormal powers, no harm is inflicted.
All the disasters of water, fire, wind, and space that arise in all worlds are transformed into an abundance of all manner of property, karmic resources, palaces, and dwellings.

Furthermore, by means of the power of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*), they manifest and transform inconceivable Buddha-fields for the sake of sentient beings; they lift them up with their right palms and transport them to immeasurable Buddha-worlds without causing them any diminution or damage;
and they manifest all Buddha-lands as naturally empty space to instruct sentient beings.
These are the ten transformations of the divine feet of a bodhisattva.
"The various powers of a bodhisattva that move and transform beings also consist of ten matters. What are these ten?
Their power moves sentient beings to open and transform them, never failing or neglecting this task."
They universally influence all lands, manifesting them through countless articles of adornment;
through the transformative power of the Dharma, all bodies enter into the bodiless;
and the force of their transformations continues uninterrupted throughout kalpas.
Through the power of the Buddha’s transformations, they awaken those who are in slumber;
through the power of their practice, they encompass all the practices of Bodhisattvas;
and through the teaching of the Tathāgata’s power, they are able to rescue and deliver the realms of sentient beings.
Through the teaching of sovereign power, one realizes that all phenomena are spontaneous by nature;
having attained the power of omniscience of supreme perfect enlightenment, one reaches the path of equality by means of the unhindered supernormal knowledges and noble wisdom;
through the transformative power of great compassion, one does not abandon sentient beings.
This is the transformation of the ten powers of a bodhisattva, by which they transform and benefit sentient beings.
If a bodhisattva attains these transformations of the ten powers, they will be without obstruction, swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and become a Most Perfectly Awakened One.
In the mere instant of generating the resolve for enlightenment, one attains the Way of the Buddha without interrupting one's practice. Why is this?
By proclaiming great vows, the bodhisattva accomplishes immeasurable dharma-gates and universally manifests the roots of virtue.
“There are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva finds delight. What are these ten?
In this regard, a bodhisattva establishes the state of a realm through the bodies of sentient beings and discerns the destinies of the forms of the common people; this is the first delight.
"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva establishes sentient beings through a manifested body of earth, yet does not allow his physical body to suffer depletion, this is the second joy.

Moreover, when that bodhisattva manifests at will the body of a Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, the bodies of śrāvakas, and the bodies of pratyekabuddhas—this is the constant manifestation of the Tathāgata’s activity, and it is the third joy."

"Furthermore, that bodhisattva manifests the towering and subtle bodies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas, yet remains unattached to the teachings of these three categories; this is the fourth joy."

"Furthermore, that bodhisattva manifests the body of conduct and the body of supreme perfect enlightenment; yet they do not cling to bodily conduct, nor is there anything to be severed—this is the fifth joy."
"Furthermore, when that bodhisattva manifests the path of perfect enlightenment, his bodily conduct does not rely upon perfect enlightenment; this is the sixth joy.
Furthermore, when that bodhisattva manifests the realm of nirvāṇa, he relies upon birth and death yet does not cling to nirvāṇa; this is the seventh joy."

"Furthermore, that bodhisattva manifests the practice of birth and death, and also manifests the attainment of parinirvāṇa, yet does not undergo eternal extinction in nirvana; this is the eighth joy."

"Furthermore, that bodhisattva, through constant and fixed stability, universally demonstrates all practices; whether going and returning, moving about, standing still, or walking in meditation, they do not abandon samādhi—this is the ninth joy."
"Furthermore, when that bodhisattva hears the True Dharma preached by a single Tathāgata, he does not perceive the perishing of his body, as he guards his samādhi concentration.

Within the immeasurable matters of the Tathāgata’s place of enlightenment, he discerns each individually; regarding all such bodies, the body in which he dwells remains unimpaired, and he does not disturb his samādhi."
Having heard the teachings expounded by the Tathāgatas, they receive and practice them accordingly.

They enter into samādhi and correctly maintain it, never ceasing to inquire into the essentials of the sūtras; remaining together with the Tathāgatas, they do not perceive the extinction of their bodies.

Each and every samādhi governs the gates of all practices, entering into countless concentrations; through such manifestations, they exhaustively endure throughout the kalpas of destruction, yet the bodhisattva’s samādhi never reaches its limit—the concentration of mind and the gates of the body—this is the tenth enjoyment.
When a bodhisattva dwells herein, they attain the unsurpassed wisdom and bliss of a Tathāgata.
There are ten matters regarding the sphere of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?
For the sake of all sentient beings, they manifest the entry into immeasurable gateways;
throughout all worlds, with their countless and manifold adornments, they guide and instruct the masses;
and while governing the realm of sentient beings, they remain free from self-conceit, preaching and exhorting those under their care.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, enters the body of a bodhisattva by means of the bodhisattva’s body, and enters the body of a Tathāgata by means of the bodhisattva’s body;
he guides all Buddha-lands by means of the realm of empty space, and guides the realm of empty space by means of all Buddha-lands;
he manifests the source of nirvāṇa through the root of birth and death, and manifests the root of birth and death through the source of nirvāṇa.
Using the voice of a single person to proclaim the teachings of all Buddhas, each entering their respective realms;
manifesting through immeasurable gateways within a single body, thereby establishing countless bodies from that one body;
and further, using that single body to pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
Sentient beings resolve their minds and, by means of a single wisdom, govern immeasurable gateways to attain supreme perfect enlightenment;
these are the ten matters.
When Bodhisattvas abide in these, they enter the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed great wisdom.
“Bodhisattvas possess ten powers. What are these ten?
They are the power of the nature of dedicated resolve, which does not share in the common dust of the various worlds;”
They cultivate the power of pure harmony, remaining unattached even to the Buddha-dharma;
they manifest the power of timely action, universally appearing in the various spheres of a bodhisattva’s skillful means;
and by the power of noble wisdom, they know the mental activities and thoughts of all sentient beings.
The power of their vows enables them to fully penetrate all things; they are endowed with the power of the practices of their original vows;
they do not sever the power of the vehicle cultivated at the primordial limit, manifesting all vehicles while never abandoning the Mahāyāna;
and through the power of all transformations, all Buddhas arise.
They purify the realms of the ten directions, manifesting the power of the path and its meaning as they tread upon it;
they awaken the minds of sentient beings so that they never depart from perfect enlightenment, possessing the power to turn the wheel of Dharma;
they proclaim a single Dharma with a voice that is neither deficient nor redundant, ensuring all is complete, thereby guiding the faculties and minds of all beings.
These are the ten powers.
When a bodhisattva abides in these, they attain the ten powers of unsurpassed universal wisdom.
There are ten matters regarding the fearlessness of a bodhisattva.
What are these ten? "They receive all things and are able to maintain all sounds.
How much more so for a bodhisattva who does not harbor such thoughts: [that they cannot do so]."

"I have come here from the east, south, west, and north to inquire about hundreds of thousands of infinite essential compendiums; yet I am perhaps not capable of receiving and answering this Great Dharma."
The Bodhisattva fully knows that nothing is unseen or unattained, and through the Great Fearlessness (mahā-vaiśāradya), he brings all sentient beings to the other shore.

When those who come to pose difficult questions listen as they please, he speaks with a courageous mind regarding whatever they wish to inquire about, never becoming weary or indolent; this is the first fearlessness.
"The sequence of sounds and words produced from all written characters flows like a stream; through the majestic power of the Tathāgata, they possess the perfection of unimpeded eloquence.
That Bodhisattva does not harbor such thoughts as:
'Should difficult questions come from the east, west, south, or north, I shall be unable to respond and resolve them.'"

"Never before has there been such a sight as this: one who is incomparable and unsurpassed, courageous and fearless, such that when all sentient beings question him at will, he remains brave, self-possessed, and his hair does not stand on end—these are the two forms of fearlessness."

“Wandering alone in the empty Dharma, the bodhisattva never allows the net of doubt to arise in the mind, nor does he calculate in terms of a self, nor does he calculate in terms of what is done or undergone, nor in terms of life-span or a person; for he is detached from the five aggregates, the sense bases, false views, and the sixty-two doubts.”
His mind is universally equanimous and equal as space; therefore, he has no such thought as:
"I might be subjected to a test that disturbs my body, speech, or mind.
The Bodhisattva possesses no such inferior view.

Why is this so? Because these true persons are free from the notions of self and person, do not manifest any conceptualizations, and move with great courage and firm skillful means; these are the three fearlessnesses.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva is established by the Buddha, abiding in the power of the Buddha and maintaining the majestic deportment and etiquette of a Tathāgata, yet remains free from conceptual construction.
He does not harbor such thoughts as:
"Will people not find fault with me, or say that my deportment is incomplete?"

Never before has there been such a case of not seeing or not attaining [the truth], yet he now walks with courageous strides through the great assembly to proclaim the Way of the Sūtras; these are the four fearlessnesses, characterized by the purity of body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore, how could that bodhisattva ever again think of eliminating unwholesome conduct, training in purity, or practicing benevolence and righteousness?
Nor does he harbor such thoughts as:
"Perhaps someone will seek out defects in my body, speech, or mind."
To preach the Way of the sutras for the sake of all sentient beings with great courage and valor constitutes the fifth fearlessness.

Because he has attained great protection—the Vajra Deity constantly holding a vajra behind the Bodhisattva; being seen and taking refuge in by devas, nāgas, spirits, and asuras; being honored and served by Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings; and being kept in mind by all Buddhas—he harbors no fear of Māras, the celestial Māras, or various heterodox teachers. No delusive or evil beings can disturb him, and he never sees such people again.

When one is a bodhisattva, through the perfection of great valor, they inspire the arising of resolve and are able to fully accomplish all the deeds of a bodhisattva; these are the six fearlessnesses.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva attains the mindfulness of the Buddha’s wisdom and never forgets it.
His faculties are always concentrated as he preaches the Dharma for the multitude, expounding the sacred words and discerning the meaning of the Buddha-way.

The Dharma he proclaims issues from the Buddha’s own mouth; it is without internal obstruction or hindrance, and nothing can obscure or veil it. No one can give rise to views that find fault with it. To uphold the Tathāgata’s teaching—this is the seventh fearlessness.

The Bodhisattva possesses clear understanding, wisdom, and skillful means; his power is infinite, and he strides alone in both advancing and retreating. In instructing and transforming sentient beings, none can restrain him. Through the vow for the Buddha-way and his boundless sagely nature, he gives rise to an unobstructed compassion, pitying the masses of living beings.

Even if one were born in a world of violence, affliction, and defilement, and were to embrace great desires, amusements, and the grand affairs of a retinue, one would teach sentient beings without giving rise to such thoughts, lest the multitude should slander one’s purity.

The Buddha-way consists of pure conduct, the severance of [defilements], meditative concentration, the gates of liberation, and right attainment; yet, through dhāraṇī and eloquence, one does not perceive these as existing.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has attained mastery over all phenomena, such that no one can obstruct the path of practice he cultivates.

That none throughout the ten directions can transgress against them; that they observe great valor and dwell in all Buddha-lands; and that they cast off all evils and embrace right vows—these are the eight fearlessnesses.

"A bodhisattva does not abandon the mind of omniscience; they dwell well in the meaning of the Path and cherish the Mahāyāna. By the power established through their various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms, they manifest for the sake of those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles a deportment and etiquette that is beyond their reach, yet they do not give rise to the thought: 'Might I not by mistake fall into the level of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha?'"
Manifesting all vehicles through great valor, their deliverance is boundless; they delight solely in the Mahāyāna and are fully endowed with its practices—this is the ninth fearlessness.

The Bodhisattva skillfully accumulates all pure dharmas, unites the roots of all virtues, and universally prepares supernatural powers; never abandoning what he has realized, he delivers beings by means of the Buddha-way.

Circulating through the bodhisattva practices, he investigates the universal wisdom of all Buddhas to transform sentient beings; he does not lose correct practice nor does he corrupt the scriptural verses.
His mind does not harbor such thoughts as:
"Sentient beings may lack the purity and maturity of their faculties, and my brilliance may not reach to manifest the realm of the Buddhas."
Since no such response has yet occurred, he observes the faculties of sentient beings with great courage and valor in order to manifest the stage of Buddhahood.
Although he transforms sentient beings, the infinite great vows practiced by the Bodhisattva remain without deficiency or omission; this is the tenth fearlessness.
When a bodhisattva abides herein, they fully attain the four fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata.
There are ten matters that are unique to the Buddha-dharmas of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?
"The Bodhisattva exerts diligent effort, being without any point of origination, and crosses over to the other shore.
He eliminates stinginess and delights in giving;
his precepts and prohibitions are pure, and he does not commit any evils."
Having perfected patience, they have cast away all resentment;
having cultivated great diligence, they never retreat from the right practice they cultivate;
their meditative concentration is firm and steadfast, as they have abandoned all distracted thoughts.
Born from wisdom, they distance themselves from evil and false views, and ultimately have no words.
What is meant by "that which arises from nowhere"?
It is to constantly and diligently practice the six perfections; this is the Bodhisattva’s first state of wordlessness.

“The Dharma of the Bodhisattva is to understand the crossing to the other shore and to encompass and protect the realms of sentient beings; they bestow both worldly gifts and the gift of the Dharma, with a serene and joyful countenance.”
The words he speaks are capable of delivering others, pure and harmonious; when the multitude hears them, there is none whose heart is not gladdened.
His principles accord with the occasion, and he clearly understands the Buddha-way; his mind is free from partiality, regarding all sentient beings with equanimity.

That which the Bodhisattva cultivates is that which is unborn; by means of wordlessness, he rescues and delivers all living beings. The realm thus cultivated constitutes the second Dharma-gift of the Bodhisattva.
"The bodhisattva’s cultivation of clear understanding and exhortation is free from expectations of reward; he leads others into the Buddha-way and takes no pleasure in worldly things.

In his cultivation of meditative practice, he does not abandon the Tathāgata’s true and holy wisdom, but exhorts and assists sentient beings for their sake. One who has nothing further to say is a bodhisattva."
To be without verbal expression while cultivating the roots of all virtues, to seek and aspire to the Buddha’s wisdom, and to bestow gifts upon sentient beings—these three are "wordless.

The karma of a bodhisattva possesses skillful means; it is the foremost practice that accords with the inclinations of sentient beings, yet it does not loathe or disdain the mundane world as one wanders therein together with them.
Within the gates of unrestrained conduct practiced by the unvirtuous, they transform and enlighten all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the common masses.

Seeking no personal peace for themselves, they thoroughly understand the advancement and retreat of dhyāna, samādhi, the doors of liberation, and right concentration, thereby attaining sovereign mastery over meditative absorption.
With tireless diligence, he examines birth and death as if on a great tour of observation.
He destroys the palaces of Māra and manifests universally throughout the realms of Śakra, Brahmā, and the four heavenly kings.

In every place where he is born, there is constant radiance; he encounters various heterodox teachers and attains complete mastery of all secular scriptures, classics, literary praises, and the arts of calculation and arithmetic.

Regarding the six matters pertaining to oneself—royal classics, ornate carvings and engravings, borrowed seals and ribbons, eloquent speech and clever rhetoric, entertainment through music and sound, and the games of *chuppo* and *liubo*—one dares to challenge all under heaven.

He also clearly understood all that was seen by the eyes: the movements of women, the gestures of men, the prediction of auspicious omens, astronomy and geography, the sun, moon, and stars, the calamities and transformations manifested therein, and the methods for transcending the world; regarding those who came to inquire about matters as Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, there was nothing he did not understand.

He traverses all worldly affairs alone without peer; the entire world gazes up at him in reverence. He manifests the majestic deportment and ritual etiquette that the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot attain, yet he never abandons the Mahāyāna.
"In the mere instant of generating the resolve, one knows the manifested practices shown by all Tathāgatas, never interrupting the transmission of the sūtras;
likewise, the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) followed by Bodhisattvas is also uninterrupted, as they reverently cultivate the roots of virtue of the tranquil Bodhisattva."

Delighting in wisdom, they attain mastery while abiding in the unconditioned; manifesting the gateway of birth and death as far as the limit of non-substantiality, they teach and transform sentient beings without ever failing or neglecting their duty.

Abiding eternally in profound stillness, yet manifesting great worldly toil among sentient beings, one employs the body of the single flavor of Dharma-wisdom to appear before sentient beings as infinite bodies and boundless gateways, just like empty space.

With great wisdom, he delights in all desires; for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he delights in a single grade of pleasure. Manifesting within the triple world, he transforms sentient beings without departing from conceptual construction. Amidst hundreds of thousands of jade maidens, he constantly amuses himself with the joy of the Dharma, adorning himself with wondrous marks and signs and hundreds of thousands of myriad virtues.

In whatever place they are born, they are always free from transgressions and calamities; they cultivate pure conduct and manifest in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, yet within the wisdom of the Buddha-way, they achieve boundless deliverance without wavering or abandoning their resolve.
The wisdom-body of a bodhisattva possesses such wisdom that it is without limit or boundary.
By this analogy, they fully understand the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone the ignorant and deluded ordinary people.
These five are beyond words.

"The activities of body, speech, and mind have wisdom as their foremost; the karmic practices cultivated by the Bodhisattva are exceedingly pure. Possessing a heart of loving-kindness and compassion for all sentient beings, he abstains from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, envy, anger, delusion, and wrong views. Cultivating right conduct and right view—all these are likewise beyond words."
That the wisdom of the bodhisattva’s actions of body, speech, and mind accords with the appropriate time is the sixth.

Not abandoning sentient beings is for the bodhisattva to practice unexcelled compassion; seeing the afflictions of sentient beings—their physical aggregates encountering suffering and their mouths undergoing hardships—they give rise to and manifest the roots of virtue.
Whether dwelling in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, they undergo bitter suffering for the sake of sentient beings without ever becoming weary or disheartened.

They transform the realms of sentient beings so that they may harbor joy, and they do not let their minds dwell upon any desires or the activities of worldly entertainment, constantly applying themselves with diligence.

To wish to deliver sentient beings from the poisons, suffering, and various pains, yet not by means of the practices cultivated by other bodhisattvas, but solely by being resolved upon great compassion and following the power of the Way—this is the seventh.

"All the common people revere, respect, and delight in him; thus the Bodhisattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings all bear him in mind. All the people behold him with complete joy, and the multitudes contemplate his virtue, never departing from it in their hearts."
Why is this so? Because these bodhisattvas, in their past lives, have practiced pure conduct and possess no sinful karma.
Therefore, when people come to see them, they never feel satiated; moreover, they do so without words. This is the eighth [mark].

"With a mind firm and steadfast, well-armored in the virtues of all-encompassing wisdom and insight, it is exceedingly difficult for a bodhisattva to exert diligent effort in practice, yet they enter among the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; their jewel-like mind of omniscience remains pure, radiant, and free from any forgetfulness."
It is like a great, bright pearl named "Pure and Further Pure," which clarifies all turbid waters.
Even if a bathing pool is extremely filthy and defiled, when this pure bright pearl is placed within those turbid waters, the water becomes clear and no longer remains mixed with impurity.

In this way, even if a bodhisattva associates with the foolish and ignorant or moves among those who are deluded and dark, they never lose the mind of omniscience, which remains precious, pure, radiant, and brilliant.

With boundless wisdom, they eliminate the false views, afflictions, defilements, and sensual desires of sentient beings; abiding in omniscience, their jewel-like, pure, and luminous mind is likewise ineffable.
"Though among evil people, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas, one does not abandon the Great Way; this is the ninth.

When the wisdom of one's own realm is sovereign within the power of the Dharma, and having crossed to the other shore, one attains mastery through the wisdom of a bodhisattva, being fully endowed without remainder, one becomes an *anāvaraṇa* (one of unobstructed rank)."
Clad in the raiment of detachment, wearing the crown and turban of the Dharma, and girded with the seal and ribbon of the Way, they do not depart from the instructions of virtuous friends.
They revere the Tathāgata without ever showing contempt, even through their silence.

The Bodhisattva teacher cultivates what has never been done before to transform and enlighten sentient beings; he does not abandon the noble teacher, always accords with the Tathāgata, and reverently takes refuge [in him]. This is the tenth teaching of wordlessness.
When a bodhisattva abides in this, they attain the state of the World-Honored One’s unsurpassed silence.
There are ten activities of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?
The world of Universal Purity is adorned as the stage of Buddhahood, establishing all the spiritual practices of the Buddhas;
with the assembly of Bodhisattvas as its leaders, they share a common root of virtue;
it opens the way and instructs sentient beings within their respective realms.
All future karma is subsumed from its branches back to its root;
thus, by means of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), one reaches the realms of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions.

Although one pervades the ten directions, one does not depart from one's own land. Through the karma of radiance, immeasurable lights are manifested, and within each light there appear various lotuses upon which individual Bodhisattvas sit.
They do not sever the Three Jewels; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they propagate his teachings and instructions without any sense of self-importance;
they travel through the worlds of the ten directions to enlighten and transform sentient beings by preaching the Dharma, causing them to follow the disciplinary teachings;
and they cultivate the practice of the Eightfold Path.
When the mind is directed toward unwholesome actions, he manifests various vows for those beings to cause them all to be fully provided with;
these are the ten karmas.
Abiding in these, the bodhisattva attains the unsurpassed path of the Tathāgata.
“A bodhisattva’s body has ten aspects. What are these ten?
A bodhisattva, in the future, understands that all bodies are entirely unformed and non-existent;”
When the body of a bodhisattva appears, one knows that the bodies of all sentient beings are ungraspable;
the body of a bodhisattva has no ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), yet it manifests as being present in accordance with worldly conventions;
the body of a bodhisattva cannot be harmed, yet it displays the ultimate reality in accordance with worldly conventions.
The body of a bodhisattva is likewise inexhaustible; throughout the limits of future ages, it is never severed.
That body is firm and solid, such that no māras can destroy it;
that body is powerful and essential, such that no heterodox studies or various external arts can move it.
His body is without marks, yet he manifests all pure marks and the merit of a hundred blessings;
his body has no [physical] excellence, for he takes the characteristics of the Dharma as his manifold excellences—to him I bow my head in salutation.
That Bodhisattva-body is universally all-pervasive, such that the Tathāgatas and Arhats of the past, future, and present are unified within a single body.
These constitute the ten bodies.
When a bodhisattva abides in these, they attain the Tathāgata’s inexhaustible karma and the infinite Dharma-body.

When these words were spoken, the trichiliocosm shook with a great trembling; a vast radiance shone everywhere throughout the ten directions; the heavens rained down myriad flowers; and lutes and musical instruments sounded of their own accord without being struck.
All those who had gathered there rejoiced individually, saying:
"We are fortunate to have encountered this boundless path of illumination through the practice of making offerings.
Desiring to attain this Dharma, what should we practice?"
The Bodhisattva replied:

“I revere all dharmas, listen to the sutras with a single mind, and make offerings to the noble assembly. I honor the Dharma Master as I would the Buddha, regard all sentient beings with compassion as if they were my own marrow and bones, and dwell within the triple world like a lotus in water, radiant as the sun, and illuminating the darkness like the moon.”
"A practitioner who acts in this way will swiftly attain the True Dharma.
When these words were spoken, countless people all resolved their minds upon the Way.

The Bodhisattva Samantaprajñā again asked Samantabhadra: "What is called bodily action? What is its essence? What..."
What is meant by "speech"?
What is meant by "purity of mouth"?
And what is meant by "thorough purity"?
What is meant by "that which is protected and well-gathered"?
What is meant by the "teachings and precepts practiced by Bodhisattvas that constantly encourage and delight the realm of sentient beings"?
And what is meant by the "equanimous mind of a Bodhisattva"?
What is meant by "arousing the intention"?
What is meant by "the mind pervading"?
What are meant by the "faculties"?
What is meant by "aspiration" (志性)?
What is meant by "harmony of nature" (性和)?
What is meant by "timeliness" (應時)?
What is meant by "that which should be believed"?
What is meant by "entrance through belief into the world-realm"?
What is meant by "entrance through belief into the realm of sentient beings"?
What is meant by abiding?
What is meant by arising?
What is meant by practicing?
What is meant by accomplishment?
What is meant by losing the Dharma of the Buddha-way?
What is meant by tranquility?
What is called the ultimate dharma?
What is called the arising of the Buddha-dharma?
And what is called a true person (saddharmapuruṣa)?
What is meant by the "path"?
What is meant by the "immeasurable path"?
And what is meant by the "work of the Way"?
What is meant by practicing the Way?
What is meant by advancing in the Way?
What is meant by "practice"?
What is meant by the hand?
What is meant by the belly?
What is meant by the internal organs?

What is meant by the armor of virtue?
And what is meant by the staff?

What is called the eye?
What is called the ear?

And what is meant by "dwelling"?
