What is meant by a chamber?
"What is meant by 'dwelling and roaming'?
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva replied, "An excellent question! Listen attentively and receive it with care."
He replied, "So be it. Samantabhadra said:
"A Bodhisattva’s physical karma consists of ten matters. What are these ten?
Being able to pervade all Buddha-fields with a single body is called physical karma."
They manifest the gateway to all realms of sentient beings;
they dwell together with all those who are born,
yet they travel alone through the worlds of the ten directions.
They also all proceeded to the sites of the bodhimandas where the Buddhas were preaching the Dharma;
they were able to cover all the three-thousandfold world systems with a single hand, grasp the great Iron Ring Mountains and the multitude of diamond mountains with a single palm,
and manifest to sentient beings all Buddha-lands as being contained within their own bodies.
Furthermore, they cause [the world] to disperse and vanish;
they take the realm of sentient beings and receive it within a single body, dwelling in solitary concealment;
and yet again, they manifest that the awakening of all sentient beings resides within their own bodies, thereby accomplishing the adornment and purification of Buddha-lands.
These are the ten bodily actions.
When a bodhisattva abides in these, they thereby attain the unsurpassed Buddha-action, instructing all sentient beings so that they may all reach the Way.
"The essence of a bodhisattva consists of ten matters."
What are the ten? They are:
being able to practice and cultivate the six pāramitās;
being able to practice the four debts of gratitude and not abandoning sentient beings;
They cultivate boundless compassion, taking upon themselves in place of all sentient beings the suffering that those beings endure;
they do not grow weary or exhausted by the heavy burden of the five aggregates;
and with a body of infinite kindness, they universally protect all beings, causing them to attain salvation.
By means of the form of merit, he causes all people to look up to him with veneration and attain peace and liberation;
by means of the matter of noble wisdom—because it is of one identical substance with all Buddhas—he achieves fulfillment;
and because he has cast off all harmful and perilous dharmas, this is called the Dharma-body.
Through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they are able to manifest all gateways, supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*), and transformations;
whatever moves the essence of a bodhisattva, they attain perfect enlightenment with mastery over the Path—
this constitutes the ten essences.
When a bodhisattva abides in this, they are able to enter the unsurpassed great wisdom of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One.
There are ten matters regarding the speech of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?
When their speech is truthful, they use these teachings to bring peace and security to sentient beings;
with pure and harmonious words, they gladden the minds of all people;
and by refraining from false speech, they speak exactly as they say, expounding words of utmost sincerity.
In this way, the Bodhisattva remains without contradiction even within a dream;
his speech is consistent with reality and does not deceive Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Heavenly Kings;
it is profound, subtle, and harmless, capable of manifesting the teaching of spontaneity.
Their speech is steadfast, proclaiming all dharmas without limit;
they expound the path, transforming and guiding through every word;
according to the actions of beings, they explain their retributions and reveal their origins and endings.
Observing the dispositions of sentient beings, he instructs and exhorts them according to what is appropriate for each;
this is the Bodhisattva’s thorough mastery of the ten modes of speech.
There are ten matters by which a Bodhisattva becomes perfectly pure.
What are the ten? To delight in hearing the voice of the Tathāgata is purity;
to reflect upon the sounds previously heard by Bodhisattvas and distance oneself from what sentient beings do not enjoy hearing; and to cast away evil speech and not direct it toward others.
One should always distance oneself from the four verbal transgressions previously described;
with a joyful heart, one should praise the Tathāgata and proclaim his great voice;
and within the Buddha’s sacred shrines, one should sing in praise of the Buddha’s virtues.
They propagate the gift of Dharma for all sentient beings by means of their pure and harmonious nature;
they perform various musical performances, lutes, zithers, and flutes in venerable shrines to delight the Buddha’s stūpas and temples;
and they personally attend upon the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, to hear the sūtras.
To accord with heavenly blessings and follow all bodhisattvas;
to personally serve and attend upon a Dharma Master if one has heard the sutras through him, while the mind renounces the heavens—
these are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva expounds the teaching for the sake of wholesome purity.
“There are ten matters by which Bodhisattvas are protected and well-sustained. What are these ten?
All the celestial kings appear and together protect them;”
The Dragon Kings and the Ghost Kings all came forth to guard him overnight;
the Gandharvas and Asuras all came to pay him homage;
and the Garuḍas and the Kinnara Kings all came to settle him in peace.
The kiṃnaras and mahoragas all turned to him in devotion;
furthermore, Śakra, Lord of Devas, together with his retinue of devas, came to protect him;
and the Brahmā King, leading the various Brahmā devas, personally took refuge at his side.
All bodhisattvas together hold them in reverent mindfulness;
all those in their final birth before enlightenment who are non-retrogressive come to attend upon them;
and all Tathāgatas currently residing throughout the ten directions protect them with their majestic spiritual power.
These are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva provides protection and skillfully gathers [beings].
There are ten matters in which a bodhisattva practices the precepts and instructions. What are these ten?

Furthermore, they constantly encourage and gladden the realms of sentient beings; they likewise transform and guide the three thousandfold great thousand-world Buddha-lands; they are also able to enter all faculties, benefiting those of intermediate capacity as well as those who are weak and inferior; they adorn and purify according to each respective land; they eliminate all cravings, afflictions, and worldly toil; they remain far removed from all defilements; they abandon objective spheres while fully perceiving the location of the will and nature; they gradually increase and cultivate their pure and harmonious nature until it universally pervades the entire Dharma-realm; and by means of this, they swiftly approach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). These are the ten matters.
"Bodhisattvas have ten matters regarding the impartial mind (*samacitta*). What are these ten?
The impartial mind is a dhāraṇī that grasps all sentient beings, gathers the roots of all virtues, and ensures they are not lost."
The mind is like the rivers and seas, immeasurable and boundless, following the infinite wisdom of the path of all Buddha-dharmas;
the mind is like Mount Sumeru, its virtue surpassing all, establishing for sentient beings the roots of all goodness;
the mind is like a bright pearl, removing all defilements, with pure intention and thought.
The mind is like a vajra, destroying all defiled phenomena;
its mind is as firm as Mount Cakravāḍa, indestructible, such that no māras or heterodox teachers can move it;
the bodhisattva’s mind is like a lotus, dwelling within the triple world yet forever free from attachment.
The mind of that bodhisattva is like the auspicious *nirmāṇa-ratna* flower, difficult to see or hear of throughout incalculable eons;
his mind is like the brilliance of the sun, traversing the void to extinguish all darkness, obscurations, and the gloom of ignorance;
his mind is like space, taking pity upon all classes of living beings.
These are the ten mentalities of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are ten matters regarding the bodhisattva’s generation of the resolve. What are these ten?
He forms this thought and says:
"I shall bring joy to all living beings; I shall eliminate the afflictions and desires of all sentient beings so that they are forever left with nothing remaining."
He then gave rise to this thought:
"Having severed all obstacles and hindrances, he is entirely free from hesitation regarding all phenomena and has attained the state of tranquility."
"I shall pacify the suffering of the five aggregates for all sentient beings; I shall sever and eliminate the evil destinies and the eight difficulties.
I shall always universally behold all Tathāgatas and never depart from their presence;
I shall always diligently study the Bodhisattva precepts and accomplish the path of all Buddhas."
“‘Beholding all sentient beings universally, one resolves the mind [to attain enlightenment] for the sake of bringing them all to accomplishment and entry into the tracks of the Path.

One should know that the drum of the infinite Dharma resounds throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, universally gathering in the mental dispositions and faculties of all people without exception.”
These are the ten matters for which a bodhisattva generates the resolve.
Furthermore, there are ten matters regarding the pervasiveness of a bodhisattva’s mind. What are these ten?
Their intention is all-pervasive, as vast as empty space;
they enter the infinite dharma-realm of all things, simultaneously pervading the three periods of time.

Whatever the Buddhas manifest, they are able to fulfill completely—whether entering the womb and being born, renouncing their kingdoms and abandoning their thrones, attaining supreme perfect enlightenment, or manifesting great parinirvāṇa—all proceed from their noble wisdom.
Entering the realm of sentient beings, he comprehends their mental dispositions and discerns their faculties;
with the light of the sages, he pervades all lands of phenomena, reaching everywhere without limit;
he perceives that the various nets of illusion have no place of origin.
As for spontaneity, it is free from inversion and cannot be calculated or measured;
one's own mind is unimpeded, causing others to be free from obscuration;
and through radiant wisdom, one attains mastery.
When the Buddhas appear in the world, they manifest supreme perfect enlightenment wherever they first resolve their minds;
this is the tenth matter of the Bodhisattva’s pervasive intention.
There are ten matters regarding the faculties of a Bodhisattva.
What are the ten? When bodhisattvas behold the Buddhas, their faculties are filled with joy and they rejoice without turning back;
they take delight in the Buddhas, revere the scriptures, and there is nothing they do not penetrate.
The Bodhisattva does not turn back any of his faculties, remaining unobstructed;
his mind is always firmly established, such that none of his practices can be abandoned;
his faculties are subtle and refined, as he clearly understands and discerns the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).
The minds of all bodhisattvas neither advance nor retreat; they exhort and instruct sentient beings with a resolve as firm as a vajra.
They digest all phenomena and destroy all evils; their brilliance is steadfast and powerful, illuminating everything without exception.
Seeing the radiance of all Tathāgatas wherever it may be, their faculties remain free from confusion.
The mind of the Bodhisattva realizes that the bodies of the Tathāgatas are unified as a single essence;
the intention of the Bodhisattva reaches the infinite limit, entering into the ten powers of the Tathāgata.
These are the ten matters regarding the faculties of a Bodhisattva.
“There are ten matters concerning the nature and disposition of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?
There is the bodhisattva whose mind is always free from attachment and does not crave the mundane world;”
His mind is pure and transparent, free from fragmentation; he does not contemplate the matters of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, he reckons that the bodhisattva’s disposition is gentle and compliant, always intent upon the Buddha-way;
his intention is pure and harmonious, having arisen through omniscience (sarvajñatā).
That which they contemplate has no peer; it subdues all Māras and various heterodox teachers;
their resolve is without flaw, purifying the site of wisdom of all Tathāgatas;
and they are constantly skilled at rescuing and gathering in the beginning and end of the mind.
They never forget the Dharma as they have heard it;
their minds are naturally free from attachment and clinging, and in whatever place they are born, they harbor neither preference nor aversion.
Their resolve is profound and subtle, enabling them universally to enter into sublime wisdom; having reflected upon it, they attain faith and understanding, thereby comprehending all Buddha-dharmas.
These are the ten qualities of the nature of a bodhisattva.
"There are ten matters regarding the harmonious nature of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?
The nature of the bodhisattva is harmonious; though his mind aspires toward the most exalted and noble states, he does not regress.

He accumulates all manner of virtues and wholesome dharmas, harbors no doubt regarding the Buddhas, and praises the fundamental and derivative qualities of the Tathāgata’s conduct, remaining steadfast in comprehensive mastery.
Acting as a great master, their vows are heard in unison;
with mindfulness fixed upon the mark of the uṣṇīṣa, they are able to universally and completely enter into the naturally pure nature of all Buddha-dharmas;
regarding all Buddha-dharmas, they attain mastery through themselves.
His intention is subtle and wondrous, able to enter the gateways to the paths of various dharmas;
as a leader among bodhisattvas, he transcends all causal conditions of existence;
he is self-reliant on the Path, and regarding the various samādhis and meditative attainments, he purifies his transformations with a mind firmly established.
To embrace the vows made in previous lives and to teach and transform sentient beings without ever resting—
this is the tenth purity of nature of a bodhisattva.
There are ten matters regarding the timely conduct of a bodhisattva.
What are these ten?
When a bodhisattva practices giving, it is timely; they give all that they possess without harboring any expectations.
They uphold all precepts, maintaining the boundaries of their moral virtue with purity and diligent cultivation; they practice in accordance with the proper time and do not look down upon others.
For the sake of sentient beings, they endure all anger, weariness, and resentment;
they eliminate notions of self and others, universally cultivate diligence without wavering according to the occasion;
they guard their body and speech, their minds remain without forgetfulness, and they set aside worldly affairs to dwell in dhyāna and samādhi.
They follow the correctness of the various gates of liberation and supernormal powers, yet do not abandon desire, worldly toil, or their retinues;
if they can practice the various perfections (pāramitās), accumulate myriad virtues without ever slackening, and cultivate great kindness (maitrī);
understanding that there are no sentient beings, they shoulder manifold sufferings, manifesting five grades of response bodies (nirmāṇakāya) without abandoning great compassion (mahākaruṇā).
To understand that all phenomena are naturally quiescent; to awaken through the Tathāgata’s ten powers according to the occasion;

to manifest for the sake of the common people with boundless appropriateness; to turn the wheel of Dharma without ever harboring thoughts of retreat; and to instruct others by perceiving their dispositions—these are the ten matters in which a bodhisattva acts in accordance with the timing.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this, they attain the unsurpassed, infinite, great wisdom of a Buddha and are thus able to act according to the occasion.
Furthermore, there are ten matters regarding a bodhisattva’s faith and understanding. What are these ten?
He has faith in the subtle and ever accords with what is appropriate;
his roots of virtue are difficult to equal, as he is steadfast in countless and manifold pure practices;
his excellence is vast and universal, perceiving the infinite minds of sentient beings.
They cultivate faith that is profoundly tranquil, entering the deep and boundless Dharma-gate;
they delight in purity, give rise to vast and far-reaching resolve, and cherish what they aspire to;
because the Buddhas have established the ten powers, they are peerlessly humble and respectful, subduing all Māras and their retinues.
Ultimate wholesome karma is equal to its retribution;
being steadfast at the gateway, one manifests according to what is pleasing;
receiving that which is received means attaining the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas.
With mastery over the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*), they act according to their own inclinations; if they wish to attain the Buddha-way, they immediately achieve perfect enlightenment.
These are the ten matters of a bodhisattva’s faith and understanding.
"There are also ten matters by which a bodhisattva enters into faith regarding the world.
What are these ten? They are:
believing that all buddha-fields enter into a single world;
and causing a single world to enter into all buddha-fields.
One believes that a single lotus flower is like a great trichiliocosm, and that a single Tathāgata’s body sits pervasively upon it throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions;
one understands and believes that all things are spontaneously so, like space,
and that all worlds are universally and completely adorned.
Within the sphere of faith, they enter the worlds of the ten directions, and their bodhisattva bodies are able to pervade them all;
they believe that the lands of the ten directions can be established within a single footprint;
and they cause all worlds to enter the body of a single person, thereby manifesting and expanding therein.
The buddha-fields extend as far as the tree of the Tathāgata, encompassing the entire circle of the site of enlightenment;
with a single voice, he addresses all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and those who hear it find joy in their hearts—
these are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva enters into faith regarding the world.
Being able to abide herein, one universally enters the immeasurable realms of the Tathāgata.
There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva enters the realm of sentient beings. What are these ten?
All bodily forms are naturally bodiless;
the realms of all sentient beings constitute a single body;
the Hall of Self-Indulgence is the place where faith enters.
The realm of all sentient beings enters the belly of a single bodhisattva;
the world of the masses assumes the forms and appearances of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings;
and one believes that the realm of sentient beings enters the body of the Tathāgata.
The inhabitants of the ten directions—the crawling, the breathing, and the human beings throughout the lands—enter into the body of a single person;
all sentient beings are able to abide within a single category of Buddha-dharma;
they manifest the realms of all living beings, appearing in the forms and likenesses of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet forever remaining free from conceptual thought.
In all worlds of the ten directions, they manifest the magnificent merits and virtues of bodhisattvas;
within the realms of all sentient beings, they manifest the physical forms, marks and signs, various bodies, and dignified deportment of the Tathāgatas to instruct and admonish the multitudes.
These are the ten ways in which bodhisattvas enter the realms of sentient beings.
“There are ten matters concerning the dwelling place of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?
To resolve upon the mind of a bodhisattva is their dwelling place;”
Cultivating the roots of all virtues, they cause all evils to cease;
transforming and enlightening sentient beings, they guide and instruct them according to the occasion;
constantly beholding all Buddhas, they never depart from the assembly of sages.
Wherever they wish to be reborn, they immediately attain their place;
they cultivate and practice the path within pure realms;
they do not deviate from the true and correct, and always maintain right aspirations.
They do not follow false vows, but are all able to observe and uphold the six perfections;
they single-mindedly and diligently contemplate the Dharma of the Equal Way;
and wherever they dwell or travel, they associate with the Buddhas.
These are the ten dwelling places of the bodhisattva.
When a bodhisattva abides in these, they cast off all worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) without remainder and attain the immeasurable state of wisdom of a Tathāgata; this is their place of residence.
"There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva gives rise to [resolve], and by these a bodhisattva severs all conditioned activities. What are the ten?
When the realm of sentient beings arises, one transforms and delivers them, leading them to ultimate completion."
If the world arises, one eliminates its defilements and constantly keeps it pure and adorned;
as the Tathāgata appears, one attains the practices of a bodhisattva;
one gives rise to the roots of all virtues through accumulation, and cultivates the marks and signs of a Buddha.
Merit arises from great compassion, which eliminates the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings and the decay of the blazing five aggregates;
it issues forth from great compassion to exhort and establish sentient beings in the peace of all-knowledge;
and it gathers together the boundless perfections and the solemn, pure practices of Bodhisattvas.
They give rise to skillful means to universally manifest the gateway to the Way and its Virtue for all beings;
they arouse the aspiration for enlightenment, their minds becoming serene and beyond measure.
To state the essential point:
All dharmas arise from the Bodhisattva; wherever they manifest transformations, they are understood through supernormal powers.
These are the ten arisings of the Bodhisattva.
"There are ten matters that a Bodhisattva should practice and uphold."

What are these ten? They are: constantly reflecting upon the various *pāramitās*; upholding and practicing the prohibitions and precepts without deficiency or leakage; following and inheriting noble wisdom without succumbing to false views; conforming to propriety and righteousness without ever losing one's integrity; honoring and exalting the Way and its teachings without following false views; ranking and categorizing according to the times without violating high principles; manifesting at the appropriate time without transgressing the teachings of the Way; drawing near to and practicing righteous conduct without wearying of instruction; upholding and correcting right awakening without following the Lesser Vehicle; and inheriting the noble practices to turn the wheel of the Dharma. These are the ten matters that a bodhisattva should practice and uphold.
“There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva achieves accomplishment. What are these ten? They are:
always maintaining sincere faith;”
By revering and honoring virtuous friends, one attains the Buddha-dharma;
with earnest devotion, one cherishes what the Tathāgata has spoken, never slandering or disparaging the teachings of the true scriptures;
their mind is immeasurable, abiding in the boundless.
They encourage and assist in the roots of virtue, reaching the realm of the Tathāgatas without limit;
with faith and joy free from doubt, they are able to universally enter the worlds of the ten directions to bring about the Buddha-dharma;
furthermore, they are unshakable within the dharma-realm, their minds as steadfast as Mount Tai.
They shall not attain mastery over the realms of Māra, but shall naturally subdue them;
they shall constantly and fully recognize and remember the realms of all Buddhas;
and in instructing sentient beings, they shall always inwardly contemplate the ten kinds of wisdom-power of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One.
These are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva achieves success.
"There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva loses the Dharma of the Buddha-way; one should always remain far removed from them. What are these ten?"
Being arrogant by nature, they slight their virtuous friends and lose the teachings of the Buddha-way;
fearing the afflictions of birth, death, and exhaustion,
they grow weary of all practices and deviate from the mind of a bodhisattva.
Toiling throughout the world, moving about and resting;
his conduct must be firmly rooted in his nature, for to deviate from right concentration is to lose the trace of equanimity.
The root of virtue he has cultivated is named:
"Thinking, 'This was done by me,' they harbor jealousy and slander the True Dharma;
they obscure and conceal the practices of all Bodhisattvas."
To delight in the teachings of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

to loathe the great practice and take no pleasure in proclaiming the Great Dharma of the bodhisattvas—these are the ten ways in which a bodhisattva loses the path. One should always remain far from them in order to enter the unsurpassed state of the bodhisattva sages.
“There are ten matters concerning the profound stillness of a bodhisattva.
What are these ten? They are:
being able to constantly and diligently cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā);”
He observes sentient beings to eliminate their various inversions;
he delivers them from the bonds of all false views;
and he never gives rise to the intent to seek after delusive thoughts, but instead transforms those who are attached and who crave delusive thoughts.
Transcending the three realms, they circulate through all worlds of the ten directions, dwelling and roaming therein;
they transform sentient beings who are attached to the various afflictions and habituated to negligence, causing them to leave behind the laws of craving and desire;
they give rise to great compassion and pity for all the multitudes, eliminating all that is possessed while yet manifesting all manner of kinsmen.
They shake all worlds, manifesting both beginning and end to demonstrate their practice;
they roam through worldly dharmas without attachment, yet they enter into those teachings according to the times;
they fully perceive the Buddha-way, never ceasing their great deeds and never fearing their original vows.
These are the ten matters of tranquility for bodhisattvas; as noble ones who have transcended the world, they gather and protect the masses, surpassing the deeds of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"There are ten matters by which bodhisattvas attain the ultimate Dharma."

What are these ten? They are: being born with sovereign mastery upon descending to earth; reaching the ultimate fulfillment of the realm of all Buddhas; achieving the accomplishment of all bodhisattva deeds; being fully endowed with all the *pāramitās*; causing the lineage of the Buddhas to flourish and be filled; surpassing the ranks of other Tathāgatas; constantly establishing the ten powers of the Buddhas; eternally reaching the ultimate fulfillment of the Great Way of the Tathāgata; understanding that all Buddhas are of one and the same *dharmakāya*; and realizing that the conduct of the Tathāgatas, the Truly Realized Ones, is non-dual. These are the ten ultimate dharmas of a bodhisattva.
“There are ten things by which a bodhisattva gives rise to all Buddha-dharmas. What are these ten?
First, taking refuge with a single mind and honoring virtuous spiritual friends, thereby giving rise to all Buddha-dharmas up to the root of a single virtue.”
Faithful delight in the Buddha-dharma gives rise to the tracks of the Path;
in the mere instant of generating the resolve, one is able to manifest all the practices of the Tathāgatas;
and by having attained the embrace of infinite great vows, one gives birth to the vast mind.
They take delight in their own roots of virtue, never forgetting or losing what they have established, and never becoming weary or disheartened;
they fully encompass all future boundless realms through the practices accumulated over incalculable eons;
dwelling and being born in immeasurable Buddha-lands, they transform sentient beings, constantly engaging in Bodhisattva practices according to the seasons, never interrupting their course.
Constantly giving rise to great compassion and manifesting the immeasurable mind, when a single thought arises, one universally perceives the void;
having attained entry into the extraordinary and sublime Great Practice, one gives birth to the vow of ultimate truth and does not lose the original intent;
upholding all the instructions of the Tathāgatas, one illuminates sentient beings to inspire the aspiration for the Way and fulfills all dharmas of virtue.
These are the ten path-ways that a bodhisattva brings forth.
There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva is designated as a "Righteous Being" (samyaksaṃbuddha). What are these ten?
Because the bodhisattva understands that the Buddha’s wisdom constitutes a single Dharma-body, he is called an *ādikarmika* (open-minded one);
because he firmly abides in the Mahāyāna, he is termed a *mahāsattva* (great being);
and because he practices the sublime Dharma, he is called a venerable person (*puruṣa*).
Because they have realized the sublime Dharma, they are called Noble Ones (*ārya*);
because they have entered into transcendent wisdom, they are called Transcendental Ones;
because they exhort others to diligent effort, they are called Superior Ones.
Because he proclaims the most sublime Dharma, he is called "Unsurpassed";
because he is fully endowed with and understands the wisdom of the ten powers, he is called a "Powerful One" (Baladeva);
because he has eliminated all darkness and obscurations, he is called "Peerless."
The peerless person, whose mind attains realization through their own effort and immediately achieves the Buddha-way, is titled "Inconceivable.
These are the ten titles of the Bodhisattvas as Righteous Persons.
"There are ten matters regarding the path traveled by Bodhisattvas.
What are these ten?
The assembly of bodhisattvas shares a single path with the One Vehicle that is peerless and incomparable, never abandoning the single mind.
That bodhisattvas possess practice, wisdom, and skillful means constitutes the path of the two natures.
"Furthermore, there are three paths:
to cultivate the foundation of emptiness and signlessness is to reach the limitless; not to rely on wishlessness, one wanders through the triple world without being defiled."
"Furthermore, there are four paths:
practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva; expounding inexhaustible karma;
and being able to encourage and assist all merits."
Bowing one's head to the Tathāgata, one should serve and revere him without slackening;
one should encourage and assist his holy wisdom and skillfully proclaim the teachings of the Way.
This increases the path of the five faculties:

He firmly establishes the faculty of faith; he exerts great diligence in all practices; he dwells in non-retrogression with a single-mindedness that is undisturbed; he possesses excellent awakening in accordance with the concentrated mind; and he is constantly and clearly aware of the practice of wisdom.
"Cultivating the six supernormal powers serves as the path:
with the divine eye, one perceives all forms and images, beholding the various classes of sentient beings throughout the worlds—those who are being born and those who are dying;
and with the divine ear, one hears the sūtras spoken by the Buddhas and upholds them."

They perceive other sentient beings as objects of discernment; they observe their own minds and behold the intentions of others. They master the countless and immeasurable thoughts from beginning to end, all of which proceed from themselves.
They recollect the roots of virtue cultivated throughout incalculable kalpas of the past, fully knowing what is appropriate for their further advancement.

Having attained great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), they manifest various transformations according to the fundamental dispositions of those to be converted, thereby instructing and admonishing sentient beings with the True Dharma.
With wisdom, they exhaust all outflows and personally perceive the original limit, yet they do not sever the practices established by Bodhisattvas.
Practicing the seven recollections is the path of the Bodhisattva:

constantly recollecting the Buddha, the guide of sentient beings who is without bound; seeing and immediately upholding all phrases [of the Dharma], and exhorting and transforming others to take refuge in the Buddha themselves.

He contemplates the sutras and dharmas, the Tathāgata, and the Truly Realized One; he never moves from a single place of practice, yet he appears universally in the assemblies of all Buddhas to manifest his own preaching of the Dharma, his voice resonating throughout the ten directions.

Knowing the dispositions and faculties of all sentient beings, he transforms and guides them. His mind and thoughts remain with the Sangha—the countless bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive—perceiving them as never departing from his count and beholding all sentient beings.
These bodhisattvas constantly contemplate giving; they bestow gifts upon other bodhisattvas, maintaining equanimity of mind, and reflect upon great generosity so that their merit may increase.
He constantly maintains the prohibitive precepts and does not abandon the bodhicitta, bestowing the roots of all virtues upon sentient beings;
he constantly remembers the devas, for the Bodhisattva is born in the Tuṣita Heaven as one destined for the single seat of succession;

being hungry and empty, he contemplates virtue and constantly thinks of sentient beings, transforming and enlightening them through great skillful means and wisdom, such that no one can obstruct his eloquence.
"As for that Eightfold Noble Path:
one upholds right view and abandons all false views;

one discards all deluded thoughts and the pursuit of various cravings, and instead constantly contemplates the wisdom of all supernormal powers. One cultivates the lineage of the Way and its Virtue, abandons the four faults of speech, and practices the lineage of the sages by proclaiming right speech. All actions of the body are performed as giving to sentient beings; one instructs and exhorts all people without weariness or indolence, never forsaking the Right Discipline."

As for their primary practice, they dwell firmly and with mastery, remaining secluded and content; they cultivate their virtue and morality, abiding in propriety and dignified demeanor, and dwelling in the True Dharma without ever erring or failing.

As for their correct means, because these bodhisattvas are brothers born of the same womb, the retinues they behold suffer no depletion; they follow and cultivate the ten kinds of power-exertion of the Tathāgata.

As for their right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), they are able to retain all sounds they hear and universally perceive the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions; their concentrated mind remains undisturbed.
As for their right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), it takes the inconceivable states of the bodhisattvas as its gate of liberation;

because of their intelligence, through a single state of concentration they pervade countless concentrations, entering the fundamental absorption of right concentration (*samāpatti*) without ever relinquishing that concentration, serving as the path of the bodhisattvas.

“Free from the traces of harm within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all that he preaches and proclaims with his voice is unimpeded; he explains the attachments of thoughts and perceptions to enlighten sentient beings and lead them into omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Having abandoned hope and relinquished all craving, he constantly desires to behold all Tathāgatas.

With a joyful heart, never wearying or indolent, he abandons the worldly karma of pleasure and pain, manifesting the noble Bodhisattvas who transcend the world. He eternally abides in the wisdom of the Path, cultivating the understanding of impermanence and the meditative concentration of formlessness (*ārūpyasamādhi*).

Whether born in the desire realm or dwelling in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), he is initially unmoving; having transcended all perceptions and the sounds encountered through right reception (*samāpatti*), his Bodhisattva practice does not become a weariness.”
"If one can contemplate the ten powers of the Tathāgata, O Son of the Buddha!
This shall dispatch you upon the path of the bodhisattvas, enabling you to constantly and clearly understand what is possible and impossible, as well as the finite and the infinite."

He perceives the retributions of all sentient beings across the past, future, and present, as well as the destinations of their transgressions and merits; he knows all their consciousnesses and faculties, discerning them with perfect clarity, and having examined the fundamental nature of their minds, he preaches the Dharma for them.

They manifest various kinds of bodies, beyond measure and each distinct, whether their aspirations are directed toward the highest, the intermediate, or the lower realms; they understand these to be boundless as they proclaim the Dharma.
Throughout all buddha-fields—wherever sentient beings dwell across the three periods of time and throughout incalculable eons—the bodies of all bodhisattvas completely pervade them.

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, manifests a state free from conceptual thought, yet he does not abandon or neglect the various bodhisattva practices or the states of meditative concentration; with a single mind in right reception, he encounters worldly afflictions and anger.

Observing their advances and retreats, he knows the causes from which they arise; abiding in the gateway of the bodhisattva, he beholds the destinies of birth and death to which all sentient beings go and explains their origins and ends.

Knowing the various perceptions and thoughts across the three periods of time, he enters into a single lifetime to comprehend the afflictions, hindrances, dispositions, and the knots of bondage or liberation of all living beings, causing them all to be completely eradicated, yet never abandoning the manifest practices initiated by a bodhisattva.
These are the ten paths; when a bodhisattva abides in them, they fully attain the supreme skillful means of the Tathāgata.
The paths traversed by a bodhisattva are immeasurable, their realization is boundless, and the purification of these practiced paths is incalculable and beyond reckoning.
Why is this so? There are ten matters regarding the immeasurable practice of the bodhisattva. What are these ten?

Observing the void, it is incalculable; within the midst of the Dharma-realm, that which turns toward the profound and possesses the profound is entirely immeasurable. Because the varieties of sentient beings are exceedingly numerous, they cannot be exhausted; because worlds have no boundaries, they are called infinite. Furthermore, all evil thoughts are bottomless, and the speech of all common folk is likewise without foundation. The body of the Tathāgata cannot be measured; the sounds and verbal teachings expounded by all Buddhas can never be fully exhausted. The power of the Tathāgata’s Way cannot be fathomed, and the sagely source of the wisdom and insight of omniscience is also without limit. These are the ten infinities of the Bodhisattva path.
Why is this so? Just as space is immeasurable, the cultivation of the Way should likewise be immeasurable;
just as the Dharma-realm is profoundly mysterious, the immeasurable accord with the meaning of the Way should likewise be so.
Just as the realm of sentient beings is exceedingly vast and inexhaustible, so too is the bodhisattva’s devotion to the Way inexhaustible;
if the worlds have no boundaries, so too is their progress on the Way;
if evil thoughts are incalculable and beyond description, so too is their compliance with the Way and transformation of others.
Just as the words of common people have no limit, so too is the conformity to the Way;

just as the practices of the Tathāgata cannot be calculated, and all sentient beings do not belong to two separate realms, such that his mindfulness is all-pervasive, so too is the practice of the Way;

just as the Buddha’s voice and verbal teachings can never be exhausted, so too is the cultivation of the Way, whereby a single word of instruction universally proclaims itself to all beings throughout the Dharma-realm.
If the power of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible, so too is the cultivation of the path through the power of the Tathāgata;
as omniscience is incalculable, so too is the bodhisattva’s accumulation of merit and cultivation of the path.
This is what is meant by the immeasurable path of the bodhisattva.
“There are ten matters regarding the path of a bodhisattva’s practice. What are these ten? They are:
there is no practice that is not practiced, and there is what should be given and what should not be given;”

Their body, speech, and mind have no point of convergence; they neither rise nor fall. Their wisdom is fundamentally pure, and thus it is made so. There is no honoring or non-honoring, no cultivation or non-cultivation;
they enter into spontaneity (*svabhāva*), which is like a phantom, a dream, a shadow, an echo, a plantain tree, a flash of lightning, a mirage, or the moon reflected in water.

Having understood all this, they harbor no dependence or seeking. They realize that the triple world is empty, signless, and wishless, entirely without a place of abode; yet, due to conceptualization and perception, there appear these three realms.
Accumulating these merits, they do not neglect their practice;
their minds possess nothing and are invisible, being without speech or instruction, and detached from all phenomena;
wherever they dwell and move, they reverently cultivate the Dharma-realm without causing any disruption.

Being able to know and observe, entering into all dharmas without losing the Tathāgata’s true reality (*tattva*) and original limit (*koṭi*)—this true reality being that which universally pervades the limits of space—one enters the wisdom, practices, powers, and activities of a bodhisattva, never becoming weary of the Tathāgata’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses;
as a treasury of omniscience, one examines all things with equanimity and contemplates all dharmas without harboring hesitation.
These are the ten matters of the bodhisattva’s path of practice.
“Bodhisattvas have ten ways of practicing the path that are adorned and purified. What are these ten?
O Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhisattva remains unmoved while in the desire realm, yet suddenly appears in the form realm; practicing in accordance with its manifestations, he enters the gate of single-minded liberation, attaining meditative absorption with a concentrated mind. In whatever place he is born, he is free from negligence; this is the first path of purity.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva beholds with his own eyes the vehicle of the śrāvakas and delivers them by means of wisdom, yet does not fall upon that path himself—this is the second path of purity."
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva contemplates and understands the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, clearly comprehends the appropriate timing, gives rise to great compassion, and attains the various powers and vows without negligence or abandonment—this is the third path of purification."
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is surrounded by a great multitude of followers and retinues; accompanied by gods and humans, pure and upright, they play hundreds of thousands of musical instruments. Countless jade maidens with lutes and harps produce harmonious and melodious sounds as they ride upon a grand carriage."
"Bodhisattvas abide within meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and right attainments, following the Way without deviation; these are the four pure paths.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

When a bodhisattva is among all sentient beings engaged in song, dance, or playful diversion, they act in accordance with what others do, appearing to participate in their activities while always maintaining a single-minded focus; the bodhisattva’s concentrated mind never becomes distracted—this is the fifth path of purification.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva has already transcended worldly dharmas and is entirely unattached to all karmic actions, yet does not abandon the path of deliverance to rescue and gather in sentient beings—this is the sixth path of purity."
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva abides in the Way, they manifest noble wisdom to enter the right path and transcend all false views. Remaining upon the wrong paths, they instruct and admonish sentient beings so that they may attain liberation; yet they do not become defiled by associating with those on the wrong paths. This is the seventh path of purification."
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no deficiency or leakage in body, speech, or mind, nor does he guard the precepts in a narrow sense; rather, he nurtures the pure prohibitions of the Tathāgata, manifests pure conduct for the sake of the masses of foolish and ignorant ordinary beings, and teaches those with evil precepts so that they may universally fulfill all pure merit."
The path by which Bodhisattvas proceed eliminates the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, leading beings to the three auspicious paths.

Even when currently lacking leisure or being born in places of manifold hardships and poverty, they reach those locations to diligently rescue sentient beings; though they roam among them, they do not become entangled with them—this is the eighth path of purity.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

That which the Bodhisattva does is not to rely upon or look up to others; rather, he attains unimpeded eloquence regarding the Buddha-dharma. He universally contemplates all Buddhas and attains the light of wisdom of the Dharma; he regards all Tathāgatas as being without distinct forms or seeds, for all Buddhas are but a single Dharmakāya."

The Buddhas guide and benefit all beings through the Dharma-gate of universal illumination for the sake of all; they abide equally within all vehicles, and the Buddhas’ dwellings and movements are all present before one’s eyes.

Although all common folk are collectively incapable of bearing this, sentient beings see their forms and hear their reprimands face-to-face, reaching a state of unprecedented wonder; yet all are universally equal, and the Dharma they seek is never forgotten.

Regarding the teachers who appear before them, they receive [teachings] from whomever and revere them all; they rise to welcome them, giving rise to wonder because of this, and receiving [the teachings] on that account.
Their practice of the Dharma is directed toward sentient beings.
Why is this? It is because of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

When a bodhisattva practices the true reality (*satya*) of a bodhisattva and abides in the path of practice (*mārga-karma*), they immediately employ skillful means to lead sentient beings so that they may follow the teachings of the discipline (*vinaya*). By manifesting these provisional paths, each being is enabled to find their proper place; this is the ninth path of purity.
"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhisattva gathers the roots of all virtues and attains the most supreme and wondrous Dharma of the Bodhisattvas. He is universally endowed with the conduct of the Tathāgata’s *anavaya* (unexcelled) state; he is the infinite liberation of the Honored One of All Dharmas. He fastens the crown of the immeasurable, stainless Dharma and ties the pure silk as his sash."
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they manifest the bodies of countless Tathāgatas, turning the wheel of Dharma without exhaustion.
Their bodies pervade all Buddha-lands; they roam among all dharmas, stride alone through the triple world, cross over to the other shore, and have attained mastery alongside all bodhisattvas.

Born in the lands of the ten directions, they appear before the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; in teaching and transforming sentient beings, they all manifest within a single Buddha-realm. Furthermore, they do not violate or lose any of the bodhisattva practices, do not become confused regarding the wisdom of the Path, and do not regress by failing to accord with the fundamental source of the virtues of an *ārya* (bodhisattva).

They tread the tracks of the Bodhisattvas without turning back; they practice the deeds of the Mahāsattvas without indolence or negligence; they do not sever the reception of the teachings of the True Beings (samyaksaṃbuddha); they do not abandon skillful means (upāyakauśalya), nor do they neglect the work of the sages; they do not contravene the power of the Bodhisattva’s conduct; they do not inflict harm upon others; and they do not distance themselves from the right practice established by the holy beings.
Why is this? Because in this way, a bodhisattva swiftly attains the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.

Thus, the bodhisattva practices non-attachment, contemplates all-knowledge, and clearly perceives the essence of the Tathāgata as being without form or appearance; these constitute the ten paths of purity.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this, they swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed great path of a Tathāgata.
"O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten practices for a bodhisattva to carry out."
What are the ten? They are:
cultivating the precepts with great and extraordinary vows until they are gradually perfected;
practicing with diligent effort, embracing all the meanings of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) without turning back.
They follow the practice of divine conduct, causing the aspirations of all beings to be individually gladdened;
they cultivate the practice of the bases of spiritual power, universally entering the buddha-lands of the ten directions and unifying them into a single realm without wavering;
they resolve to uphold purity and harmony, thereby attaining entry into the sublime and wondrous.
Their vows are firm, such that all their undertakings are accomplished;
if they receive a submissive victory, they do not transgress the commands of their honored teachers;
in seeking to hear the scriptures, they act without weariness, and in reverently practicing the Dharma proclaimed by the Buddhas, they do not regard it as toil.
Revering the sacred nature of the Dharma, they traverse all assemblies and sites of enlightenment with courage and without timidity;
they engage in the purity of infinite great practice and understand that all things are fundamentally unarisen—this constitutes the ten practices.
When a bodhisattva abides in this, they travel universally through all buddha-lands in the ten directions without any hindrance.
There are ten kinds of hands of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?
That is to say:
the hand of profound faith, which believes in the teachings of the Tathāgata with single-minded devotion and joy that is inexhaustible;
and the hand that makes offerings to all Buddhas and Perfectly Awakened Ones, accumulating great merit and increasing it without weariness.
The hand of relinquishment, which causes all seekers to find joy and fulfills their aspirations;
the hand of greeting that precedes speech with "Excellent!
(Sādhu); the right palm extended, the hand of vast learning that severs all hesitation, the web of fetters, and brings tranquility to the three realms.
The Great Roaming Hand: love and desire are impermanent; with this great hand, one should transform the realms of sentient beings and bestow what is given.
The Hand Abiding in the Ground of Peace: awakening to the four torrents; the Arm of the Infinite Crossing: comprehensively gathering the inner treasury.

Practicing impartial conduct as the teacherless Dharma, transforming all sentient beings without giving rise to a harmful mind, and expounding the sutras; the Hand of Clear Knowledge of Mundane and Transcendent Dharmas: able to eliminate all calamities and ailments of body and mind.
With the jewel-hand of wisdom, they extinguish the afflictions and manifest the radiance of the light of immeasurable dharmas;
these are the ten kinds of hands of a bodhisattva, by which their hands of the Way extensively cover all things.
“A bodhisattva’s abdomen has ten qualities.
What are these ten? They are as follows:”
Their mental disposition is vast, and their thoughts are pure and harmonious;
they possess a storehouse of integrity and straightforwardness, free from flattery and devoid of false pretenses, remaining entirely without attachment;
they have no realm of causal conditions and take no delight in any worldly activities whatsoever.
Having eliminated all worldly afflictions, one takes wisdom as the womb;
the mind is pure and free from blemish;
one contemplates the severance of all sustenance, reflects upon the Dharma of the True Truths, and observes that all phenomena are non-existent.
Because they have clearly understood the twelve links of dependent origination, they discern all karmic actions of birth and death;
because their will and nature are supple and pure,
they eliminate all extreme and heterodox views.
To serve as the womb for bodhisattvas, universally causing all sentient beings to enter the treasury of the Buddha-way;
these are the ten matters that constitute the womb of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas have ten treasuries.

What are these ten? They are: not severing the Buddha’s teaching; abiding in the bodhisattva practice; honoring the teachings of all Buddhas; attaining the manifestation of the blazing Dharma-instructions through non-negligence;
being the womb for bodhisattvas; abiding in infinite wisdom; manifesting transcendence from the world; and following the noble assembly.
To be the embryo of a bodhisattva, abiding in non-retrogression while turning the wheel of Dharma, necessarily arises from the remnants of the wholesome dharmas of sentient beings;

to be the embryo of a bodhisattva, dwelling at all times without losing the seasonal rhythm of the Way, ultimately transforming and enlightening those sentient beings who remain in a state of indecision;

to be the embryo of a bodhisattva, establishing retributions for each so that they may cross over, ensuring there is no interruption, and giving rise to great compassion for sentient beings situated upon the ground of false views.

As the womb of a bodhisattva, one gives rise to and kindles the ten powers of the Tathāgata of Infinite Radiance in the future, cultivating and practicing their retributive responses so that they are fully perfected;
as the womb of a bodhisattva, one subdues all māras, possessing peerless roots of virtue and great fearlessness, and utters the lion’s roar;
thus, abiding in the single station of the bodhisattva-womb, one gladdens sentient beings, causes them to be free from all doubt, and attains the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

To serve as the womb for bodhisattvas, benefiting all through the path of noble wisdom; to encourage and assist the Buddha-way wherever the teachings of the Buddhas exist throughout the lands of the ten directions;
to serve as the womb for bodhisattvas, giving birth to them without distinction and causing them to enter into a single wisdom—these are the ten wombs of a bodhisattva.
"The mental karma of a bodhisattva has ten aspects. What are these ten?
As for the karma of their thoughts, everything they undertake is immediately accomplished."
With a mind free from cowardice, he accumulates merit and cultivates the primary and secondary marks;
with great compassion in his stride, he subdues all the hosts of Māras;
acting with compassion according to the occasion, he eliminates all worldly afflictions and sensual desires.
They cultivate non-retrogression and never turn back from their practice of great compassion;
reaching the Buddha’s place of enlightenment, they manifest primordial purity and radiance, with minds that reach nowhere and are entirely without dependence;
out of pity they enter among sentient beings, transforming them according to their inclinations.
They cultivate the great Brahma-conduct and enter into all Buddha-dharmas, taking no pleasure in other paths while rescuing and delivering sentient beings;
through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they reach the state of non-existence, abandoning all false views yet not forsaking the triple world;

they manifest all manner of adornments as a vajra-realm, firm and indestructible, such that even if all beings were to become Māras, they could not shake a single hair of the virtuous conduct initiated by the Bodhisattva.
These are the ten forms of compassion.
"There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva dons the armor of virtue. What are these ten?"
Donning the armor of great compassion, they protect and sustain the common people;
cultivating infinite pity, they endure all manner of suffering;
and donning the armor of their vows and aspirations, they are fully able to exhaustively master all skillful means.
Donning the armor of exhortation and assistance, they personally uphold the pure conduct of all Buddhas;
raising the armor of merit, they cause all sentient beings to receive its grace;
through all the perfections (pāramitās), they ferry across the multitudes.
The armor of noble wisdom eliminates all afflictions and sensual desires;
through skillful means and expedient methods, one plants the roots of myriad virtues;
leading and benefiting all through universal gates, the mind of omniscience remains untroubled and undisturbed, its intent unchanging.
First is the armor of resolute virtue, maintaining mindfulness of the Dharma in one's heart without negligence;
this is the tenth armor of virtue of a bodhisattva for subduing all māras.
There are ten matters concerning the staff of a bodhisattva.

What are these ten? The staff of giving subdues all stinginess and greed; the staff of practicing the precepts destroys and eliminates all transgressions and manifold evils; the staff of equal exhortation through the Dharma dispels delusive thoughts; the staff of wisdom cuts off the afflictions and desires of sentient beings; the staff of right livelihood distances one from all ignorant means of subsistence; the staff of skillful means universally manifests within the confusion of lust, anger, and ignorance; the Bodhisattva uses these Dharma-staves to dissolve all the gates of desire and defilement in sentient beings; when amidst birth and death, they use the power of wisdom to sever defiled conduct and transform others; the staff of preaching the One Dharma destroys all dependencies; and the gate of omniscience is able to eliminate all rebellious tendencies—these are the ten staves wielded by the Bodhisattva.
“A bodhisattva has ten attributes regarding the head. What are these ten?
Having no pride as their foremost quality, no one in the heavens or the world can see the crown of their head;”
He bows his head in reverence to teachers and elders and is filial and obedient to his parents; throughout the heavens and the world, all prostrate themselves before him.
His head is excellent and sublime; throughout the trichiliocosm, there are none who do not look up to him with veneration.
He is the root of all virtues and the sovereign leader; the sentient beings of the three realms all come to take refuge in him.
He bears the heavy burden on behalf of all sentient beings; as the foremost among those who rest their heads upon him, he is always able to lift his head and survey the ten directions.
He does not disparage the heads of others; his gait and movements are far superior to those of the multitude;
he is the foremost in the Perfection of Wisdom, with the Dharma King upon his crown.
The foremost of skillful means, universally manifesting the practice of equality toward all sentient beings;
the foremost in transforming the populace, guiding and encouraging sentient beings so that they all attain universal peace;
and the foremost in cultivating the teachings of all Tathāgatas, constantly honoring the Triple Gem so that it shall never be interrupted.
These are the ten heads possessed by a bodhisattva.
"The eye of a bodhisattva has ten aspects. What are these ten?

Thus, with the fleshly eye, one sees all forms; with the divine eye, one universally perceives the thoughts and intentions of sentient beings; with the wisdom eye, one observes the faculties of the masses; with the Dharma eye, one sees the ultimate destination of all phenomena; with the Buddha’s eye of perfect awakening, one fully perceives the ten powers of a Tathāgata; with the noble wisdom eye, one sees the elimination of all unrighteous matters; with the light-emitting eye, one manifests the Buddha’s majestic brilliance that shines everywhere; with the guiding and benefiting eye, one abandons all arrogance and conceit; with the unconditioned eye, what is perceived is unimpeded; and with the all-knowing eye, one universally perceives all dharma-gates throughout the ten directions—these are the ten types of eyes of a bodhisattva.
"Bodhisattvas have ten matters regarding their ears. What are these ten?
Hearing the praise of virtues, they sever all fetters and attachments."
If one hears slander and defamation, one eliminates all that has been received;
if one hears matters concerning the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, one feels neither joy nor aspiration for them;
if one hears praise of the conduct of Bodhisattvas, one experiences immeasurable delight.
They block off the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals;
even if one is born into the eight adversities of poverty and calamity, they arouse great compassion for them.
Hearing that one may be born among gods or humans in a state of peace, they know all such states are impermanent, and their will aspires to the Great Way.
If they hear the praises of the merits and virtues of the Buddhas, they will increase their diligence and fully accomplish these deeds;

furthermore, if they hear of the various *pāramitās*, the four debts of gratitude, and the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas, they will be able to thoroughly master and fully comprehend all these matters through diligent cultivation.
Sons of the Buddha, you should know that the sons of enlightenment hear all the teachings on the principles and activities proclaimed by the Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Whatever he hears, he understands as being non-existent.

Furthermore, all the teachings heard by that bodhisattva’s ear are equal and of one taste; from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree to become a Buddha, he never ceases to transform and guide sentient beings.
These are the ten matters concerning the ear of a bodhisattva.
There are ten matters concerning the nose of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?

If they encounter pleasant fragrances, they do not take pleasure in them through consciousness; if they encounter foul stenches, they do not feel aversion or weariness. They examine fragrance and stench with equanimity, without distinguishing one from the other, observing that all fragrances and stenches are ultimately non-existent.
Regarding clothing, bedding, the fragrance or stench of ritual etiquette, and the matters of lust, anger, and delusion, they enter among these sentient beings with a mind of equality.
They observe all great treasuries, trees, and various perfumes, knowing that no such fragrance exists.
From the Avīci Hell below up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven above,
all the various named fragrances therein were entirely free from attachment, and they all explained their origins and endings;
they attained the hearing of the śrāvaka precepts and prohibitions, as well as extensive learning.
They bestow the fragrance of the Dharma of the path of wisdom;
they aspire to all-knowledge with a mind that never wavers;
and having attained the practices of all bodhisattvas, they cultivate wisdom equal to the stages of the Tathāgatas.
If one possesses the fragrance of wisdom regarding the realm of the Tathāgata, one does not sever the sublime and wondrous practices of the bodhisattva path;
this is the tenth pure fragrance of a bodhisattva.
"The tongues of bodhisattvas have ten qualities."
What are the ten? They are:
expounding through speech the inexhaustible conduct of sentient beings;
and proclaiming the teachings of immeasurable sūtras.
They extol the boundless merits of all Buddhas;
they sing praises of the inexhaustible eloquence of parinirvāṇa;
and they chant the limitless deeds of the Mahāyāna.
The words of his speech pervade the void of the ten directions;
his great radiance illuminates all Buddha-lands;
and every word spoken from his mouth causes sentient beings to each attain understanding.
The words they utter are praised by all the Buddhas of the ten directions;
all demons, external adversaries, afflictions, and the cycle of birth and death are naturally eliminated, leading to the ultimate quiescence of the unconditioned.
This is the eloquence of speech of a Bodhisattva.
“There are ten matters concerning the person of a bodhisattva.
What are these ten? They are as follows:”
When receiving a human body, one transforms others through human speech;
likewise, one instructs and guides those with non-human forms;
and one causes those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals to follow the teachings of the Vinaya.
Born in the bodies of devas, he further instructs the forms of all devas—those in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm;
for those still in training, he guides them through the stages of training toward the state of no-more-learning;
and for them, he manifests the state of an Arhat who is free from attachment.
When appearing in the form of a pratyekabuddha, he acts as a guide for those who should follow the discipline of a pratyekabuddha;
when appearing in the form of a bodhisattva, he demonstrates the practices of the Mahāyāna;
and the Tathāgata, the Arhat, whose wisdom is infinite, preaches and manifests according to the occasion, perceiving all forms of self-conceit and inspiring them through skillful means.
The Dharma-body is without outflows and is entirely non-existent, yet it universally manifests all bodies;
these are the ten bodies of a bodhisattva.
"A bodhisattva has ten mental practices."
What are the ten? They are:
mindfulness of all past lives and deeds;
establishing the mind upon the foundation of manifold virtues; and constantly upholding the essential meaning.
As for the entry of the mind: one constantly directs the will toward the Buddha-way;
reaching the ultimate limit of the fundamental source, one takes pity on the bodies of sentient beings;
maintaining mindfulness without agitation, one severs all worldly afflictions.
His mind is luminous and radiant, never becoming conjoined with adventitious defilements;
he contemplates and selects virtuous conduct, examining it according to the occasion so as not to commit any transgression;
he observes carefully the nature of sin and merit, refraining from creating any calamity or offense.
To contemplate the roots of all virtues, to have the faculties in tranquil concentration, to exercise restraint and avoid negligence;
to maintain a mind of detachment and seek the meditative intent of the Buddha—
these constitute the ten mental practices of a bodhisattva.
“There are ten matters regarding the gait of a bodhisattva. What are these ten? They are:
delighting in attending Dharma assemblies to listen to and receive the meaning of the sutras; and when approaching [the assembly], doing so without noise and without being obscured.”
Free from lust, anger, delusion, and fear, his mind is always focused and contemplative;
whenever he preaches the Dharma, it is for the sake of all sentient beings,
reaching even into the realm of desire to transform and enlighten the masses.
If they reach the realm of form or the formless realm, they immediately return by means of the concentrated mind of an image;
they manifest universally throughout the five destinies to instruct and edify the multitudes;
and with the wisdom of supernormal powers, they visit all Buddha-lands to behold the Tathāgatas, prostrating themselves and inquiring after their well-being.
Whatever they traverse is entirely for the gift of Dharma;
by virtue of this, they attain great wisdom, manifest entry into nirvana while not severing the cycle of birth and death, and circulate through the realms of those to be saved;
they are endowed with all Buddha-dharmas and never cease or abandon the practices of a bodhisattva.
These are the ten matters of the bodhisattva’s wandering.
Abiding in these, there is no place where the bodhisattva does not wander; by means of this, they universally reach the conduct of all Tathāgatas and emerge uniquely throughout the ten directions.
“Bodhisattvas have ten stations. What are these ten?
They are the stations that a bodhisattva’s mind never forgets.”
He dwells in the practice of the perfection of effort;
he does not seek to satisfy himself by gathering a multitude of followers, but attains penetrating wisdom;
he abides in seclusion and achieves great meditative concentration.
In accord with all-knowledge, possessing the virtue of contentment, and tranquil like the noble ones;
abiding in freedom from manifold conceptualizations and devoid of expectations;
practicing the sphere of the Dharma, they do not distance themselves from the true meaning.
When returning to the Tathāgata through ritual, one is able to fully possess the majestic deportment and ceremonial etiquette of all Buddhas and Perfectly Awakened Ones;
emerging from the realm of supernormal powers, one is thoroughly endowed with great wisdom and attains the patience of the Dharma, fulfilling the wisdom bestowed upon them;
seated at the site of enlightenment, one reaches the powers and fearlessnesses, filling all the teachings of the Buddhas.
These are the ten stations of a bodhisattva.
"A bodhisattva has ten seats. What are these ten?
The merit of this shall lead to the throne of a Wheel-Turning King;
by cultivating the ten virtues, one shall not lose one's place among the heavens or the world of humans;
and one shall attain the rank of the Four Heavenly Kings, bestowing the honored Dharma of the Buddha upon all under heaven.
Upon attaining the status of Lord of Devas, he transcends the multitudes, the Brahmā heavens, and the Īśvaras;
he can influence the minds of others according to his own will;
he ascends the lion throne and causes the assembly of the Dharma to flourish and manifest.
Having attained the seat of the True Dharma and achieved the power of dhāraṇī, they universally illumine all things;
their resolve is firm and strong, and the right vows they establish are all-encompassing, penetrating the ten directions;
by means of the seat of great compassion, they cause those harboring anger and resentment to attain joyful countenances.
Sitting upon the seat of great compassion, one endures all suffering and affliction without regarding them as calamities;
sitting upon the Vajra-seat, one subdues all Māras and external enemies—
these constitute the ten seats.
"There are ten matters concerning the sleeping and resting of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?
They are: dwelling in tranquility, with body and mind serene and detached, lodging in solitude."
Contemplating meanings in accordance with the Dharma, he does not miss the proper timing;
established in right concentration, his body and mind are tranquil and silent;
dwelling in the Brahma-heaven, he is able to gladden both himself and others.
They cultivate their practice well, yet harbor no distress or feverish anxiety regarding future lives;
they resolve upon impartial conduct and harbor no malice;
they abide in the path of practice and understand how to rely on virtuous friends.
They dwell in the sublime and subtle, encouraging and assisting the roots of virtue;
they attain the source of all principles and meanings, and are able to reach their ultimate consummation;
they accomplish the Way and its teachings, not seeking profit from wealth or worldly affairs, for this is the virtuous conduct cultivated in past lives.
These are the ten matters concerning the sleeping and resting of a bodhisattva.
There are ten matters regarding the dwelling of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?
With boundless loving-kindness, they regard all sentient beings with an impartial mind;
through the practice of great compassion, they do not slight those who have not yet studied;
through the practice of great sympathetic joy, they eliminate all forms of unhappiness and maintain a serene and joyful countenance.
They practice the stage of great protection, regarding the conditioned and the non-existent as equal;
they take the mind of enlightenment as the foremost among the perfections;
they are fully endowed with the practice of emptiness and understand how to act according to the occasion.
Practicing signlessness, they do not dwell in cessation;
practicing wishlessness, they give rise to utmost sincerity;
their minds practice composure, fully perfecting patience.
By practicing these various dharmas, one attains the prediction of enlightenment;
these are the ten matters that constitute the dwelling of a bodhisattva.
"There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva dwells and travels."
What are the ten? His mind dwells and abides in the four foundations of mindfulness;
his conduct and dwelling fully comprehend the destination of all phenomena.
The direction of his intent is solely to delight in all Buddhas;
he is fully endowed with the perfections (pāramitās) and all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñatā), and cultivates the practice of the four debts of gratitude;
he transforms and enlightens sentient beings, dwelling within birth and death to give rise to the roots of virtue.
He gathers the multitudes of common people without indulging in worldly clamor, delivering them according to their inclinations;
he manifests spiritual powers and practices to awaken sentient beings, discerning their extraordinary faculties through skillful means;
with the perfection of wisdom, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of the multitude.
"Roaming to the sites of enlightenment, one attains all supernormal powers and wisdom;
fully preparing for the bodhisattva practices, one’s conduct remains uninterrupted—these are the ten matters of a bodhisattva’s roaming and dwelling.
When these words were spoken, the trichiliocosm shook with a great trembling.

Bodhisattvas from the ten directions all came to offer praise and recitation; carrying celestial flowers as vast as Mount Sumeru, they scattered them all over the Buddha, and there was none who was not filled with joy.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits all came to pay him homage.

Lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; the pearl bracelets of the women all produced sounds on their own; and the flying birds and wild beasts all joined together in joyful clamor.

The blind gained sight, the deaf gained hearing, the lame were able to walk, the humpbacked became straight, the bent were stretched out, the insane regained their composure, the weak became strong and healthy, and the sick were healed.
The entire assembly leaped for joy, deeply congratulating themselves that their past merits were so abundant as to have brought about this radiance.
Countless people attained the state of non-arising, resolved upon the Great Way, and all perfected their virtues.
*Sūtra on the Chapter on Transcending the World*, Scroll Four;
*Sūtra on the Chapter on Transcending the World*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.

And what is the establishment of a Buddha?

What is meant by abandoning the kingdom and renouncing kingship?
What is meant by practicing asceticism with diligent effort?
What is meant by "approaching the site of enlightenment"?
What is meant by "sitting beneath the tree"?
And what is meant by "attaining the unprecedented Dharma while beneath the tree"?
What is meant by "subduing the palace of Māra"?
What is meant by "attaining the Way of the Buddha"?
What is meant by "turning the wheel of Dharma"?
"What is meant by the transformation of pure and white dharmas?
What is meant by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, attaining great parinirvāṇa?
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva replied to Samantajñāna:
“Excellent is your question! For the sake of all beings, I shall once again expound upon this meaning; how joyful this is!
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; together with the great assembly, receive these instructions and listen.”
Samantabhadra said:
“There are ten matters through which a bodhisattva contemplates existence. What are these ten?
Contemplating its ultimate truth, one establishes wholesome karma;
seeing subtle and wondrous forms, one fully realizes their origin;
observing those who have reached the end of life as well as those being born, one does not crave or cling to the clamor of worldly assemblies.
They perceive all faculties and discern them, transforming all impaired faculties;
they observe all phenomena without destroying the dharma-realm;
they behold all phenomena face-to-face and attain the Buddha-eye.

Having attained the sagely wisdom, they preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate, being without any point of origin; they reach the ultimate stage of the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*).

They attain the stage of non-retrogression in the teachings of all Buddhas, eliminating all afflictions (*kleśa*), the various hardships of the triple world, and all paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Contemplating the state of *anavaivartika* (non-regression), they attain mastery over all Buddha-dharmas.
To manifest the Dharma of joy, skillfully understanding the intent of the Way and being able to universally manifest all that exists in the ten directions—
this is the Bodhisattva’s tenth contemplation.
“There are ten matters regarding the Bodhisattva’s retrospective gaze.
What are these ten?
Seeing those who beg, one harbors no harmful intent, but fulfills their wishes so as to bring them joy;
seeing those who violate prohibitions, one establishes them all in the precepts of omniscience.
Seeing sentient beings harboring thoughts of anger and resentment, they resolve them to the state of patience and lead them forward through the benevolence of the Buddha;
seeing those who are indolent, they do not abandon their practice but encourage and assist them, causing them to study the Mahāyāna;
beholding those whose minds are distracted, they transform and establish them so that they do not lose the ground of awakening.
Those who possess penetrating and wise discernment regarding evil wisdom have never harbored false views, having eliminated them without remainder;
