While remaining firmly within the mother’s womb, he manifested the practice of diligence and arduous asceticism; he appeared to proceed to the site of enlightenment and sit beneath the tree to attain perfect buddhahood;
furthermore, while still in the womb, he manifested the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
and while remaining in the womb, he manifested the attainment of parinirvāṇa.

While dwelling within the mother’s womb, he proceeded with dignified composure to encourage entry into the Great Way; remaining there in the womb, he universally manifested the practices of all bodhisattvas, establishing the Tathāgata’s boundless Great Way and embracing the gateway to the Path.
These are the ten matters of the dignified conduct manifested by a bodhisattva.
"There are ten matters for a bodhisattva to cultivate regarding birth. What are these ten?
The Bodhisattva fully understands their intent and remains serene, manifesting a birth that is pure and harmonious;
he radiates great light that pervades the trichiliocosm.

At the ultimate end, he does not undergo further rebirth, yet manifests what appears as birth—because there is neither arising nor ceasing, it is called "birth. He contemplates that the recipients of birth within the three realms are like illusions and transformations.
Manifesting bodies born within the worlds of the ten directions;
his body displays the attainment of all-knowledge;
the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, universally radiates majestic brilliance, issuing commands to all who possess a body.
Having accumulated great wisdom and attained the meditative absorption of samādhi, he was then born;
as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, he shook all Buddha-lands, causing all classes of sentient beings to feel joy in their hearts;
he extinguished the evil realms and eclipsed the works of all Māras, so that each was struck with wonder and cried out:
"Today, the Bodhisattva has come from such-and-such a place.
These are the ten things produced by the cultivation of the Bodhisattva.
"There are ten matters for which a Bodhisattva smiles.
What are these ten?

"Observing that those in the mundane world are bound by greed and entangled within it, with no one capable of pulling them out, [he thinks]: 'Only the strength of my own body can bear to shatter this faction.'"
"It is for this reason that he smiles.
Worldly people are often deluded by the afflictions of defilement; they claim their own wisdom is such that none can equal it. For this reason, the Bodhisattva smiles with joy."

"From great self-indulgence and negligence, my own name and title are thus unsurpassed; the Tathāgata has thereby manifested the essential core of the Dharma-body throughout the three periods of time, causing each person to give rise to the aspiration to attain this."

"The eyes of all Bodhisattvas are unimpeded; from the lands of the ten directions up to the palaces of the Brahma heavens, and even further to the Mahābrahmā devas, they observe both the origins and the ends of all things, and then reflect to themselves:
'The multitude of these sentient beings are thus defiled, yet the power of the Bodhisattva's wisdom perceives them all clearly.'"

"Furthermore, he sees that people who have accumulated the roots of virtue in past lives fall back again; he sees those who plant small merit yet hope for immeasurable retribution; and he beholds the path of the Equal Enlightenment, the true and correct Way, which is free from deception."

"Observe our former friends and fellow students from the past who were resolved upon the bodhisattva path; each cultivated purity, yet while they had not yet perfected the Buddha-dharma, I have already attained it."

“Observing the devas and people dwelling in their original abodes, as well as those on the ground of ignorance who do not understand the True Dharma, his mind remains unshaken and he does not consider it a hardship.
Thus, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, emits a radiance called ‘Great Tranquil Shaking’ and sends forth this great brilliance.”
These are the ten matters for which the Bodhisattva smiles with joy.
"When the Bodhisattva walks seven steps, there are ten matters. What are these ten?
At that time, the Bodhisattva manifested himself as a young child; taking seven steps, he demonstrated the possession of the seven riches and displayed his extraordinary distinction,
desiring to fulfill the aspirations of the earth deities.
He manifested that his virtue transcended the triple world, walking alone without peer.
His movement was like that of a dragon king, his stillness like that of an elephant king, and his every gesture and step like the gait of a lion.
In all his comings and goings, wherever he arrived, the Bodhisattva’s walking, circling, and every movement surpassed all others.
At that time, heaven and earth were transformed into vajra.
The remaining ordinary grounds were immovable, yet they were capable of supporting the Bodhisattva and nurturing all beings of the various stages.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva took seven steps with his feet.

Furthermore, because all people do not understand the meaning of the Way, the Bodhisattva again took seven steps—corresponding to the seven factors of enlightenment—to awaken those who were unawakened, thereby attaining the True Dharma and having nothing upon which to rely or depend.
Regarding the World-Honored One, I am without peer; with my own mouth I have declared:
"In the heavens above and the world below, I shall deliver them all.
These are the ten matters of the Bodhisattva’s conduct.
“There are ten further matters concerning the Bodhisattva’s manifestation of the stage of a young child. What are these ten?

He is fully proficient in writing, calligraphy, arithmetic, calculation, practical applications, and the art of responsive speech; there is nothing he does not master, and thus he displays these skills to all people.”

Furthermore, he manifested himself riding superior horses and elephants, traveling back and forth by chariot, and excelling the multitude with divine arts and incantations; whether in games of dice, gambling, music, or song and dance, he surpassed all others.
“His body, speech, and mind manifest both transgressions and blessings yet remain free from calamity or fault, being devoid of arrogance.
Through the correct reception of samādhi, he pervades immeasurable Buddha-worlds to enlighten and transform sentient beings currently living therein.”

"The manifested virtues of the Bodhisattva surpass those of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings; they all come to take refuge in him."
Furthermore, he manifests the physical appearance and forms of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
He also manifests in the form of a bodhisattva to reveal his spiritual accomplishments.

The bodhisattva appears in various ways among the people: for those sentient beings who indulge in greed, pleasure, desire, and frivolity, or who are distressed and agitated by sorrow, he manifests joyfulness, causing them to delight in the Dharma.
"Always through the assembly of the Dharma, they find growth and benefit, revering and honoring the Tathāgata.

Surveying the ten directions, they manifest serenity through the radiance of the Dharma and the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata; in peaceful harmony and silent stillness, they thereby transform sentient beings."
This Bodhisattva manifests as a young child within the inner palace, providing great relief and succor; the Bodhisattva dwells in the central palace among the ladies-in-waiting.
Furthermore, there are ten matters.
What are these ten?

"He dwelt in the inner palace because he had previously studied together with these beings in past lives; it was because the Bodhisattva wished to transform these sentient beings and manifest his roots of virtue that he remained there."
“Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva must strive to rescue those who have planted roots of virtue, he manifests a harem.

When gods and humans are arrogant, self-indulgent, and ostentatious in their wealth and status, the Bodhisattva manifests great magnificence and noble causes in order to transform them through such means.”
"In this world of five turbidities, he guides and advances beings according to the times, transforming and delivering them throughout the Buddha-lands.
Although he dwells within the inner palace, he does not abandon samādhi; his power is peerless."
"In the distant past, sentient beings established vows; because the Bodhisattva wishes to cause them all to be fulfilled according to their intent, he manifests within the inner palace.
He does so to ensure that the original vows of his parents, household, and kinsmen are fully realized."

"With the sound of the Great Dharma, with music, songs, hymns, the *konghou* lute, and various musical instruments, they shall reverently make offerings to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, and cause all others to follow their example."

"At that time, while the Bodhisattva was within the inner palace, he fully realized the Way of the Buddha; with a concentrated mind, unwavering from beginning to end, he attained supreme perfect enlightenment and turned the wheel of Dharma until his great parinirvāṇa."
"Therefore, he manifests the protection of beings through the Dharma, rescuing them from peril and distress, and causing them to enter the Great Way.
This constitutes the final stage of a Bodhisattva’s life within the inner palace; thereafter, he abandons his kingdom and renounces kingship, enters the mountains, and attains the Way."
“There are ten further matters concerning a bodhisattva’s renunciation of his kingdom. What are these ten?
To demonstrate weariness with worldly desires, he manifests the act of leaving the household life.”

Seeing that worldly beings are largely defiled by attachments, he desires to lead people away from clinging to flaws, manifesting the righteous and true traces of the noble ones and the meaning of compliant conduct;

as for the bodhisattva’s dwelling and practice, he desires to propagate the transformation of the Way and extol the virtue of leaving the household life, employing skillful means to manifest within the two extremes;
and for those fallen into the sixty-two views of various doubts, he pulls them out and causes them to emerge.

Sentient beings are diligently devoted to the pursuit of security; to manifest the manifold difficulties and cause them to abandon their attachment to the notion of security and bliss, he appears as one who has gone forth from home.
For those various classes of beings who are attached to the three realms and run wild, he manifests the initial response of renunciation;
thus, his resolve is exalted, having nothing upon which to rely or depend, and because that reliance is incalculable, he manifests going forth from home.
Furthermore, he demonstrates the attainment of the Tathāgata’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses, teaching according to the occasion;
finally, reaching the ultimate, he manifests what is appropriate for one about to achieve Buddhahood.
These are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva abandons his country and renounces his kingship.
“There are ten further matters concerning the Bodhisattva’s manifestation of diligent ascetic practices. What are these ten?
Desiring to transform and instruct those of inferior capacity, he manifested six years of subsisting on only one grain of hemp and one grain of rice.”
Furthermore, desiring to exhort and encourage those who are attached to various heterodox views— the sixty-two [wrong] views—
and for the sake of the multitudes of sentient beings who have lost their virtue, he points out their karma and the retribution of sin and merit;
and for the sake of the defiled and deluded world, he provides timely exhortation and guidance, manifesting his own toil and suffering.
They are able to subdue sensual desires and demonstrate the karma of the two equalities;
for this reason, they receive the Dharma of the True Truths;
while those who greedily grasp at desires seek their own heavy self-comfort, these beings cause those who are running wild to purify their minds.
Furthermore, he manifests the diligence of a bodhisattva, striving with arduous resolve for the Way;
yet, in the final age when he is about to attain Buddhahood, he demonstrates that he will not be born again.
Because of his diligence, he causes the gods and people—whose faculties are not yet pure—and even those of external heterodox paths to follow his instruction.
These are the ten ascetic practices demonstrated by the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are ten matters concerning the Bodhisattva’s approach to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). What are these ten?
"Manifesting a great radiance that illuminates the ten directions so that the multitudes may know [of me], I have therefore come beneath this tree.
Furthermore, I wish to move the Buddha-lands and manifest my own body, so that all Buddha-lands may behold me together."
Furthermore, he clearly revealed the past deeds of all the bodhisattvas and sentient beings, causing them all to come from afar to prostrate and receive instruction.
He manifested his site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), with the tree beneath which he sat adorned and pure.
“In accordance with the fundamental dispositions of the multitude, he manifests his body at the appropriate time with dignified deportment and ritual propriety.
While the Buddha-tree remains serene, he causes the Tathāgatas and Arhats of all worlds to each manifest their own bodies—performing every act of walking, lifting the feet, and setting them down.”
"Constantly cultivating samādhi, he never departs from a concentrated mind.
Fully awakening to the Noble Path, he does not transgress it for even a moment.

Devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings appear and come to pay him homage; upon seeing him, all people do not fail to resolve their minds [for enlightenment]."

“Mahāmati, with unimpeded mastery, Bodhisattvas universally observe the ten directions and mindfully contemplate all Tathāgatas; they clearly understand all quarters and manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment within all lands.”
This is the Bodhisattva manifesting his arrival at the tree of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are ten matters concerning the Bodhisattva sitting beneath the tree of enlightenment. What are these ten?
They sit beneath the trees because they move all Buddha-lands through countless means;
they do so because they desire to illuminate the worlds of the ten directions and to completely eliminate all evil realms.
Furthermore, they establish all realms and lands as being entirely of vajra;
they contemplate all Tathāgatas seated upon lion thrones, with thoughts as vast as space;
and they manifest their physical presence and deportment in accordance with the times.
They take refuge in the samādhi of the Vajra-maṇḍala;
they receive purity in the abodes where all Tathāgatas dwell;
and by relying on their own power, they advance toward the roots of virtue.
To exhort all classes of sentient beings to establish themselves [in the path];
these are the ten matters for sitting beneath the Bodhi tree.
"There are ten ways in which a Bodhisattva attains the unprecedented while sitting beneath the Honored Tree."
What are these ten?
"When sitting at the Bodhi tree, he attained the unprecedented, spontaneous Dharma.
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the worlds in the ten directions each manifested their countenances, extended their right palms, and each offered praise:"
"May the Guide attain victory.
To attain victory is the first unprecedented phenomenon.
"Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva sits beneath the Bodhi tree, all Buddhas collectively keep him in mind and dispatch their majestic spiritual power to him; this is the second matter."

"When he sat beneath the Bodhi tree, his former fellow students and all the bodhisattvas came together to surround and guard him; they dwelt in the gate of meditative concentration and made offerings to him with various things—this is the third matter."

"When he was beneath the tree, the grasses, trees, flowers, fruits, and all medicinal plants throughout the worlds of the ten directions—though they possess no consciousness—naturally bent their forms; they all bowed their bodies together toward the Bodhi tree and prostrated themselves in homage. This is the fourth matter."
“There is a great state of meditative concentration called ‘Accumulating the Dharma Realm,’ which transcends all bodhisattva practices.
When one attains this state of meditative concentration, its merit and radiance surpass those of all other bodhisattvas; these are the five matters.”

"At that time, the Bodhisattva establishes his body in the field of the ocean-treasury, stainless radiance, and dhāraṇī, causing all Tathāgatas to proclaim the great rain of Dharma; this is the sixth matter."
Then, with a supple and upright head, he departed to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
"The Bodhisattva sat beneath the tree and traveled throughout all lands, reaching everywhere; this is the seventh matter."

"When a bodhisattva sits beneath the Bodhi tree, his practice is also like that of the noble being Hui-shang (Wisdom-Supreme): he universally perceives the fundamental mental intentions and thoughts of all sentient beings; this constitutes the eighth matter."
"When sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, he naturally and skillfully attains the noble Buddha-concentration of awakening.
Upon attaining this concentration, he universally pervades the infinite matters of the three periods of time, just like empty space; this is the ninth matter."

"When sitting at the Bodhi tree, he personally and clearly perceives the three periods of time; his great and holy wisdom is peerless, and he radiates the light of detachment—these are the ten matters of unprecedented dharmas."
“What is meant by a bodhisattva subduing the hosts of Māra?
There are ten matters for subduing the retinues of Māra. What are these ten?”

Sentient beings are equally attached to the dust of the mundane world and suffer the afflictions of birth and death; they take no pleasure in battle. For this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests great power to subdue the retinues of Māra.
As the devas and people are arrogant and seek fame, he desires to sever for them the hardship of self-inflation.
The Buddha wishes to transform and enlighten both Māra and his hosts, as well as the devas and people, so that they may all rejoice together and assemble in one place.
Transforming them through these means, the Bodhisattva’s power and majesty are without peer;
he likewise manifests these displays desiring that people may know them, and desiring to encourage and gladden all sentient beings;
he reveals these beneficial discourses, also wishing to take pity on future generations of worldly people.
When he descended upon the Bodhi tree to subdue the hosts of Māra, he had already completely transcended all realms of Māra;
being free from worldly desires, he was neither possessed of power nor lacking in power, yet perceiving those of feeble strength, he manifested the roots of virtue;
demonstrating the power of a compassionate mind, he subdued the retinues of the Māra hosts.
In an age characterized by desire, worldly toil, and greed, he encourages and gladdens beings according to the times, transforming them through the Dharma.
Contemplating these ten meanings, the Bodhisattva thus subdues the retinues of Māra.
"When a Bodhisattva attains supreme perfect enlightenment, there are ten matters that demonstrate the powers of a Tathāgata.
What are these ten? They are:
being able to subdue all demonic activities and the defilements of worldly afflictions, and being fully endowed with the practices of a Bodhisattva."
They delight in all the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the bodhisattvas to enjoy themselves, entering the hall of noble wisdom of the superior assembly of *bodhisattvas*;
they have ultimately accomplished all pure dharmas and the meaning of all practices;
and they act with skillful reflection for the sake of all worlds.
His body pervades the worlds of the ten directions, manifesting its resonance;
with an impartial mind toward all sentient beings, he fully exerts his majestic spiritual power to establish them;
regarding the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Arhats of the past, future, and present, his body, speech, and mind are equal and free from all expectations or conceptualizations.
In a single moment, one universally penetrates the three periods of time;
there is a samādhi called "Awakening to the Awakening Mind," and when this concentration is attained, one enters the ten powers of a Buddha.
By being able to give rise to this, one possesses power everywhere, reaching as far as the wisdom that exhausts all outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*).
This is how the Bodhisattva, through the ten powers of a Tathāgata, achieves supreme perfect enlightenment.
When abiding in these powers, all Buddhas arrive everywhere; therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata has already attained perfect enlightenment.
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, turns the wheel of Dharma by means of ten aspects. What are these ten?
He attains the four fearlessnesses, enters pure wisdom, and proclaims the sound of wisdom;”
Possessing the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), they further skillfully understand that which transcends the Four Noble Truths;
they dwell in the unimpeded gate of liberation of perfect enlightenment;
and with a vast mind, they compassionately regard all living beings.
It eliminates the afflictions of adversity, oppression, suffering, and dejection, as well as the hardships of lack of leisure;
it does not contradict the past immeasurable compassion;
and its pure, harmonious speech pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
Throughout incalculable kalpas, they proclaim the Dharma without weariness or indolence;
they skillfully discern and understand the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment;
and with single-minded joy, they enter the gates of dhyāna and samādhi.
These are the ten aspects by which, upon attaining perfect enlightenment, one turns the wheel of Dharma through immeasurable meanings.

Having already become a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, one turns the wheel of Dharma; observing that the minds of sentient beings are turbid and restless, one gladdens their wills and causes them to attain clarity.

What are these ten? They are: being brought about by the power and force of vows made in previous lives; not violating one's original vow; establishing infinite great compassion through majestic spiritual power; not abandoning sentient beings but rescuing and aiding them; manifesting holy wisdom and preaching the Dharma for them; establishing and proclaiming it according to the appropriate time; causing them to understand it at the right moment so that there is no deficiency or omission; clearly knowing and understanding the wisdom of the three periods of time; the conduct of one’s body being forever free from karmic creation; the proclamations of one’s mind being devoid of conceptual forms; and the wisdom one expounds being understood immediately upon hearing the sound. These are the ten matters of pure and white dharmas by which the Wheel of Dharma is turned.
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, having performed the work of a Buddha by contemplating ten meanings, manifests the Great Parinirvāṇa. What are these ten?
He constantly manifests the contemplation of the definitive truth of impermanence;..."
All conditioned phenomena appear like inhalation and exhalation;
he universally attains the true state of the unconditioned and eliminates all fears.
Because gods and humans are attached to the form-body (*rūpakāya*), he manifests the form-body as thus impermanent, while distinguishing it from the eternally abiding Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Union must end in separation; all conditioned phenomena pass away in the blink of an eye and possess not the slightest solidity.
All that exists within the triple world is like an illusion or a magical transformation;
all mental constructions are precarious and fragile, while the unconditioned is most solid.

To manifest that the Dharma of the Path is indestructible, and that all habitual tendencies and separations are ultimately unestablished; to demonstrate that the disintegration of phenomena is their very nature;
and because the Buddha-deeds performed by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are already fully perfected, they skillfully turn the Wheel of Dharma to resolve all doubts;
causing beings to follow the teachings of the Vinaya, bestowing the prediction of enlightenment upon Bodhisattvas, so that there is no advancing or retreating as they cultivate Great Nirvana.
"These ten meanings of contemplation are such that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, has attained parinirvāṇa, yet there is no passing away or transformation.
Samantabhadra further said:
"This is it, O Son of the Buddha!"
This is called the Dharma-door of the Bodhisattva’s Practice of Purifying the Great Path of Dharma.

What I have now expounded is but a rough outline of the essentials of this Dharma-door; the meanings proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, are immeasurable, bringing joy to those of clear wisdom.
"The practices of all bodhisattvas are sustained by great vows and have never been interrupted.

If anyone hears this and rejoices with faith, and if their mind harbors such faith, they will practice and uphold it, thereby accomplishing this meaning; all shall swiftly attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and become the most perfectly awakened ones."
Why is this? Because one calculates that the path of a bodhisattva takes practice as its essence and has never been apart from practice.
Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in practice.

By being able to practice these meritorious deeds of a bodhisattva—entering into the discernment of meanings and being as pure as a lotus flower—one is immediately able to enter the infinite, holy chamber of all dharma-gates and the path that transcends the world, thereby departing from the paths of the śrāvakas and all pratyekabuddhas.
Transforming all sentient beings without harboring any partiality, one illuminates all dharmas through the sutras and dharma-gates to exhort the multitudes, enabling them to attain long-term benefit.

One should listen with a sincere mind to the Dharma-gate for Transcending the World; one should receive, uphold, recite, and contemplate with single-mindedness the Chapter on the Dharma for Transcending the World; and one should cultivate the gateway to the eye of the Path, reverently following one's vows.
Having practiced in this manner, that which the bodhisattva seeks will ultimately not be difficult to attain, and he shall swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

When this sutra was spoken—when this Dharma-gate was proclaimed and this chapter on the Teaching of the World-Transcending Dharma was expounded—the immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions were greatly shaken; all of this was brought about by the transformative power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority.
When this Dharma is proclaimed and this sutra is attained, all Buddha-lands naturally tremble, and a great radiance shines everywhere without exception.
The Buddhas of the ten directions each manifest their bodies and offer praise from afar to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva:
"Excellent, excellent!"
O Son of the Most Victorious!
How delightful it is that you expound at the appropriate time the meritorious virtues of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas and discern the true meaning!

You have opened up, elucidated, and proclaimed this chapter on the Dharma for transcending the world, just as you, Son of the Buddha, have originally studied the True Reality and attained mastery of this Dharma.
What you have now well expounded, we have fully understood through the majestic power of this sutra and the essential points of this pure and radiant scripture;
so it is with all Buddhas, and we likewise join in praising this sutra.
The present Buddhas of the ten directions bestow such vast and compassionate grace upon all future Bodhisattvas and those who have not yet heard the teachings; is it not truly so?

Thereupon, the Great Being Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, receiving the holy mandate of the Buddha and sustained by the protection of the sages of the ten directions, surveyed the ten directions, observed the various assemblies, and gazed universally upon the Dharma-realm, speaking these verses:

"Having cultivated for thousands of billions of trillions of eons, Diligently honoring that which is immeasurable, Taking refuge in hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, One thereby gives birth to the sons of the Dharma."
He transforms and enlightens all sentient beings, establishing the Way without limit or depth;
let everyone listen with one mind and praise the Buddha’s peerless excellence.
His offerings to the Buddhas are boundless, yet he remains unattached even to the Buddha-way.
Understanding the desires of the masses, he does not conceive the notion that there is a person.
Seeing the merit of the Buddha, he does not rely on his name or fame;
he praises the noble conduct of the Honored One, rejoicing in the world’s greatness.
Having already eliminated the dust of sin and the Māras, he manifests universally throughout the three periods of time;
his virtue surpasses that of all sages as he displays extraordinary and powerful conduct.
Having incinerated all actions of ignorance and craving, his will and nature abide in profound stillness.
The present activities of the assembly are now limited; I shall now extol his meritorious achievements.
That which the Most Holy One has transcended—sentient beings' destinies are like illusions—and he manifests various transformations to cause people to eliminate their arrogance.
At the very moment he first resolved his mind, he was able to understand everything completely;
now I praise those meritorious deeds, which all sentient beings honor and revere.
Beholding sentient beings in distress, suffering from birth, old age, and illness within the five realms of existence—
In the end, one perishes through sorrow, grief, and peril, harmed by the afflictions of desire.
Out of compassion for those who yearn to cross over these, he has established this vast and honored wisdom;
you should praise this meritorious achievement and listen together with a single mind.
Generosity, precepts, patience, diligence, And concentration to delight oneself—
these are the perfections of skillful means and wisdom, With generosity characterized by infinite compassion.
Delighting in the Dharma with compassion and joy, you have protected your practice for hundreds of thousands of kalpas;
now I shall praise this conduct, so listen to the merits I describe.
For the sake of seeking the Buddha-way, you have sacrificed bodies numbering in the trillions.
Not begrudging one’s own body or life—this is the true supreme path.
Diligently acting for the sake of sentient beings while always protecting them as one would oneself;
praising the transcendent conduct of the Muni, with a mind resolved upon compassion and loving-kindness.
Even if one were to spend countless billions of years, praising his name throughout kalpas,
And were to take up water from the great ocean with a single hair until it was exhausted,
The merit of the virtue of his practiced diligence would still surpass this beyond comparison.
Furthermore, listen to the realm of the Buddha, which manifests out of compassion for the multitudes;
for the sake of all sentient beings, it perpetually purifies the roots of white virtue.
Its nature and disposition are neither impetuous nor violent, and it never tires of the joy found in the Dharma.

Establishing the dwelling place for sentient beings, The river of wisdom and the deep pool of knowledge, The World-Honored One is like heaven and earth; All living beings constantly revere and look up to him.
Compassionate moisture and pity are his roots; Guarding the precepts and benevolence are his trunk.
The venerable one’s merit is like the petals of a flower of wisdom, and the fragrance of his precepts is exceedingly pure.
He awakens those whose minds are unawakened; his conduct is loved and revered by sentient beings.
Like an unattached lotus, sentient beings see him and take refuge in him.
Liberation is the seed-grain; the body’s fundamental nature harbors compassion.
With wisdom and skillful means, one crosses to the other shore by means of the five branches.
Meditation is the leaf, supernatural powers are the flower, and all-encompassing wisdom is the fruit.
The Dharma-tree of the Honored One with Divine Power broadly covers the three realms.
Having fundamentally cultivated the traces of purity, he nurtures the meaning of vast wisdom.
With a neck and jaw like a lion’s, his mindfulness is steadfast; his head is adorned with the pure silk of wisdom.
The meaning of the wisdom of emptiness is foremost; Compassionate and merciful, he is a light that delivers the world.
Being selfless like a lion, He can roar to subdue all demons.
Having transcended the vast wilderness of birth and death, He brings the various people’s heterodox defilements and desires to an end.
Having transcended all worldly affairs, they uphold the essential practice to eliminate delusion.
Showing the correct path to those who are confused, they reveal the unsurpassed way of the Buddha.
Resolving their minds without fear, they become supreme guides.
Sentient beings, with their lust, anger, and delusion, And various defilements of the dark dust,
follow conditioned existence through the long night, Afflicted by suffering and troubled by their parents.
Seeing the multitudes born into this world, he heals their craving with compassion;
preaching eighty-four thousand teachings, he uses them to cure and cast away all ailments.
Thus subduing the dust of Māra, he instructs sentient beings through the Dharma.
Abandoning evil, one has nothing further to practice; one seeks the majestic and pure virtues of a Buddha.
Understanding the Dharma, the Sovereign of the Two-Legged, the Honored One of All-Wisdom, uses the wealth of the noble and holy to truly and extensively awaken the masses in darkness.
Delighting in the precepts and samādhi, with the noble and pure wisdom,
one uses the blade of penetrating insight to cross over the dust of the world without fear.
Performing transformations through the illusion of dharmas, one thereby turns the supreme wheel of Dharma.
Nor do they ever retreat or turn back, nor can the minds of any heterodox teachers prevail.
Having fully realized profound and ultimate wisdom, they universally produce the flavor of the Dharma;
with the jewel of the awakened mind and the power of spiritual feet, they open the way for those difficult to transform among the common people.
Abiding in the power of a thousand supernormal knowledges, you purify the three realms as their sovereign;
you are an ocean of great wisdom, whose peerless teaching is inexhaustible.
Having transcended the mundane world, you do not cling to the multitudes of the three realms.
Having perfected meditative concentration and supernormal powers, his wisdom is as immovable as a mountain.
There is none who can equal his purity; none can surpass the brilliance of his wisdom.
His virtuous sanctity exceeds Mount Sumeru; out of compassion, he dwells for the sake of those who look up to him.
His nature is as firm as a diamond; all that he cultivates is essential and solid.
His mind cannot be destroyed; he honors the Dharma and serves universal wisdom.
Wandering amidst the dust and desires of the various māras, he dwells in this world without fear.
Extinguishing the blazing fire of craving and affection, he gathers in the multitudes of worldly beings.
He spreads the rain of universal compassion and radiates the brilliant light of pity;
with the thundering sound of the four bases of psychic power, the Muni proclaims his voice of tranquil clarity.
Raining down the fourfold analytical knowledge, The pure and harmonious eightfold path;
With this great rain of dharma, It purifies and extinguishes all worldly afflictions.
Taking wisdom as the wall and shame as the moat, It erects the banner of the Dharma as its pennant.
The Noble One understands the gate as a wall, and his intention guards the gatekeeper.
The Four Truths form the path; with pure supernormal powers, he adorns his tracks.
Taking the illusion of dharmas as the city walls, he rules the three realms and subdues Māra.
With the heart of a tree rooted in omniscience, Firmly established, he travels through the air;
Like a bird wandering alone, His compassion serves as his radiant light.
In teaching and transforming others, he is like a phoenix, Whom no sentient being can ever equal.
He pulls others across the ocean of birth and death, resolving his mind upon the supreme Nirvana.
By means of the dharma-grounds of precepts and meditative concentration, he brings forth the pure garland of the flowers of wisdom;
through clarity, he dispels worldly toil and dries up the flow of craving and affection.
Increasing the power of the medicinal roots, purifying the supreme path of the Buddhas for the multitude, they then raise the sun of Dharma to illuminate the realms of sentient beings.
The field of the Dharma-realm is equally pure; they do not abandon the equality of all beings.
Illuminating all vehicles— the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha—
my mind universally perceives the three periods of time. Dissolving the fluctuations of thought,
my noble wisdom transcends the ordinary, and I comprehend sentient beings as being like space.
Attaining mastery over all phenomena, he abides amidst the assembly with a majestic and virtuous form;
as the Illuminator, the Vajra-holder, he ever stands firm upon the ground of Dharma.
His physical marks are manifold and sublime, pure and transcending all worlds.
For the sake of the multitude, he has accumulated the scriptures—the most honored Dharma for all beings.
Having transcended the three periods of time, the net of craving, and all worldly afflictions, he takes pity on all mundane beings;
delighting in the Dharma, he acts as a compassionate protector.
Manifesting his body within the three realms, he proclaims the Dharma to all;
pure as Brahmā, he delivers those with wrong views from their lack of joy.
Purely crossing over birth and death, his sphere of activity is the majestic and honored Dharma.
No longer shall he retreat; with great resolve, he gathers all that moves.
The Dharma-Honored One transcends the world, embracing the multitudes with wisdom.
His every merit is supreme, and his great renown flows everywhere throughout the world.
Spontaneously like space, removing all inversions,
Standing out as extraordinary among the multitudes, never clinging to any realms.
Universally entering pure conduct, they also establish sentient beings.
His wisdom is most profound and subtle; this insight is pure and further purified.
His skillful means are as vast as the earth, universally reaching all beings of the five destinies;
his compassion is like water, washing away the dust of all desires.
With wisdom he eliminates craving and desire, uprooting the leaks of all beings;
the World-Honored One is without limit or bottom, wandering through the three realms like the wind.
This assembly is like a treasure, providing the path for those who are poor and destitute.
Like a diamond, peerless, he has abandoned all views regarding the three realms.
His manifold voices universally adorn the triple world with virtue;
as venerable as a night-bright pearl, his conduct stands as the crown upon the head.
Their meritorious deeds are like a multitude of flowers, and they delight themselves with the awakening mind;
these are like flower garlands, transcending the world through their vows and right aspirations.
Their fragrance of precepts is pure, complete and without flaw.
With the fragrance of the Dharma of pure anointing, wisdom is spread across the three places;
his conduct is like a lofty parasol, covering away the dust of worldly toil and desire.
He stands firm as a banner of wisdom, holding his intent without dual tracks.
Adorning their conduct with variegated banners and streamers, they cultivate wisdom while suspending insight;
wearing the raiment of truth and shame, they cover all sentient beings with virtue.
Dwelling in vehicles within immeasurable realms, they traverse and roam through the three periods of time.
With concentration as steady as a dragon-elephant, his mind remains ever firm and abiding.
With supernormal power he traverses the three times and casts off the great heavy burden;
like a great dragon king, he spreads forth clouds of Dharma-water.
They are like the auspicious *ariṣṭa* flower, difficult for the multitude to encounter.
These ones are like brave heroes who subdue Māra and uproot the afflictions;
they are also like the wheel-turning monarch, as proclaimed by the Teacher.
Appearing to all beings from beginning to end, like a torch in the darkness;
their virtue is like the great rivers, following its course like flowing water.
These ones are like bridges, constantly bearing up and carrying all across.
Like a finely adorned vessel, he crosses the abyss with wisdom and vows;
he is also like a helmsman, dwelling at the pinnacle of the stage of universal illumination.
While others wander in the pleasures of the night, he reveals true bliss for the sake of the multitude.
By means of the gates of liberation through wisdom, one adorns the pure palace of wisdom.
It is also like various medicines that eliminate the diseases of worldly toil;
like the diverse medicinal herbs of the Snowy Mountains, wondrous wisdom serves as one’s dwelling place.
His conduct is like that of a Perfectly Awakened One; his wisdom awakens all who sleep.
His path is the awakening of equality; with an impartial mind, he understands all sentient beings.
As for the place from which he comes, it is like supreme practice and sincere faith.
Just as one with all-encompassing wisdom enters the chamber of universal gateways,
so do these many who transform others and deliver various sentient beings;
by means of the sovereign Buddha-wisdom, they roam throughout the realm of all-encompassing knowledge.
His power is immeasurable, such that none can withstand it;
his wisdom is fearless, and through the understanding of wisdom, he enlightens all sentient beings.
Among all the various forms of people, their features, and their names, there is nothing that can compare.
All forms are equal; transcending all categories of letters and all sounds, they manifest apart from names and voices.
Among all classes of sentient beings, none are capable of proclaiming their radiant virtue.
Cultivating these meritorious deeds, he abandons what is false and establishes the Dharma.
Being the father of wisdom in the present, he remains far removed from the extremes of existence and non-existence;
thus he becomes the All-Knowing One, the foremost illumination of wisdom.
Alas! Entering the practice of non-attachment, you honor and delight the world;
you have understood all dharma-doors as being like illusions, eternally empty and quiescent.
Out of compassion for your past vows and practices, and also by upholding the holy intent of the Buddha, [you have come forth].
Leaving behind arrogance, they reveal the gateway of wisdom, manifesting various transformations.
Listen all with one mind to the meritorious achievements of the Bodhisattva;
for with a single physical form, he extensively manifests countless virtues.
Beyond the realm of mind and consciousness, sentient beings do not perceive the mind.
Emanating a single sound that transcends all realms of language,
it is proclaimed through speech in accordance with all classes of beings.
Having relinquished the bodies of sentient beings, he seeks to repay the essence of his practice;
understanding that sounds are non-existent, he articulates the teachings of all voices.
His mind is tranquil yet radiant, awakening to the truths as empty as space.
The common people differ from age to age, and thus various manifestations are shown.
Since ultimately there is no body, how can a physical form still appear?
According to the births of sentient beings, the fruits of retribution are established.
They enter into all places of birth, yet they do not cling to those births;
their own bodies are like space, and they do not conceive of themselves as being many persons.
Their bodies are immeasurable, yet through clear wisdom they can manifest them all.
I pay homage to the Honored One among gods and humans, and take refuge in the All-Knowing One of the world.
With flowers, incense, various powdered perfumes, music, silken banners and canopies,
and even casting my own body and life upon the ground, I make offerings to the Most Holy Honored One.
Abiding beneath a single most excellent tree, they all stand before the Buddhas;
beholding the dwellings of the multitudes, they constantly inquire of those who are peerless.
Hearing the Dharma, they attain samādhi; upon a single platform are infinite gates.
Abiding in what has been studied from the beginning, their resolve manifests immeasurably.
Through the karma of skillful means and wisdom, they cross over to the other shore;
understanding that sentient beings are like illusions, they personally attain the Way of the Buddha.
Universally perceiving diverse minds and immeasurable forms and sounds, they enter into the conceptualizations of seeking and longing; unattached, they appear everywhere among the multitudes.
Or again, they manifest as the foremost, revealing their minds for the sake of sentient beings.
There are those who practice the Path, seeing immeasurable multitudes;
practicing giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom;
some receiving the practices of the Brahma-traces, others manifesting supreme and wondrous conduct.
Some have perfected their practice and attained patience, yet manifest anger;
some have reached the ultimate state of birth, or are *avaivartika* Buddhas;
some appear in the form of *śrāvakas*, or again as *pratyekabuddhas*.
The realms of billions of worlds appear to perish, yet they do not truly pass into extinction;
nor do these Kṛṣṇas, Śakras, Asuras, Brahmā Kings, jade maidens, and their various retinues.
Or again, they may wander alone, the bhikṣu’s mind in profound stillness;
or they may act as sovereigns of nations, entering the realm of wisdom within the net of the Dharma;
or they may manifest wondrous forms and features, descending from the heavens to appear in this world.
Sometimes manifesting in the form of a woman, they deliver beings to the infinite;
sometimes appearing as a naked ascetic;
or dwelling in the meditative concentration of vast desire.
If one accumulates the karma of patience and awakens to the stage of ultimate truth, one perceives directly the movements of the mind:
sometimes manifesting entry into a womb, attaining perfect enlightenment within the womb,
and then turning the wheel of Dharma;
Some manifest passing into parinirvāṇa, while others study various arts and crafts; among women, they enter samādhi.
Having fully perfected all karmic deeds, they manifest the renunciation of their kingdoms and the abandonment of kingship;
or else, beneath the Bodhi tree, they attain the realization of supreme, perfect enlightenment.
Sometimes they manifest the turning of the wheel of Dharma, revealing various chapters;
sometimes Buddhas transform sentient beings throughout billions of lands,
manifesting the practice of non-retrogression.
The Buddha likewise has no karma of stillness; through the perfection of concentration (*samādhi-pāramitā*), he dwells throughout billions of kalpas.
Manifested by a single mind, his sphere of experience spans hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Whether amidst various perceptions or the absence of perception, he manifests the number of kalpas for the sake of sentient beings.
Without doubt and without anything to be said, yet manifesting in active engagement;
seeing the performance of deeds that lead to tranquility, he universally brings down grace upon sentient beings.
All this arises from supreme subduing; in that state, there is profound stillness.
The Buddha-lands and the realms of sentient beings enter into the retributions of all dharmas.
Even after an ultimate hundred billion kalpas, that which is proclaimed can never be exhausted.
Entering into sentient beings in this way, the one of vast wisdom enlightens the masses.
Thus, with a single body, he assumes immeasurable transformed forms;
likewise, by means of a single illusory artifice, he constantly pervades all things.
This is called the Perfection of Deliverance, which instructs those who have not yet learned.
Understanding that the faculties are all-pervasive and sharp, their fundamental state is one of meditative balance;
when the faculties attain mastery, sentient beings are free from karma.
One faculty enters into all faculties, yet each harbors its own attachment and craving.
The cessation of dhyāna is most subtle and wondrous; it is that in which the various sense bases and faculties abide.
This is the nature of liberation through the faithful offerings of others; it does not cease from the activity of sensory desires.
The past and future minds are likewise, and the present is also thus.
Sentient beings cross to the other shore, Neither going nor coming;
Fully understanding the practice of the true reality, They expound the supreme Dharma for the sake of the multitude.
The mind is thus manifold, Yet the mental activities are free from outflows.
With single-mindedness, they enter the right path and profoundly understand all-knowledge.
Their minds abide in the Buddha’s state of no-mind, dwelling in the supreme, highest wisdom.
In the mere instant of a single thought-arising, they discern and realize spontaneous wisdom.
The perfection of the divine feet distinguishes all the sages;
in the mere blink of an eye, they reach lands of immeasurable eons,
traveling everywhere in this same manner.
Throughout hundreds of billions of nayutas of eons, he proclaims immeasurable wisdom; his power is unshakable and universally penetrating.
Like a magician seeking wealth and occupation, he perceives various forms within the assembly;
though there is no form, he perceives various forms, yet for the magician, nothing at all exists.
Skillful wisdom is likewise so: entering the illusion of the vast Dharma, it manifests various transformations throughout the world.
Like the sun in the sky, pure and free from even the slightest cataract;
Just as in clear, pure water, one sees everything on the bottom; so too,
when the field of the Dharma-realm is pristine and still, the light of wisdom shines afar,
perceiving the purity of the realm of sentient beings, and the mind does not dwell in false views.
Just as various thoughts in a dream vanish upon awakening, so too, though countless billions of years have passed, the long night cannot be exhausted.
The nature of phenomena is likewise thus; it universally manifests all meanings.
Having remained for a hundred thousand kalpas, one must at once exhaust all wisdom.
Dwelling in the worldly customs of the realm, like a threshold upon a mountain peak,
one should not conceive of oneself as expounding wisdom when all sounds are being proclaimed.
The Bodhisattva understands this: all phenomena are naturally so;
following the verbal expressions of sentient beings, they manifest the sound of the Dharma without conceptualization.
It is like the days of spring and summer, when people give rise to the perception of a mirage.
Rushing about, one thinks there is water, yet the thirst becomes even more intense;
when sentient beings’ desires arise in this way, they should set their will on seeking liberation.
Having attained wisdom and the notion of non-self, their compassion and pity increase all the more.
The Buddha taught that form is like foam, Sensation is like a water bubble,
Perception is entirely like a mirage, And formations are like the trunk of a plantain tree.
The mind is like an illusion, Where consciousness manifests various transformations.
Manifesting the five aggregates in this manner, the one who attains realization has no attachments.
The various sense bases (*āyatana*) are empty by nature;
according to what one does, they are equal to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), manifesting as a realm free from sentient beings.
The six sense-bases are quiescent and the ultimate truth; to speak of various indeterminacies is the analytical understanding.
Regarding all phenomena upon which one relies and clings, there is no place from which they come, no place to which they go, and no place where they abide eternally.

The retribution for affection and love, and the turning of sins and blessings through the three periods of time, arise from the differentiation of causes and conditions; there is nothing that abides and yet can be uprooted.
Reaching the ultimate fulfillment of seeking the beginning and the end, one relies upon that which is non-existent.
Realizing that the three periods of time are of one and the same nature, he manifests manifold forms all at once.
Abiding in the realms of desire and formlessness, he is universally able to manifest his lands;
through his practice, he attains the three protections and delivers beings from the three states of existence.
Praising and proclaiming the Three Vehicles, they return to the One, the All-Knowing;
analyzing the various aspects of the Dharma, they enable beings to cross over the source of all faculties.
Having already liberated themselves from the realm of worldly toil, they dwell and travel everywhere with sovereign ease.
Consciousness recollects past events; the clear-eyed one extinguishes worldly toil.
The Buddha’s vast wisdom and ten powers likewise do not grasp at those powers;
awakening to the mind that all is empty, he presently contemplates the dharmas of sentient beings.
Free from the leaks of craving and desire, yet not seeking total extinction, he enters into all places of birth;
with vast wisdom, he does not lose the multitude.
The Son of the Victor dwells courageously here, skillfully bestowing and composing the practice of exposition.
The path is neither deficient nor wavering; his mind never forgets it.
He delights in the concentration of diligent effort, and wisdom eliminates all defilements.
Having fully established the protection of the dharmas of wisdom, he now manifests throughout the three periods of time.
The Dharma of loving-kindness is the companion of all beings;
Unconditioned and without attainment, those who practice this dharma-gate Attain the proclamation of virtue.
I have briefly set forth its meritorious achievements, Adorning all ultimate meanings.
To praise his conduct would be inexhaustible for billions of kalpas;
to briefly cite its essential benefits is like taking a single speck of dust from the earth.
Relying upon the holy wisdom of the Buddha, he dwells in thoughts never before conceived.
With diligence, firmness, and a compassionate heart, they transcend and follow all karmic deeds.
Exhorting and transforming the multitudes, their meditative concentration and precepts remain unshakable;
having attained the practice of right resolve, they are all called sons of the Buddha.
Pervading and entering the merits of the Buddha, He contemplates the conduct of sentient beings in the lands;
Entering into non-dual thought, His wisdom transcends all weariness and difficulty.
Attaining the power of discernment and dhāraṇī, He delivers others through the meaning of the True Truth.
Praising the peerless mind, one attains the state of supreme perfect enlightenment.
Universally contemplating the renown of the Sage’s merit, one vows to practice the Honored One’s sublime conduct;
through compassion and conditions, one cultivates loving-kindness, drawing near to the Honored One’s pure and wondrous path.
Understanding purity, one reaches the ultimate limit; through skillful means, one attains final nirvana.
Discerning and gaining power, one achieves the supreme path;
understanding leads to universal equanimity, as one proclaims the most sublime Dharma.
Transcending virtues, he donned the armor of the noble; abiding on the Path, he followed the station of the Dharma.
Ultimately dwelling in the holy intent, his equanimous mind silenced the thunder of worldly sounds.
Governing with wisdom, he transformed the traces of arrogance and attained the harmonious Buddha-way.
Establishing wisdom in the state of non-conception, one reaches the hall of nurturing and protection.
Abiding in profound tranquility and valor, one dispels the doubts of sentient beings;
through the sequential dharma of reflection and wisdom, this is the perfection of excellent retribution.
Entering the level path below, the wise division awakens to universal wisdom;
having transcended fragmented knowledge, they find delight in their own supernormal powers.
Radiant illumination liberates them from worldly toil, serving as a pleasure grove for all sentient beings.
In the palace of pure conduct, he manifests various wondrous deeds;
showing the multitude that there is nothing to be purified, his mind remains unshaken.
Thoroughly fathoming the clarity of the nature of the will, he is skilled in preaching the Perfection of Eloquence.
Within the vision of the pure and adorned path, he radiates the brilliance of awakened wisdom;
peerless and without timidity, his mind is like Mount Sumeru.
His virtuous conduct reaches the ultimate limit, and his wisdom is as inexhaustible as the ocean.
If one is like a diamond treasury, firmly abiding in the armor of great virtue;
if what is established is exceedingly vast and well-understood such that it cannot be destroyed;
and if one is destined for the path of enlightenment by virtue of dwelling in a vast mind—then one shall receive the prediction of future Buddhahood.
Attaining the Buddha’s inexhaustible treasury, awakening to the realization of all-knowledge,
constantly guarding sovereign wisdom, and clearly understanding the manifestation of transformations;
regarding sentient beings, lands, and the dharma-realm, they abide in wisdom to manifest skillful means.
The body vows to establish its wandering;
wisdom’s transformations are likewise, manifesting billions of immeasurable forms.
Displaying the power of supernormal flight, one thoroughly masters the power of joyful play.
Having attained the realm of awakening, they are fearless and courageous in transforming those sentient beings who are difficult to convert; their wisdom is adorned yet remains beyond words.
All are children of the Buddha, and their bodies are utterly pure.
The substance and activity are exceedingly vast and long; the words spoken by the mouth are also pure.
Delighting in the establishment of wisdom until its fulfillment, the Most Victorious One performs the ten karmas.
With every thought he gives rise to that mind, manifesting it everywhere as supreme.
With a concentrated mind, he disciplines the faculties; superior to all origins, he dwells steadfastly.
Pure and free from flattery, his nature and conduct are ever upright. Thus he attains entry into liberation, manifesting various transformations.
Abandoning one's dwelling place, One maintains the highest grade of karma,
Accomplishing what is virtuous, And attaining the understanding of all-knowledge.
Without forsaking the state of tranquility, One dwells in supreme serenity.
Born to manifest meritorious deeds, he skillfully studies the Great Way.
Seeking the mind within immeasurable karma, he practices with non-attachment.
He manifests the profound depths of the various streams of the Path, firmly establishing himself to enter among sentient beings.
His conduct serves as his hands; his abdomen is the supreme strength of wisdom.
His mind is like a diamond, armored with compassion and the purity of the noble ones.
With wisdom as his head, he contemplates all phenomena; through his knowledge of the path, he possesses vast learning.
The fragrance of precepts is pure; in movement and stillness, it is supreme.
When body, mind, and speech are at ease, wisdom of the mind is most excellent.
Proceeding toward the path of the Buddha, one sits upon the lion throne.
The traces of the Brahma-conduct lie in sleep; the supreme emptiness is unconditioned action.
Clarity leads to the realm of peace; such is the illumination of its light.
Observing and knowing sentient beings, one perceives their various activities and postures.
Through giving, one leaves behind stinginess and greed;
by not disparaging the precepts, one practices patience and abandons anger. Diligence is supreme;
through meditative concentration and wisdom, one attains mastery. With a heart of loving-kindness, one regards all sentient beings as equal.
Compassionately pitying all without weariness, he purifies himself and exhausts all afflictions;
his meaning is tranquil as he accords with the Dharma, bestowing blessings upon sentient beings.
His noble wisdom is as sharp as a rhinoceros horn, and his clear intelligence shines forth far and wide.
Insatiable in broad learning, fearless and uprooting delusive thoughts,
he restrains himself and establishes himself in practice; having escaped the paths of Māra,
he honors with his head bowed the Buddha’s wisdom-work which he cultivates, his will and nature being thus dedicated.
Cast aside arrogance and pride, always adhering to the Way and its righteousness;
exhort yourself when beset by Māra, following the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
Let your great intent follow the teachings of the Dharma, and by synthesizing these meanings, reach the Unsurpassed.
Deeds performed follow one later; this is the infinite excellence of the Adornment of Progression.
His birth manifests as noble and honored; at his first birth he takes seven steps.
He universally displays all arts and skills, yet demonstrates dwelling within the inner palace.
Renouncing the home with no lingering attachments, he cultivated the Way to reach the fundamental source;
drawing near to the radiance of emptiness, he practiced the vast karma of utmost sincerity.
Having subdued Māra and attained the supreme path, he left behind the traces of turning the Wheel of Dharma.
He manifests as dwelling on the stages of the Buddha-way; the Great Teacher is without peer.
This practice has no limit or bottom; its manifestations may be coarse or vast and far-reaching.
Having accumulated these practices for billions of kalpas, he takes this as his delight.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings, Diligently cultivating and abiding in the virtues of a Buddha,
Understand that in the Dharma there is no person, Nor attachment to any conditioned phenomena;
This practice accords with the meaning of wisdom, And they delight themselves in supernormal powers.
Billions of lands throughout thousands of worlds, for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas,
he carries them all upon the palm of his hand and travels about; yet these billions of lands do not weary him,
and he can return to their original places at will, without causing distress or affliction to any sentient being.
The adornments and purity of all Buddha-fields, though appearing as if they were limited,
are caused to enter a single pore of every class of sentient being;
likewise, the four great oceans are made to reside within a single pore.
Neither increasing nor decreasing, they benefit all beings without causing distress.
Grasping the Great Iron Ring Mountains with their palms, they treat billions upon billions as if they were a single speck of dust;
shifting the earth of billions of Ganges sands, they restore it once more to its original place.
Taking the kingdom along with its lands, even where there may be destruction, one subdues them through a mindless state; that which enters therein is inexhaustible.
Even if a hundred thousand suns and all the moons were to shine upon the multitudes, [the light of this wisdom would not be surpassed].
With the great blazing light of a bright pearl, And all the devas and asuras,
He radiates light from a single pore, Its brilliance surpassing that of a billion worlds;
Having expounded the unsurpassed Dharma, All evil destinies in the world are extinguished.
Through various kinds of speech and sounds, and all the words of sentient beings without exception,
once the teaching of a single voice has been proclaimed, it completely pervades all instructions.
Hearing this gentle sound, billions of beings rejoice.
The sounds of the Dharma preached by the Buddha, all listen to them together.
Calculating the kalpas of the past, they behold the events of the future;
whether regarding the future or the present, they reveal the deeds of the past.
He manifests the boundaries of all Buddha-fields, Which are perilously ruined and yet restored;
By means of billions of sentient beings, They are all fully contained within a single hair-pore.
Through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, They are established so as to attain transcendence.
All are the true manifestation of one's own body, appearing through transformation by means of spiritual resonance.
The wise abide in non-arrogance, clearly understanding the minds of sentient beings;
they manifest according to their forms, remaining free from defilement and without craving for themselves.
The bodies, speech, and mental inclinations of all people—
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, the various devas and worldlings,
as well as those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles— all emerge from the Buddha’s body.
Manifesting the practice of the Buddha-way, reaching all-encompassing wisdom, they enter entirely into the realm of thought; within purity, there is no defilement.
Establishing universal wisdom, they constantly manifest the land of the Buddha-way.
Mindfulness, discernment, and reflection—these comprise the sovereign wisdom of the world.
Following its fundamental path of practice, the land becomes that which is cultivated in the present;
such is the nature of its resonance, as vast and excellent as it manifests.
Beyond the reach of worldly understanding, he manifests such teachings as these;
yet that which is manifested is nothing manifested, for who could ever surpass it?
According to the dispositions and conduct of sentient beings, he reveals the activity of ultimate truth.
His body is equal to space, and his name is renowned throughout the three periods of time.
Clothed in the self-perfumed fragrance of precepts, adorned with the majesty of tranquility,
draped in the stainless silks of the Dharma, he possesses the wish-fulfilling jewel of universal wisdom.
Having fully mastered clear wisdom, his meritorious deeds abide in universal knowledge;
having attained the wheel of the infinite transcendence, he constantly bestows the most supreme spiritual powers.
His divine feet of wisdom are unimpeded, reaching the supreme bright jewel of ultimate knowledge.
Her conduct is pure and wondrous, a woman of sublime excellence who gathers others through the four means of attraction.
She guides with skillful means; her virtue is the root of the Dharma-wheel, and she dwells as a venerable one in the concentration of emptiness.
With the bow of wisdom and the mind as the handle, the clarity of the faculties serves as arrows;
establishing himself as a canopy for the world, he raises the banner of noble insight.
Having subdued the hosts of Māra, he humbles them through the power of patience.
The earth-element is the dhāraṇī that encompasses all; The practice of wisdom is the tree of profound knowledge.
The flowers of the factors of enlightenment and samādhi, Adorned by the play of the supernormal powers, Emptiness is the bathing pool, And the gates of liberation are the essential pure wife.
They partake of the nectar-food of the Dharma and delight in play through the Three Vehicles.
This conduct is most supreme; nothing more wondrous exists than this.
For billions of koṭis of hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they have never once given rise to weariness or indolence.
Reverently honoring the holy pure land, he enlightens the multitude with the joy of non-abiding;
establishing wisdom and all wondrous delights, he is endowed with omniscience.
With valor he surveys all lands, as the celestial rain washes away all impurities.
All wonders may yet be exhausted, and even empty space may be traversed;
Yet in a single moment, one can understand the mental thoughts of all beings.
I praise these sons of the Buddhas, whose virtues remain inexhaustible for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Desiring to bring about pure merit and virtue, with wisdom beyond surpassing,
one delivers others from all suffering and affliction, establishing them in eternal peace.
Reaching the inexhaustible state of equanimity, one dwells securely in body, speech, and mind.
"One should make one's mind firm, performing deeds like a vajra.

When the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra spoke these words, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; a great radiance shone universally throughout the ten directions, and lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.

Among the devas and humans, there were none who did not rejoice; the śrāvaka disciples all came to take refuge in him; the bodhisattvas all praised his sincerity; and the entire assembly was filled with joy, as they all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
The Bodhisattva Puzhi again addressed the Buddha,
saying, "Does the Way result from speech or from silence?
The Buddha said:
"It is both through words of existence and words of non-existence. [Beings] fall into the perils of birth and death within the five destinies;

they are bound by the fetters of the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six decays (*āyatana*), and what is perceived; they are agitated and restless by the twelve links of dependent origination and the sixty-two views; or they remain in the twelve seas, unable to cross to the other shore. Because of these various activities and hundreds of thousands of kinds of maladies, the Buddha established the teaching and bestowed the medicine of the Dharma—the categories of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; the four immeasurables, the four debts of gratitude, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the six perfections (*pāramitā*), the twelve divisions of scripture, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the four truths, the three doors of liberation, and the Three Jewels—using these to treat and cure all such defiled ailments."

Medicine is administered for the sake of illness; where there is no illness, there is no medicine. The three poisons and various defilements constitute grave illnesses, while the attainment of ultimate, true wisdom is called being free from illness.

Because those bound by causes and conditions fail to understand the Way, the Buddha provides extensive explanations through parables, speaking of masses of foam, water bubbles, plantain trees, mirages, shadows, echoes, illusions, dreams, the moon, and the fleeting—thereby elucidating their meaning.
All these matters are empty and arise from delusion.

By not craving the mundane world and practicing the medicinal dharma of the Way—the various practices of the six perfections, the four immeasurables, and the four debts of gratitude—one attains the Way by carrying out these deeds.

One understands that all verbal teachings are fundamentally wordless; for there may be buddha-fields where the five aggregates, the six sense-decays, the three poisons, and the bonds of causes and conditions do not exist, and thus no written explanations are found.

Without body and without speech, empty, still, and silent, one realizes the non-existence of the three realms; not abiding in the conditioned, not dwelling in the unconditioned, and not dwelling in between—this is called "attaining through wordlessness."
Samantaprajña asked again:

“Now this assembly has gathered here; some have profound understanding and their faculties are clear and penetrating, some are of middling capacity who may advance or retreat, and some are of inferior rank who do not know where they are headed.”
Those who have attained realization have no doubts, but those of middling and inferior capacity all harbor hesitation. Why is this?
Having heard that when I previously asked two hundred questions, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva answered with two thousand, each thinks to themselves:
"The phenomena are so manifold that I do not know which things should be honored and which should be relinquished.
I pray that the Buddha will analyze and explain their meaning.
For what reason are there two hundred matters to which two thousand answers are given?"
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent! How delightful is what you have asked!
It resolves the doubts of those to come and ensures that all students do not harbor misconceptions regarding the scriptures.”
The Buddha said, "Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall explain for you the direction in which this meaning leads. He replied:
“I shall receive the instruction. The Buddha said:
“Because there are two [aspects] involved, I have asked two hundred questions.”
What are these two?
There is a spirit that craves the body and calculates the existence of a self; there is the internal and the external, existence and non-existence—therefore, two hundred questions are asked.
He asked again: "Since it is because of this calculation that there is birth and death,
for what reason do you repeatedly ask about these two hundred matters?"
The World-Honored One replied:

"Regarding those two hundred matters you have inquired about, they all involve the removal of self, internal and external, and existence and non-existence. Thus, through skillful means and wisdom, one transforms beings boundlessly; by not apprehending internal or external, one attains the ultimate Way and transforms all."
Samantajñāna again asked Samantabhadra Bodhisattva:
"For what reason do you answer by repeating these two thousand matters?
The World-Honored One said:
"All those from the ten directions have gathered here; their minds differ and their mental activities vary.
Those who have attained realization understand the ultimate Way upon hearing the essentials.

For those who cannot yet attain such realization, one must employ extensive discourse, elucidating through literary explanations and drawing out the underlying meaning; by using the forms perceived by the eyes as metaphors for their intent, they may finally attain liberating wisdom."
It is like a garment with many stains: it must be washed with strong lye several times before it becomes clean; only then can it be dyed so that its color is bright.
It is also like a person who wishes to build a house, yet the ground is uneven and not level, and is filled with latrines, snakes, vipers, and venomous insects.
One levels the high and low, removes impurities, banishes snakes and vipers, builds walls and foundations, and only then erects a dwelling.

In this same way, the Bodhisattva eliminates the five aggregates (*skandhas*), the six sense-fields (*āyatanas*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the various hindrances of the self; practicing great compassion and skillful wisdom, he becomes a shelter for all dharmas, a protector of the world, and a refuge for the world.
Prajñāpāramitā asked again:
"What is meant by the 'Dharma-abode'?
The World-Honored One replied:

"To transform and guide all beings so that they enter the wisdom of emptiness, being without increase or craving, with a mind free from delusive thoughts, and thus liberating sentient beings—this is the Dharma-abode."
Prajñāpāramitā again asked:
"What is meant by 'platform'?
The World-Honored One replied:
"By means of the six supernormal powers, they perceive and behold the mental activities of the ten directions; they hear clearly all that has form and also observe that which is formless.
Their bodies pervade the ten directions without coming or going; through the mind of the Way, they behold that the source and root of all things are fundamentally without location."

Having seen the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), one does not abide in existence or non-existence, does not dwell in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and does not rest in extinction (*nirvāṇa*); opening the mind so that all reach the Great Way—this is called the Terrace.
"What is meant by 'protection'?
The World-Honored One replied:
"To transform beings according to the time, entering the five destinies to purify the five eyes."

What are the five? The first is called the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*); abiding in the world, it manifests as a body composed of the four great elements, and by means of this, it transforms and delivers sentient beings.
What is called the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)?
To those in the heavens and those in the world who have not yet realized the ultimate Way, he manifests the three vehicles, each enabling them to find their proper place.
What is meant by the "eye of wisdom"?
It is that which cannot be understood through ordinary knowledge; he brings all such beings to transformation and enlightenment, causing them to enter into great wisdom.
What is called the Dharma-eye?

It is that which, though operating within narrow confines, cannot fail to expand and transform all beings; it understands that the Dharma-body is entirely devoid of past, future, or present, being equal throughout the three periods of time.
What is called the Buddha-eye?
Those who are deluded do not recognize the true and real; they are shrouded by the five hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), as if in deep sleep.

To them, he demonstrates the four immeasurables (*brahmavihāra*), the four acts of kindness (*catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*), and the practices of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom. Through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), he transforms beings according to the time, advancing or retreating as appropriate without missing any opportunity, so that each finds their proper place and all resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed, true, and real path to enlightenment.
Samantaprajña asked again:
"Why is this sutra named 'The Chapter on Delivering the World'?
The Buddha said:
"All sentient beings are confined within the world.
What is meant by 'confined'?
They are shrouded by the five aggregates (*skandha*) and the six sense-fields (*āyatana*), entangled in birth and death, unable to extricate themselves."

By means of the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, one eliminates the five aggregates, casts off the six sense-fields, does not conceive of a self, does not abide in birth and death, and does not dwell in extinction.
Just as the sun and moon radiate their light throughout day and night, so too are expedient means and wisdom: they appear suddenly yet leave no trace.
Their virtue is like empty space, beyond all analogy.
"For this reason, it is titled 'The Chapter on Delivering the World.

When the Buddha had spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva Samantamati, and all those who had gathered—the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, spirits, and asuras—heard what the Buddha taught and were all filled with joy, prostrating themselves before the Buddha.
The Scripture on the Chapter of Delivering the World, Scroll Six.
